title: Do Americans Need a Visa for Vietnam?
content:
Yes. If you hold a US passport, you need a visa to enter Vietnam. There is one narrow exception, and there is a lot of confident misinformation online telling you otherwise — so it is worth being precise about what applies to an American passport and what does not.

The short answer for US passport holders

American travelers need a visa for Vietnam, and almost all of them use the electronic visa. The State Department states the rule without qualification: a visa is required, and you must apply before you travel. The main exception is a stay of 30 days or less on the island of Phu Quoc, which you can do without a visa if you fly in and out of Phu Quoc directly. A second, narrower exception for Vietnamese-Americans is covered below.

The mechanics of applying are covered step by step in our Vietnam e-visa walkthrough. That exception is narrower than it sounds. Fly to Phu Quoc via Ho Chi Minh City and clear immigration on the mainland, and you have entered Vietnam — the exemption no longer covers you.

Why you keep reading that Vietnam is visa-free

Vietnam does run a unilateral visa-exemption scheme, most recently widened to twelve more European countries in August 2025. It covers a list of mostly European and Asian nationalities for stays of up to 45 days. United States, Canadian and Australian passports are not on that list. Articles that say "Vietnam is visa-free for 45 days" are usually accurate for somebody — just not for you.

There is one group of Americans who are treated differently. Overseas Vietnamese holding the relevant Vietnamese documentation can obtain a five-year visa-exemption certificate instead of applying trip by trip. If you have Vietnamese parentage, that route is worth asking about before you pay for an e-visa.

What the e-visa actually gives you

The Vietnamese e-visa is issued online by the Immigration Department and costs $25 for single entry or $50 for multiple entry, payable by bank transfer. Validity runs up to 90 days, and processing usually takes 3 to 5 working days once the department has your completed application and payment.

Treat the processing window as a floor rather than a promise. Vietnam's own embassy in India publishes a far wider range, and the figure stretches during holidays and application surges. Apply weeks ahead, and do not buy non-refundable flights against an assumption that it will land in three days.

Ninety days is a ceiling, not a default

Vietnam usually grants exactly the period you request, so the 90 days is the maximum available rather than what you automatically receive. Ask for less than you need and you cannot top it up later.

There is also a passport rule that almost nothing online mentions. Your e-visa's validity must be at least 30 days shorter than your passport's remaining validity. In practice it never binds a tourist: a 90-day visa needs about four months of validity, and Vietnam already requires six at entry, so meeting the entry rule automatically satisfies this one. It is worth knowing only because the wording alarms people who find it.

Your passport: how much validity you need

Vietnam requires your passport to be valid at entry with six months' validity beyond your arrival date, plus blank pages for stamps. The State Department's own page is internally inconsistent on the page count, saying one blank page per stamp in one section and at least two in another, so treat two as the working minimum.

One more trap worth knowing if things go wrong mid-trip: Vietnam may not accept the 12-page US emergency passport for e-visa entry. If you lose your passport elsewhere in the region and replace it at a US embassy, the replacement may not get you into Vietnam.

The second form nobody tells you about

Separately from the visa, Vietnam operates an online pre-arrival declaration at the Immigration Department's own portal. Filing is free, takes about ten minutes, and is done no earlier than three days before you arrive. The two governments describe its status differently: the State Department says air travelers on a non-Vietnamese passport must complete it, while Vietnam's portal presents it as advice that reduces waiting time at immigration.

We are not going to resolve a disagreement between two governments for you. The practical answer is to file it: it is free, it takes about ten minutes, and on Vietnam's own account it shortens the queue you would otherwise stand in.

Where your e-visa is actually valid

An e-visa works at 83 designated border gates — 17 airports, 27 land crossings and 39 seaports — after Vietnam added 41 of them in December 2025. That covers every international airport in Vietnam, so Noi Bai, Tan Son Nhat, Da Nang, Cam Ranh and Phu Quoc are all eligible. Note that eligibility is a separate question from the port you select on the form, which is dealt with below.

Where it does bite is overland. If you plan to cross into Cambodia or Laos and come back, or enter by road from either, the crossing has to be on the approved list — and plenty are not.

Two ways a valid visa still fails

Your entry and exit points must match what you selected on the application, so a visa naming Hanoi will not get you through Ho Chi Minh City. And you must print the thing: the official instruction is to carry a paper copy with your passport. Both failures happen before you leave home, and both are free to avoid.

What this decision actually sits inside

Notice what happened across all of that. The visa question looks like paperwork, but every answer above quietly locked something else in place: how long you can stay, which airport you fly into, whether you can loop through Cambodia, whether a Phu Quoc beach week is exempt or not. You chose your route when you chose your visa, and most people do it in the opposite order.

That sequencing — what you book first and what it silently forecloses — is worked out end to end in the complete Vietnam decision manual, alongside the rest of the connected decisions a first Vietnam trip turns on.
excerpt: Yes — US passport holders need a visa for Vietnam, and the widely repeated 45-day visa-free rule does not apply to you. Here is what you actually need.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam E-Visa: How to Apply Step by Step
content:
The Vietnamese e-visa is genuinely straightforward to apply for, and the application takes perhaps twenty minutes. A few of its fields are more binding than they look, though, and the mistakes worth knowing about are the ones you cannot correct once you have landed.

Use the official site and nothing else

Vietnam's e-visa is issued by the Immigration Department, and the fee is $25 for single entry or $50 for multiple entry, paid by bank transfer. The department runs it on two official domains, evisa.gov.vn and thithucdientu.gov.vn; evisa.gov.vn is the one to use. Beyond those, you are dealing with an intermediary, and the market around this particular visa is unusually aggressive.

Plenty of those intermediaries are legitimate agents doing real work. The problem is that their markup is rarely presented as a markup — sites styled to look governmental will charge several times the state fee for submitting the same form you could submit yourself. Paying an agent is a choice; paying one without realising you had the option is not.

Whether you need a visa at all, and the one narrow exception for US passports, is covered in our guide to Vietnam visa requirements for Americans.

What you need before you start

Have your passport scan, a passport-style photograph, your travel dates, your intended port of entry and your first night's address ready. The form will not let you save your way around a missing field, and sessions time out.

Choosing your dates and duration

Vietnam usually grants exactly the period you ask for rather than defaulting to the maximum, so the duration field deserves more thought than it looks like it does. Validity runs up to 90 days, but asking for three weeks gets you three weeks even if you later wish you had more.

Build in a buffer at both ends. Arriving a day or two later than planned is fine as long as you are inside the validity window — what you cannot do is arrive before it opens or leave after it closes, and neither is fixable from the airport.

One rule you can safely ignore

Your e-visa's validity has to be at least 30 days shorter than your passport's remaining validity. A 90-day visa therefore needs about four months of validity — and since Vietnam separately requires six months at entry, anyone eligible to enter already clears this. It sits in the official FAQ and it worries people who find it, which is the only reason it is here.

Picking your port of entry

The application asks which border gate you will use, and that answer is binding. Your entry and exit locations must match what you selected, so an e-visa naming Noi Bai in Hanoi will not get you through Tan Son Nhat in Ho Chi Minh City.

Two different rules are at work here and they are easy to confuse. The first is which gates accept an e-visa at all: 83 of them since December 2025, including every international airport in Vietnam, so flying in is never the problem. The second is the one above — your selected port is binding whichever gate you choose. Overland crossings into Cambodia and Laos are where the first rule still bites, because many crossings are not on the list.

Paying and waiting

Processing normally runs 3 to 5 working days from the point the Immigration Department has both your completed application and your payment. Weekends and Vietnamese public holidays are not working days, and Tet shuts the calendar down for a week or more.

Do not treat that window as a guarantee. Vietnam's own embassy in India publishes a substantially longer range, and the honest planning advice is to apply several weeks out. One thing worth knowing: the US Embassy states that it cannot change your e-visa information or speed your application up, so your own consulate is not a shortcut if it stalls.

Check the document before you celebrate

When your e-visa arrives, read every field against your passport, character by character. A mismatch in your name, passport number or date of birth can mean being refused entry on arrival, and the State Department warns you may then have to pay a travel agency at the airport for an expensive visa sponsorship — a remedy that is neither guaranteed nor cheap.

Then print it. The official instruction is to carry a printed copy alongside your passport, and a sheet of paper is a cheap hedge against a flat phone battery in an immigration queue.

The separate form you also need

Vietnam runs an online pre-arrival declaration independently of the visa, filed at the Immigration Department's portal no earlier than three days before you arrive. It is free and takes about ten minutes. The State Department describes it as required for air arrivals on a non-Vietnamese passport; Vietnam's own portal frames it as advisory. Do it regardless.

What you cannot do later

An e-visa cannot be renewed or extended from inside Vietnam. The Immigration Department allows in-person extensions for other visa categories, but the electronic visa is not one of them, which makes the duration you choose at application the final word.

Anyone selling you an e-visa extension is therefore selling a service the government says does not exist. If you genuinely need longer, the answer is a different visa type arranged before you travel, not a fix applied once you are there. That is worth knowing before you choose a duration, because it is one of the places where the order you plan things in matters — something the complete Vietnam decision manual works through in full.
excerpt: The official Vietnamese e-visa costs $25, takes 3 to 5 working days, and has four ways to fail at the border. Here is the whole process.
author: Editorial

title: Is Vietnam Safe for Americans?
content:
Vietnam is a safe country to travel in, and the US government says so in the plainest terms it has. The more useful question is not whether it is safe but which risks are real — because the thing most American visitors worry about is not the thing that actually sends them home early.

What the official advisory says

The State Department places Vietnam at Level 1 — Exercise Normal Precautions, the lowest of its four levels. That is a lower advisory than the Department currently assigns to France or Germany, both of which sit at Level 2. For an American audience whose mental picture of Vietnam was shaped by a war that ended fifty years ago, that single data point is worth sitting with.

Level 1 is not a promise that nothing goes wrong. It means the baseline caution you would use in any unfamiliar city is the appropriate level of caution here. The advisory itself is short and worth two minutes of your time before you fly.

How Americans are actually received

Warmly, and more warmly than most first-time visitors expect. The median Vietnamese citizen was born long after 1975, Vietnam and the United States are significant trading partners, and American visitors are commonplace. In Vietnam it is called the American War, museums present it from the Vietnamese side without much softening, and that is a national account of a national trauma rather than a comment on you standing in the room.

The crime risk: petty, persistent, avoidable

Petty theft is the dominant crime risk, and the State Department is direct about it: Vietnam is generally safe for travelers, but petty crime is common, especially in popular tourist locations. Violent crime against foreigners is rare. What is not rare is losing a phone.

The signature method is a snatch from a moving motorbike — your phone leaves your hand while you are standing on a sidewalk reading a map, and the bike is gone before you have registered what happened. Ho Chi Minh City is where this is most common. The defense is unglamorous and effective: do not walk and scroll, keep your phone in your hand only when you have stopped and have your back to a wall, and wear bags on the traffic-away side.

Scams are price-ambiguity, not theft

Nearly every common Vietnamese tourist scam is the same trick wearing different clothes: a service begins before a price is named, then the price arrives. Taxi meters that run fast, cyclo rides quoted per person rather than per trip, an unsolicited shoe repair in Hanoi's Old Quarter, a motorbike rental with pre-existing scratches charged at return. One habit prevents most of them — agree the number, in dong, before anything starts. Grab and Xanh SM remove the taxi version entirely by fixing the fare in the app. The exception is the motorbike-rental damage claim, where the price was never the issue: that one needs photographs of the bike before you ride off.

The risk nobody writes about

Road traffic is what actually injures visitors to Vietnam, not crime, and the gap between those two risks is not close. The country's roads are crowded and chaotic, most people are on motorbikes, and a tourist on a rented scooter with no local riding experience is the highest-exposure person on the road.

Two things compound it. US driver's licences and International Driving Permits are both invalid in Vietnam, and riding without a Vietnamese licence can void the travel insurance that would otherwise pay your medical bills. We have written up what that means in practice in our guide to renting a motorbike in Vietnam, and it is the single most consequential safety decision on a Vietnam trip.

Crossing the street is a skill

Walk at a slow, constant, predictable pace rather than darting, and keep watching the traffic as you go. Riders read your trajectory and steer around it, so sudden changes are what cause collisions — the rider has to re-solve the problem mid-manoeuvre. Predictability is the technique, not a guarantee: cars and buses do not swerve the way scooters do, so wait those out, and crossing alongside a local is the easiest way to learn the rhythm.

Legal risks worth taking seriously

Drug offences carry severe penalties, and the mechanics are worth understanding if you are coming from a state where cannabis is legal. Police sometimes test blood for drugs, and substances used legally in another country can still lead to arrest in Vietnam if they are detectable in your system on arrival. Ingredients in some ordinary prescription medicines, including common ADHD treatments, may also be illegal — a reason to travel with documentation for anything you are carrying.

What makes this weigh more than it otherwise would is the aftermath. Consular access to detained Americans is routinely delayed, often by several weeks, so the embassy may not reach you quickly. Overstaying your visa compounds similarly: fines, then delays obtaining permission to leave.

Unexploded ordnance, in proportion

Wartime ordnance remains in the ground in parts of Vietnam, and the risk is real but narrow. The greatest exposure is at construction sites, and landmine risk is low in urban and populated areas, including tourist destinations. On a DMZ tour or a rural trek, stay on marked paths and do not pick up metal objects. In Hanoi, this is not something to think about.

Health, air and emergencies

Tap water is not drinkable anywhere in Vietnam and bottled water is cheap and universal; ice is a judgement call we work through in the health guide. Air pollution is a genuine consideration — the State Department flags it as a significant problem in major cities, Hanoi above all, and advises travelers with respiratory conditions to speak to a doctor first. Vaccination questions are covered in our Vietnam health and vaccines guide.

Emergency numbers: 113 for traffic police, 115 for an ambulance. Be aware that these are frequently answered only in Vietnamese, and for a serious medical event in Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City you are usually better off going directly to an international hospital than waiting for dispatch.

Taken together, the pattern is that Vietnam's real risks are ordinary ones handled badly rather than exotic ones. The largest of them — how you move around the country — is partly settled weeks before you arrive, when you choose between riding, hiring a driver and flying the long legs. the complete Vietnam decision manual works that set of choices through in sequence.
excerpt: Vietnam sits at the State Department's lowest advisory level. The risk Americans worry about and the risk that actually hurts them are not the same thing.
author: Editorial

title: Renting a Motorbike in Vietnam: What to Know
content:
Renting a motorbike is the classic Vietnam experience, and for a lot of travelers it is the whole point of the trip. It is also the one decision on a Vietnam itinerary where the gap between what is easy and what is legal is wide enough to end badly. Here is the honest version.

The legal position, stated plainly

US driver's licences and International Driving Permits do not work in Vietnam. The State Department puts it without hedging: driving without a Vietnamese licence can mean a fine, arrest, or jail, and renting a moped or motorbike without one is illegal. That is the US government describing the law to its own citizens, not a cautious lawyer's reading.

You will not feel any of this at the rental shop. Shops routinely hand over a bike against a passport photocopy and a cash deposit, ask nothing, and check nothing. The absence of a check is not permission — it only means the consequences arrive later, if they arrive at all.

Why the IDP you bought does not help

Americans often arrive holding an International Driving Permit from AAA, reasonably assuming it is the universal solution. Vietnam does not recognise it. The permit the United States issues is not the standard Vietnam accepts, and the State Department simply lists both your licence and your IDP as not working. Buying one before you fly is money spent on a document that changes nothing here.

What this does to your insurance

Travel medical insurance is where the legal question turns into a financial one, and it is the reason this article exists. If you are in an accident while riding without a valid licence, the State Department warns that your travel insurance may not pay your medical bills.

Sit with what that means. Road safety is the hazard the State Department warns about at greatest length in Vietnam, and a bad motorbike accident can mean a medical evacuation costing well into six figures. Riding without a licence means finding out whether your policy pays at the worst possible moment — the State Department's wording is that it may not, which is a risk you are accepting rather than a certainty you are buying.

Can you get a Vietnamese licence as a visitor?

Realistically, no. Converting a foreign licence requires residency documentation — a temporary residence card issued by the Immigration Department — which a tourist on an e-visa does not hold and cannot obtain for a two-week trip. The lawful route exists for people who live in Vietnam, not for people visiting it.

Traffic law, and how much it is enforced

Vietnamese law requires helmets, speed-limit compliance and zero alcohol while driving — zero, not a blood-alcohol threshold like the 0.08 you are used to. One beer with dinner puts you over the limit. You must also carry your licence, the vehicle registration and identification while riding.

Enforcement is tightening rather than relaxing. The government is deploying cameras and raising fines in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, and traffic police increasingly have speed detectors and some English. The State Department also notes that informal payments are sometimes solicited for minor violations, and advises insisting on an official receipt.

If you ride anyway

Plenty of travelers make this choice with their eyes open, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. If you are going to, reduce the things that are actually within your control.

Photograph the entire bike with the renter present before you ride off, including every existing scratch, or expect to be charged for them at return. Never surrender your actual passport as a deposit — offer a photocopy and cash. Wear a real helmet rather than the plastic shell supplied, which is not designed to survive an impact. Ride outside the cities before you ride inside them, and do not start in Ho Chi Minh City traffic on day one.

The alternatives that are not a compromise

Riding pillion with an experienced local — the easy-rider model — is how a large share of the Ha Giang loop is actually done, and it removes the licence problem entirely while improving the experience: you get a guide, and you get to look at the scenery instead of the road. A car with a driver costs roughly what bare car rental costs in the US and covers the long legs comfortably. Grab's motorbike taxis handle short city hops for a couple of dollars.

What you are really deciding

Look at what just happened across all of that. This reads like a question about renting a vehicle, but every answer above was actually about something else — which parts of Vietnam you can reach, whether Ha Giang and the mountain passes are on your itinerary at all, how your long north-to-south legs get covered, and what your insurance is worth on the day you need it. The bike was never the decision. The shape of the trip was.

Travelers who sort transport first and route second tend to end up with an itinerary built around a vehicle instead of a vehicle chosen for the itinerary. Which way those choices should run, and what each one forecloses, is worked out in order in the complete Vietnam decision manual. If you are still weighing the broader risk picture, our honest assessment of safety in Vietnam covers the rest.
excerpt: Rental shops will hand you a bike without checking anything. That does not make it legal, and your travel insurance may not cover what follows.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Health and Vaccines for Travelers
content:
Vietnam asks nothing of you medically at the border, which is a different statement from saying you need nothing. The distinction between what is required to enter and what a doctor would recommend is the whole of this subject, and conflating the two is how travelers end up either under-prepared or paying for medication they will never need.

Required versus recommended

No vaccinations are required to enter Vietnam. The State Department states it in exactly those words, and no proof of vaccination is needed at the border for a standard tourist arrival from the United States.

That is an immigration fact, not medical advice, and it is where most articles stop. The CDC maintains a separate and longer list of vaccines it recommends for Vietnam — recommendations that carry no border consequence whatsoever but exist because the diseases do. Nobody will stop you boarding without them.

What the CDC actually recommends

For Vietnam the CDC recommends Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, and typhoid for most travelers, alongside keeping routine vaccinations current. Hepatitis A and typhoid are both food-and-water transmitted, which is the relevant route in a country where the best eating is done at street stalls. Hepatitis B is recommended for unvaccinated travelers of all ages.

Several others are conditional rather than universal, and the distinction saves money. Japanese encephalitis is aimed mainly at people moving to affected rural areas or spending long periods there, though CDC also says to consider it for shorter trips with significant rural or outdoor exposure, or accommodation without good mosquito protection. Rabies is weighed on animal contact and remoteness. The CDC's Vietnam page lists the full set with its reasoning.

Malaria: probably not your problem

Most visitors to Vietnam do not need antimalarial medication, which contradicts the blanket advice people are given about Southeast Asia. The CDC is specific: transmission is rural only, with rare cases in the Mekong and Red River deltas, and there is no transmission in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang, Hai Phong, Nha Trang or Quy Nhon.

Read that list against a normal itinerary. Hanoi, Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City are named on it outright, and the rest of a standard first trip — Ha Long Bay, Hoi An — is coastal and urban rather than the rural forest where transmission sits. For most city-and-coast itineraries that makes prophylaxis a question to raise with a travel clinic rather than an automatic purchase.

When it does apply

Rural and forested areas are a different matter, and the far north is rural. Sapa, Ha Giang and extended time in the central highlands are not covered by the city exemption above, and if your trip is built around trekking rather than cities the calculation changes. Chloroquine and mefloquine resistance is present in a named set of provinces — Binh Phuoc, Dak Lak, Dak Nong, Gia Lai, Khanh Hoa, Kon Tum, Lam Dong, Ninh Thuan and Tay Ninh — where the CDC points to atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline or tafenoquine instead. Elsewhere its options are wider. Which applies depends on exactly where you are going, which is a conversation for a travel clinic with your actual route in front of them.

The mosquito risk with no vaccine

Dengue is the mosquito-borne illness most likely to affect a visitor to Vietnam, and unlike malaria it is urban, seasonal and not preventable by medication. Cases rise during and after the rainy season, and the Aedes mosquitoes that carry it bite during the day rather than at dusk.

Bite avoidance is therefore the whole strategy, and it is the same strategy everywhere: repellent with DEET or picaridin applied to exposed skin, long sleeves in the evening, and air conditioning or a screened room. This matters more in the south and during the May-to-November wet months.

Food, water and the stomach question

Tap water is not drinkable anywhere in Vietnam, including the major cities. Bottled water is cheap and sold everywhere, and most hotels and many cafes will refill a bottle. Brush your teeth with bottled water if you are being careful, though many travelers do not and are fine.

Ice is the judgement call. The CDC's advice is to avoid ice, on the basis that it may be made from untreated water. In practice most cafes and restaurants in Vietnamese cities use commercially produced ice — the cylindrical kind with a hole through the middle — and iced coffee is close to unavoidable if you want to drink what the country drinks. The honest position is that the industrial product is widely used and widely consumed without incident, that neither its shape nor its popularity proves how it was handled, and that the cautious choice remains the CDC's. Be stricter in rural areas and anywhere the ice is loose chipped rather than uniform.

How to choose a street stall

Turnover is the most useful signal available to you. A stall with a queue of locals is selling food that has not been sitting around, which removes one of the commonest problems — though it says nothing about water, storage temperature or cross-contamination, so treat it as evidence rather than proof. Beyond that: prefer food cooked to order in front of you, and be more cautious with pre-cut fruit and anything lukewarm that ought to be hot.

Medical care and what to bring

International-standard hospitals exist in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang, and they expect payment up front — frequently by card before treatment begins, with reimbursement your problem afterwards. Outside those cities, facilities drop off sharply, which is the practical reason travel insurance with medical evacuation cover matters on a Vietnam trip.

Bring any prescription medication in its original labelled packaging with a copy of the prescription. Some ingredients in common prescription drugs, including certain ADHD treatments, may be illegal in Vietnam, so check anything you depend on before you fly rather than at customs. A basic kit of rehydration salts, loperamide and plasters covers the overwhelming majority of what actually goes wrong.
excerpt: No vaccines are required to enter Vietnam, several are recommended, and most travelers do not need the antimalarials they are told to buy.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Money and Costs for Americans
content:
Vietnam is one of the cheapest countries an American can fly to, and the gap between travelling carefully and travelling comfortably is unusually small. What catches people out is not the price level. It is the shape of the money: a currency with three extra zeros, two banknotes that look alike, and a card network that stops working earlier than you expect.

The currency, and the mistake everyone makes

Vietnam uses the dong, and it trades in the tens of thousands to the dollar, so every price carries three more zeros than your instincts expect. A bowl of pho priced at 50,000 looks alarming for about two days and then stops registering. Check the current rate before you go rather than memorising one, because it moves.

The expensive mistake is not arithmetic, it is colour. The 500,000 dong note and the 20,000 dong note are both blue-ish polymer, and they are separated by a factor of twenty-five. Learn those two notes specifically before you land. Handing over a 500,000 believing it is a 20,000 is an easy mistake to make in dim light at the end of a long day, and an expensive one.

What things actually cost

Rough daily budgets, excluding international flights. These are planning brackets rather than quoted prices, and they move with the region and the season: around $30 to $45 a day travelling cheaply on street food, dorms or basic guesthouses and buses; roughly $60 to $100 for a private room in a good mid-range hotel, restaurant meals and the occasional internal flight; and $150 and up for upper-tier hotels, private drivers and guided days.

Individual prices sit where you would expect from that: a bowl of pho or a banh mi for a couple of dollars, a local beer for about one, a mid-range hotel room for a fraction of the US equivalent. Intercity transport is cheap in absolute terms, though the gap between a sleeper bus and a flight is real money on a tight budget and worth comparing rather than waving away.

Where cards work, and where they stop

Cards work in hotels, chain supermarkets, malls and mid-to-upper restaurants in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang and Hoi An. Beyond that, Vietnam runs on cash: street food, markets, most independent cafes, motorbike-taxi fares paid in person, locally bought train and bus tickets, and very nearly everything outside the big cities.

The part Americans are least prepared for is QR payment. You will watch everyone around you pay by phone, because VietQR is near-universal among Vietnamese — and it is tied to a domestic bank account, so it is effectively unavailable to a visitor. Apple Pay is not the equivalent. Plan to carry more physical cash than you would anywhere in Europe.

Getting cash without paying twice for it

Vietnamese ATMs charge a flat fee per withdrawal rather than a percentage, and they cap how much you can take out at once. Those two facts together decide what cash actually costs you, and the rule that follows is simple: withdraw the maximum your bank and the machine allow, as rarely as you can stand.

The arithmetic is worth seeing once. A fixed fee on a small withdrawal can run several percent of the amount; the same fee on a large withdrawal is a fraction of one percent. Five small withdrawals cost five fees. Your US bank's own foreign-transaction charge stacks on top of whatever the Vietnamese machine takes, so check what your own card charges abroad before you travel — that half is within your control and is often the larger one.

Practical habits that save real money

Decline the machine's offer to bill you in dollars. Dynamic currency conversion looks like a courtesy and is a worse exchange rate every time; always choose to be charged in dong. Beyond that: tell your bank you are travelling, carry a second card in a different pocket, and keep a small reserve of clean US dollars for emergencies rather than for spending.

One habit that is not about money at all: tipping. It is not customary in Vietnam and leaving nothing is normal, which surprises most Americans — our practical guide to tipping in Vietnam covers the few situations where it genuinely is expected.

Changing money, and what not to do

Gold and jewellery shops are the traditional place Vietnamese people change money and often give better rates than banks, which is legal and ordinary. Airport exchange counters are the worst rate you will see all trip, so change only what you need to reach your hotel. Never change money with someone who approaches you on the street.

Count what you are handed before you walk away, every time. This is not about dishonesty so much as the zeros: in a stack of similar-looking notes, a miscount is easy in both directions.

What your money decisions are really deciding

Look at what runs underneath all of this. Cash is needed everywhere in Vietnam, including in the middle of Hanoi, but the further you get from the big cities the fewer alternatives there are when you run out — so how much you carry and where you can withdraw quietly set how far off the main corridor you can comfortably travel. How you pay also shapes which transport you can book on the spot versus in advance.

In other words, your money setup quietly draws the boundary of your itinerary, and most people decide it last — after the flights, after the route, after the bookings that assumed they could pay. Which decisions depend on which, and the order that keeps them from colliding, is worked out in the complete Vietnam decision manual.
excerpt: Vietnam is cheap, but the dong has three extra zeros and cards stop working sooner than you expect. Here is how the money actually behaves.
author: Editorial

title: Tipping in Vietnam: A Practical Guide
content:
Tipping is not customary in Vietnam, and walking out of a restaurant having left nothing is a completely normal thing to do. For American travellers that takes some unlearning, because the reflex runs deep and the anxiety about getting it wrong is usually larger than the stakes.

The default: no tip, no offence

Vietnam has no tipping culture in the American sense. Service staff are not paid a sub-minimum wage topped up by gratuities, the price on the menu is the price, and nobody is calculating a percentage as you leave. At a street stall, a local pho shop, a bahn mi cart or a neighbourhood cafe, you pay what you owe and you go.

That is the baseline to start from, because the common American failure mode here is not stinginess. It is over-tipping from nervousness, which is a small problem rather than a large one but adds up across three weeks and quietly distorts prices in heavily touristed places.

Why the advice online disagrees with itself

Tourism has imported the habit into tourist-facing businesses, so you will find confident articles saying tipping is expected and equally confident ones saying it is not. Both describe something real. The honest version is that tipping is absent from ordinary Vietnamese life and present at the tourist interface, and knowing which one you are standing in is the whole skill.

Where it genuinely is expected

A short list covers nearly everything. Private guides and drivers hired for a day or longer, spa and massage therapists, hotel porters who carry bags, and cruise crews on Ha Long Bay overnight boats, where the convention is a pooled envelope collected at the end rather than individual tips. In those situations a tip is anticipated and its absence is noticed.

Amounts are modest. As customary gestures rather than fixed rates, and indicative as of October 2026: 20,000 to 50,000 dong for a porter or a spa therapist; 100,000 to 200,000 dong per day for a private guide or driver, more if they have gone well beyond the job; and in a Western-facing restaurant with no service charge, rounding up or around ten percent. A pooled cruise envelope is usually a few dollars per passenger per day.

The useful rule underneath those numbers is proportionality: a tip in Vietnam is a gesture, not a percentage, and it should feel small relative to what the service cost.

Restaurants and the service charge

Mid-range and upper restaurants, especially in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, increasingly add a service charge to the bill, often alongside VAT. When that line is there, the tipping question is already settled and anything further is optional. Read the bottom of the bill before reaching for extra.

In Western-facing restaurants and bars without a service charge, rounding up or leaving small change is common and welcome. Nobody will chase you down the street if you do not.

Hotels

At a budget guesthouse nobody expects anything. At a mid-range or upper hotel, porters who carry bags to your room are tipped a small note, and housekeeping is sometimes left something at the end of a multi-night stay rather than daily. Neither is obligatory, and a Vietnamese guest would often leave nothing.

Taxis, Grab and the rounding habit

Taxi drivers do not expect tips, and rounding up to avoid fiddling with small notes is the normal gesture. Grab fixes the fare before the ride, which at least removes any argument about the price; tipping is a separate question, and the app has a tip option that drivers appreciate on long or awkward trips. Some Grab rides are still settled in cash to the driver.

One thing worth knowing: with a metered taxi, drivers frequently do not carry much change. Having small notes is more useful to everyone than a tip, and it prevents the familiar standoff where a 500,000 note cannot be broken.

Barbers, nail salons and small services

These sit on the boundary and the honest answer is that it depends who is around you. In a neighbourhood shop where the clientele is local, pay the posted price. In a salon on a tourist street with English signage and prices to match, a small tip is common and expected. Judge the room rather than the service type.

How to tip without making it awkward

Hand money directly to the person rather than leaving it on a table, use both hands or your right hand supported at the left elbow, and do it quietly. A tip presented with ceremony can read as a performance of generosity rather than thanks, which lands badly.

Tip in dong rather than dollars. Foreign notes have to be changed, small denominations often cannot be changed at all, and a few dollar bills are worth less to the recipient than the same value in usable local currency. The exception is a pooled cruise envelope, where dollars are commonly accepted.

The one that is not a tip

If someone performs an unrequested service and then names a price — a shoe repair begun while you are standing still, a photograph taken with a conical hat and a shoulder pole — that is a transaction you did not agree to, not a tipping situation. Decline before it starts rather than paying afterwards. Our wider look at how prices get set in these moments is in our honest assessment of safety in Vietnam, and the same habit of fixing the number first is one strand of the cash-and-cards planning that the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: Tipping is not customary in Vietnam and leaving nothing is normal. Here are the few situations where it genuinely is expected.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Visa Extension Guide
content:
Most articles on this subject explain how to extend a Vietnamese visa. This one has to begin by correcting the premise, because for the visa almost every American actually holds, extension is not a procedure with a difficult process. It does not exist.

An e-visa cannot be extended from inside Vietnam

The State Department states it plainly: Vietnam does not allow you to renew or extend an e-visa while you are in the country. There is no office to visit, no fee to pay and no form to file. The e-visa you were granted is the stay you have.

One corollary matters just as much. Vietnam usually grants the period you requested rather than defaulting to the maximum, so a three-week request will generally come back as three weeks even though 90 days was available. Ask for what you actually need.

What that means for anyone selling you an extension

Agencies do advertise e-visa extensions, and the service they are selling is one the government says is not available. In practice what they can offer is a different thing wearing the same name — usually an exit and re-entry, or a new visa of another category arranged through a sponsor. That may be legitimate work, but it is not an extension, and the distinction is worth insisting on before money changes hands.

If you have not applied yet, the duration question is covered alongside the rest of the requirements in our guide to Vietnam visa requirements for Americans.

Who can extend, and where

Extension exists as a real procedure for other visa categories — sponsored business visas, work-linked visas, and holders of temporary residence cards. For those, the Immigration Department handles it in person: you must appear at the office with jurisdiction over where you are actually staying, not whichever office is nearest or most convenient.

The three offices are in Hanoi at 69 Mac Thai To in Yen Hoa Ward, in Da Nang at 78 Le Loi in Hai Chau for central Vietnam, and in Ho Chi Minh City at 196 Nguyen Thi Minh Khai in Xuan Hoa Ward. The same offices handle overstays.

If you want longer than your visa allows

The answer is to decide before you fly. Request the duration you actually need, with a buffer at both ends, and remember the fee is $25 for single entry or $50 for multiple entry — a small premium for a lot of flexibility if your plans are loose.

The other route people use is a border run: leave to Cambodia, Laos or Thailand and come back on a fresh e-visa. This works, but it is not free of friction. You need the new visa approved before you return, your overland crossing must be one of the gates where e-visas are accepted, and the round trip costs a day or two plus the fee. Treat it as a plan rather than an improvisation.

Making a border run work

If you do plan to leave and re-enter, two details decide whether it goes smoothly. The new e-visa has to be approved before you travel back, which means allowing the 3 to 5 working days the Immigration Department usually takes — a border run improvised over a weekend is how people end up stranded on the wrong side. And two separate port rules apply: the crossing must be one where e-visas are accepted at all — every international airport, but only some land crossings into Cambodia and Laos — and it must also match the entry point you named on the new application.

Flying to Bangkok or Phnom Penh is the simpler version, because every international airport is an eligible gate, whereas only some land crossings are. It is not automatically the cheaper one — that depends on where you are and what fares look like. Whichever route you take, the binding constraint is the visa, not the travel: get the new one approved before you go, and treat the trip as open-ended rather than a two-day errand.

Overstaying is the expensive version

Overstaying is not a quiet administrative matter in Vietnam. The State Department warns that if you cannot leave on time for any reason, including a medical emergency, you will likely pay overstay fines and face delays getting permission to leave. Vietnam requires valid status to exit as well as to enter — a valid visa, a residence card, or Immigration Department approval — so an expired visa means obtaining that approval before you can fly, not simply apologising at the gate.

Check your entry stamp against your visa when you land. The stamp occasionally grants less time than the visa does, and that discrepancy is the commonest way a careful traveller overstays without realising. Photograph it.

What Phu Quoc does and does not change

The island's visa exemption covers a stay of 30 days or less, arriving and leaving Phu Quoc directly. It is not an extension mechanism and it does not reset anything: fly from Phu Quoc to the mainland and you have entered Vietnam proper, which needs a visa like any other arrival. Treat it as a separate short trip rather than a way to add time to an existing one.

The decision this really belongs to

Because nothing can be adjusted from inside the country, the visa form stops being paperwork and becomes one of the first real commitments of the trip — made before you have settled the route, often before the flights. Changing your mind later means leaving and applying again, not filing something locally. How long you ask for, single or multiple entry, and which port you name all shape what the itinerary can later become, which is one of the sequencing problems the complete Vietnam decision manual works through in order.
excerpt: There is no such thing as extending a Vietnamese e-visa from inside the country. That single fact reshapes how you should fill in the application.
author: Editorial

title: Hiring a Driver vs Riding Yourself in Vietnam
content:
This looks like a question about preference and budget — do you want the freedom of your own bike, or the comfort of someone else driving? The legal position narrows it more than most articles admit, so it is worth putting that on the table before the comparison.

The constraint that frames the choice

A US licence and an International Driving Permit are each invalid in Vietnam, and driving without a Vietnamese licence can mean a fine, arrest, or jail. Converting a foreign licence requires residency paperwork a tourist does not hold, so for a two-week visitor there is no lawful route to ride their own motorbike.

That does not stop anyone — rental shops ask for a passport photocopy and nothing else — but it does change what the decision is. You are not choosing between two equivalent options. You are choosing between a legal one and one where your travel insurance may not pay your medical bills after an accident.

Why insurance is the deciding number

Road safety is what the State Department warns about at greatest length for Vietnam, far more than crime. A serious motorbike accident can mean evacuation costs in the six figures. Riding unlicensed means finding out at the worst possible moment whether your policy pays — a risk you are accepting rather than a cost you have budgeted.

What hiring a driver actually gets you

A car with a driver is the standard product in Vietnam, and it costs roughly what bare self-drive rental costs in the United States. For the long legs — Hanoi to Ninh Binh, Hue to Hoi An over the Hai Van Pass, anything in the Mekong Delta — it is comfortable, air-conditioned, and removes both the licence question and the navigation.

The trade is the obvious one. You lose spontaneity, you are on someone else's schedule, and a car cannot take the narrow lanes and paddy tracks that make the countryside worth seeing. Most drivers will wait while you wander, which recovers some of that.

The easy-rider middle ground

Riding pillion behind an experienced local rider is how a large share of the Ha Giang loop is actually done, and it is the option most first-timers underrate. You get the motorbike experience, the mountain roads and the stops a car cannot reach, with none of the licence exposure. You also get a guide, and you get to look at the scenery instead of at the road surface.

For short city hops, Grab's motorbike taxis do the same job for a couple of dollars. Over a two-week trip that covers most of what people imagine they need a rented scooter for.

When self-drive still makes sense

Being straight about it: plenty of travellers rent anyway, and in quiet places — the lanes around Hoi An, a loop of Cat Ba, the flat roads of Ninh Binh — the practical risk is lower than in Ho Chi Minh City traffic. If that is your choice, make it knowingly rather than by default.

Reduce what is in your control. Photograph the whole bike with the renter watching before you ride off, so that existing scratches cannot become your problem at return. Never hand over your actual passport as a deposit; offer a photocopy and cash. Wear a proper helmet rather than the token shell supplied. And note that Vietnamese law requires zero alcohol while driving — not a 0.08 threshold, zero.

The option this comparison usually forgets

For the genuinely long legs, neither riding nor hiring a driver is the obvious answer — flying or taking the train often is. Hanoi to Da Nang is roughly an hour and a quarter in the air against fourteen hours or more on the ground, and domestic fares are low enough that the arithmetic rarely favours the road.

The train earns its place on one stretch in particular. The Hue to Da Nang leg over the Hai Van Pass is a sight in its own right, costs very little, and gives you the coastal views that are the whole reason people consider riding that road. Taking the train there and a car elsewhere is a common and sensible split.

How to decide

A useful split: fly or take the train for the longest hops, hire a car with a driver for the regional legs where the road itself is worth seeing, use Grab in the cities, and take an easy-rider for the one mountain route you actually came for. That covers the whole country legally and costs less than most people expect.

What makes this worth deciding early is that it is not really a transport choice. It determines which places are reachable, how long each leg takes, and therefore what the itinerary can contain — which is why it belongs in the same conversation as your route rather than being sorted out on arrival. the complete Vietnam decision manual works that sequence through in order. The licence and insurance detail sits in our guide to renting a motorbike in Vietnam.
excerpt: Riding without a Vietnamese licence is illegal for most visitors, and your insurer may refuse the medical bill. That makes this less of a preference question than it looks.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Customs and Duty-Free Rules
content:
Vietnamese customs is straightforward for an ordinary tourist, and most people walk through the green channel without speaking to anyone. The allowances are worth knowing anyway, because two of them — cash and alcohol — are easy to exceed without noticing, and the rules are more generous and more precise than the summaries online suggest.

Alcohol: three limits, pick one

Vietnam's duty-free allowance on arrival gives each traveller, per entry, 1.5 litres of spirits at 20% ABV or above, or 2 litres under 20%, or 3 litres of beer. These are alternatives rather than a combined total — you get one of the three, not all of them.

There is a sensible overflow provision most sources omit. A single bottle that goes over the limit by no more than one litre passes duty-free in its entirety; past one litre over, only the excess is dutiable. In practice that means a standard bottle bought in an airport duty-free shop on the way in is almost never a problem.

Tobacco

The tobacco allowance is 200 cigarettes, or 250 grams of shredded tobacco, or 20 cigars per entry, and again these are alternatives. The limits do not apply to anyone under eighteen, who has no allowance at all rather than a reduced one.

Everything else: a value cap, not an item list

Beyond alcohol, tobacco and a reasonable quantity of personal belongings, other goods come in duty-free up to a total customs value of 10,000,000 dong per entry. The figure is set in dong by decree, so its dollar equivalent drifts with the exchange rate — check the current conversion rather than trusting a number you read somewhere.

For a normal holiday this is not a constraint. It becomes one if you are bringing gifts in quantity, carrying new electronics still in their boxes, or travelling with professional equipment. Anything above the allowance has to clear customs as imported goods rather than as luggage.

The rule that works in your favour

One provision is worth knowing before you reach the counter: if you are over the allowance, you choose which items count inside it and which are declared. The decree gives that choice to the traveller, not to the officer. If you are carrying one expensive item and several cheap ones, you can put the expensive one inside the allowance and declare the rest — provided that item is itself within the 10,000,000 dong ceiling, which the choice does not override.

None of this replaces the entry requirements themselves, which are a separate matter — passport validity, the pre-arrival declaration and the visa are covered in our guide to Vietnam visa requirements for Americans.

Cash you must declare

There is no limit on how much money you may bring into or out of Vietnam, but above either threshold you must declare it in writing: more than 15,000,000 dong, or more than 5,000 US dollars in foreign currency. The same figures apply on the way out.

Note what the obligation actually is. You are not asking permission and you are not being taxed — you are filling in a form. A competing figure of 7,000 dollars circulates online and traces back to a superseded notice from 2005; the current thresholds are the ones above.

What you cannot bring

The prohibited-import list is set by decree and changed on 5 September 2026, when Decree 292/2026 replaced Decree 69/2018. The categories that matter to a tourist are the predictable ones: weapons and ammunition, narcotics, and politically sensitive publications or material deemed contrary to Vietnamese cultural norms.

Two practical notes. Drones frequently attract attention and may require permission, so research before packing one rather than discovering the rule at the airport. And prescription medication should travel in its original labelled packaging with a copy of the prescription, because some ingredients in common prescriptions, including certain ADHD treatments, are controlled in Vietnam.

The allowance resets each entry

The duty-free allowances above — alcohol, tobacco, the goods value — are per person, per entry, granted against your passport. If your trip includes a hop to Cambodia or Laos and back, you arrive with a fresh allowance on the return, which matters more for someone doing a border run than for a single-entry visitor. The cash thresholds work differently: they are reporting triggers rather than allowances, and they apply on the way out as well as in.

The personal-belongings category is deliberately written as a reasonable quantity rather than a list, which gives officers discretion and gives you latitude. Clothes, a laptop, a camera and a phone in ordinary numbers are luggage. Six identical new phones in retail packaging are not, whatever their total value, because the question shifts from what they are worth to what they are for.

Taking things home

The allowances above govern what comes in. On the way out your constraint is mostly your own country's: US Customs sets what you may bring back duty-free and that figure has nothing to do with Vietnam's. The one Vietnamese restriction worth checking before you buy is on genuine antiques and certain cultural objects, which require documentation to export — a reproduction lacquer piece is fine, a genuinely old one may not be, and a reputable dealer will tell you which you are holding.

Green channel, red channel

If you are inside every allowance and carrying nothing restricted, you take the green channel and keep walking. If you are over on any of them, or carrying cash above the thresholds, take the red channel and declare. The paperwork is short, and declaring is not itself a penalty — though goods over the allowance may still attract duty, as with the alcohol rule above. What declaring does cost you nothing in is trouble: being found over the line after choosing green is a different conversation entirely.
excerpt: What you can bring into Vietnam duty-free, the cash you must declare, and the one rule that works in your favour at the red channel.
author: Editorial

title: Best Time to Visit Vietnam
content:
Vietnam runs about a thousand miles from north to south, and that length is the whole answer to this question. At any given moment the country is running three different climates, so a month that is perfect in one region can be the worst of the year in another. The useful question is not when to visit Vietnam but which Vietnam you are visiting.

The short answer, if you want one

March and April are the best single compromise across the whole country. The north has warmed up and dried out, the centre is in its reliable dry run, and the south is still in its dry season. Prices sit in shoulder territory and the crowds are manageable. If you are flying from the United States and can only choose one window for a two-week trip that touches all three regions, this is it.

October and November are the other strong window, and in the north they are arguably better than spring: clear air, comfortable temperatures, and the Sapa rice terraces at their most photogenic. The catch is the centre, and it is a real one — see below before you commit.

Why most articles get this wrong

Search for this question and you will get a single month as an answer. That only works if your trip stays in one region. Once your itinerary includes both Hanoi and Hoi An, some months serve both well and others force a trade — and spotting which is which is the actual decision.

The north: four real seasons

Hanoi, Ha Long Bay, Ninh Binh and Sapa get a genuine winter. From December to February expect temperatures in the 50s and 60s Fahrenheit with a persistent grey drizzle the Vietnamese call mua phun — not heavy rain, but damp, overcast and colder than almost any American expects of Southeast Asia. Sapa can approach freezing and occasionally sees snow.

Summer runs hot and wet: June through August brings the 90s with high humidity and the year's heaviest rainfall. The shoulders are the sweet spots. October and November are reliably clear and mild, and March and April warm steadily without the summer downpours.

The air-quality caveat nobody mentions

The State Department notes that air pollution is a significant problem in Vietnam’s major cities, especially Hanoi, and the worst stretch overlaps the cool dry months that are otherwise the north's best — roughly November through March, when still air traps pollution over the Red River delta. That is not a reason to avoid Hanoi in winter, but if you are asthmatic or travelling with someone who is, it belongs in the decision. Check a live air-quality reading rather than a figure printed in any article, including this one.

The centre: a short, violent wet season

Hue, Da Nang and Hoi An are driest from February to August, and that is when their beaches work. The complication is September to November, which is typhoon season on this coast. Hoi An's old town floods in most years, boat trips get cancelled at short notice, and Hue is the wettest major city in the country during this window.

This is the single biggest planning conflict in Vietnam. October and November are excellent in Hanoi and unreliable in Hoi An. Storms are forecastable a few days out but not months ahead, so an autumn trip spanning both regions is a bet rather than a plan you can optimise: keep slack in the central leg, book refundable where you can, and be prepared to lose more than a beach day if a typhoon lands.

The south: wet and dry, not hot and cold

Ho Chi Minh City, the Mekong Delta and Phu Quoc are warm year-round, typically in the 80s and 90s, and the seasons are defined by rain rather than temperature. Dry season runs December to April. Wet season runs May to November, and it is less disruptive than it sounds: the pattern is a heavy afternoon downpour for an hour or two rather than all-day rain, and mornings are usually clear.

Travelling the south in the wet season is a reasonable trade for lower prices and thinner crowds, provided you plan activities for the morning. Phu Quoc is the exception where the sea gets rough enough to matter for boat trips.

Festival timing as a reason, not an obstacle

Two dates are worth bending an itinerary for. The rice harvest in the northern terraces falls around September and October, which is when Sapa and Ha Giang look the way they do in photographs, and the northern weather in that window is reliably good. The Mid-Autumn Festival, usually September, is at its best in Hoi An — but it sits inside the central coast's storm season, so it is the one case here where the festival and the weather pull against each other.

When not to go

Tet, the Lunar New Year, is the one period that can genuinely derail a trip. The dates move with the lunar calendar — in 2027 Tet falls on 6 February, with the public-sector holiday announced as 4 to 10 February — and the disruption runs wider than the official week. Popular domestic flights and trains book out well in advance and fares rise sharply, many family-run businesses close for several days, and cities empty while the countryside fills. Always verify the dates for your own year before booking.

The other date to know is the Reunification Day and Labour Day pair at the end of April, when Vietnamese travellers fill the beaches and hill towns and prices spike for a long weekend whose exact shape is set by government announcement each year.
excerpt: There is no single best month for Vietnam. The country spans three climates at once, and the right answer depends on which third you are visiting.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Weather by Region and Month
content:
Vietnam's three climate zones rarely line up, so the practical way to read its weather is month by month and region by region rather than as a single national season. What follows is that grid, written for someone deciding when to fly rather than someone studying meteorology.

December to February: cold north, dry south

The north is cool and damp — Hanoi in the 50s and 60s Fahrenheit, grey more often than not, with a fine persistent drizzle. Sapa is genuinely cold and the mountain passes can be fogged in. Pack layers and a waterproof shell, which first-timers heading to Southeast Asia almost never do.

The centre is transitional and improving, with Hue and Hoi An drying out through January. The south is at its best: Ho Chi Minh City, the Mekong and Phu Quoc sit in the heart of the dry season with warm days, low humidity by local standards and reliable sun. This is peak season in the south and prices follow.

The Tet exception

Whatever the weather is doing, Lunar New Year overrides it as a planning factor. In 2027 Tet falls on 6 February with a public-sector holiday announced for 4 to 10 February, and the travel surge runs well past the official days. Check the dates for your year before fixing anything in February.

March to April: the national sweet spot

This is the window where all three regions are simultaneously good. The north warms into the 70s and sheds the winter drizzle, the centre is firmly dry with beach weather arriving, and the south is still dry before the May rains. Humidity is tolerable everywhere and the light is clear.

If your itinerary covers Hanoi, the central coast and Ho Chi Minh City in one trip, this is the period that asks you to compromise least. The trade is that others have worked this out too, so book accommodation earlier than you otherwise would.

May to August: hot everywhere, wet in two places

The north turns hot and humid, with the 90s common in Hanoi and the year's heaviest rain falling in July and August. Sapa stays cooler and becomes a genuine escape, and the rice terraces are green and growing through this period.

The centre is the surprise: this is its dry, hot season, and Da Nang and Hoi An have their best beach weather of the year. If your trip is beach-led and must happen in summer, the central coast is the answer. The south is in wet season, which in practice means clear mornings and a heavy afternoon hour of rain rather than washed-out days.

What the summer heat actually feels like

Temperature alone understates it. Humidity in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City in July regularly makes the mid-90s feel like well over a hundred, and midday sightseeing stops being enjoyable. The local rhythm adjusts for this — early starts, a long flat middle of the day, activity again after four — and copying it makes summer travel far more pleasant than fighting it.

September to November: the split

These months divide the country more sharply than any others. The north is excellent: October and November bring clear skies and comfortable temperatures, with the terrace harvest falling around September and October. The south is drying out and improving through November.

The centre, meanwhile, is in its typhoon season. Hue and Hoi An take the brunt, Hoi An's old town floods in most years, and coastal boat trips including Ha Long cruises further north can be cancelled on short notice. Storms are forecastable a few days out but not bookable around months in advance, so autumn itineraries through the centre need slack built in.

Ha Long Bay has its own rules

Cruises run year-round, but the bay is weather-sensitive in a way the rest of the north is not. Summer brings the risk of storm cancellations, and winter brings the mist that makes the karsts atmospheric in photographs and invisible in person. October and November give the best odds of clear water and clear air, which is one reason the north's autumn is worth protecting in an itinerary.

How to use this grid

Work backwards from the region you most want to see rather than from the month. If Hoi An and the central beaches are the point of the trip, February to August is the stretch that reliably works, and September to November is the one to avoid. If Sapa and the northern mountains are the point, aim for September to November or March to April. If you want all three regions, March and April is the least compromised window — October is excellent in the north and south but remains a gamble on the central coast, which no amount of sequencing fixes.

One practical note that applies all year: Vietnam has a single time zone and does not observe daylight saving, so the gap to the United States shifts by an hour twice a year rather than staying fixed. Check it when you book rather than assuming.
excerpt: A month-by-month read of Vietnam's three climate zones, so you can see where the good weather actually is when you want to travel.
author: Editorial

title: Traveling Vietnam During Tet (Lunar New Year)
content:
Tet is the Lunar New Year and the most important date in the Vietnamese calendar, and the honest framing for a visitor is that it is not a festival laid on for the public. It is the entire country travelling home to be with family. Understanding that one fact explains everything else about what works and what does not.

When Tet falls, and why the dates move

Tet follows the lunar calendar, so it shifts every year, usually landing between late January and mid-February. In 2027 Tet day is 6 February, with the public-sector holiday announced as 4 to 10 February. Always confirm the dates for your own year before booking anything — they are set each year and widely misreported in travel articles written well in advance.

The official holiday is the smaller number. The practical disruption window is roughly a week either side, because people travel home before and back after. Vietnam Airlines, for instance, treats a span running into the third week of February as its return-surge period for routes from Ho Chi Minh City to the north.

What closes

Family-run businesses — which is most of the good food in Vietnam — close for several days, sometimes a week. Small restaurants, independent cafes, market stalls, tailors in Hoi An, local tour operators. Museums and official sites close on the main days. Hotels, international chains, larger restaurants and the bigger tour companies stay open, which is why a package trip feels the disruption far less than independent travel does.

What happens to transport and prices

Popular domestic flights and trains book out well ahead and fares on the busiest routes rise sharply. This is the part that catches people: it is not that travel is inconvenient during Tet, it is that on the days and routes everyone wants, the seat may simply not exist. Intercity buses fill too, and the roads around the major cities become congested in the days before.

Accommodation behaves differently by region. City hotels can actually be cheaper, because business travel stops and the cities empty. Coastal and resort areas go the other way as domestic holidaymakers arrive. Expect the reverse of the usual pattern.

Cash, and the one thing that always bites

Banks close, and ATMs in smaller towns can run empty and go unrefilled for days. Whatever you think you need in cash before the holiday starts, take more, and take it out in a city. It is a common and largely preventable way for a Tet trip to go wrong, and it costs nothing to prepare for.

What Tet is actually like, if you go

It is quiet, and that surprises people expecting a street carnival. The public spectacle happens in the days before — flower markets selling kumquat trees and peach blossom, families buying in bulk, a genuine buzz in the markets — and then on the day itself the streets empty as everyone goes indoors to eat with family. Hanoi's Old Quarter at Tet is the stillest you will ever see it.

There are real rewards. Temples and pagodas are full and alive. The cities are navigable in a way they never otherwise are. If you have any Vietnamese connection, or are invited into a home, it is the warmest possible time to be there. And the flower markets in the week before are a genuine sight.

If you are going anyway

Book flights and intercity transport the moment your dates are fixed, months out. Stock cash before the holiday begins. Base yourself somewhere with enough open infrastructure — a larger city or a resort area rather than a small town. Lower your expectations about eating: have a hotel with food, or accept that your favourite-looking place will be shuttered. And learn chuc mung nam moi, which will be received very warmly.

A little etiquette goes a long way

Red envelopes of lucky money, li xi, are given to children and sometimes to elders; small crisp notes in a red envelope are the form, and the amount matters less than the gesture. Avoid giving anything black or sharp as a gift. The first person to enter a home in the new year is traditionally significant, so do not let yourself be the uninvited first foot through a neighbour's door on the morning of Tet. None of this is expected of visitors, and a foreigner who gets it wrong is unlikely to cause real offence — but knowing it changes how the week reads.

What this decision is really attached to

Notice what Tet actually does to a trip. It does not simply make one week inconvenient. It pushes your transport bookings much earlier than you would otherwise make them, which means committing to a route before you have finished choosing it. It raises the cost of any plan that leans on a single mid-trip internal flight, because that is the link most likely to fail. It inverts the usual price relationship between cities and coast. And it rewards planning you would otherwise leave until you arrived.

In other words, a single date on the lunar calendar quietly reorders the sequence in which the other decisions have to be made. How that sequence works, and which choices are worth locking before which, is set out in the complete Vietnam decision manual.
excerpt: Tet is not a festival you attend as a tourist — it is the country going home. Here is what actually closes, what sells out, and when it is worth it anyway.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Festivals Calendar Beyond Tet
content:
Tet absorbs most of the attention, and reasonably so, but Vietnam's year has a dozen other dates worth knowing. Some are worth planning a trip around. Two of them will close things and fill beaches whether you planned for them or not.

The two that affect your logistics

Reunification Day on 30 April and International Labour Day on 1 May fall together and function as a long domestic holiday. Vietnamese travellers fill coastal resorts, Da Lat and Sapa, prices rise sharply, and domestic flights and hotels book out. The exact length of the break is set by government announcement each year because it depends on how the dates land against the weekend, so check it rather than assuming a fixed span.

National Day on 2 September is the other one, and it follows the same pattern: domestic travel surges and the beaches fill. Its length also depends on how the date falls against the weekend, so check the year rather than assuming it is the shorter of the two. Hanoi holds official ceremonies around Ba Dinh Square, which is worth seeing but closes roads.

Why these matter more than the cultural dates

Festivals mostly add something to a trip. Public holidays subtract capacity from it. If you are choosing between two weeks and the only difference is that one contains a national holiday, that is a real reason to pick the other.

The lunar dates worth planning around

Most Vietnamese festivals follow the lunar calendar, so their Gregorian dates shift each year and need checking for your own travel year.

The Perfume Pagoda festival runs from shortly after Tet through to around the third lunar month, drawing very large crowds to the boat-and-cave pilgrimage southwest of Hanoi. Going outside the festival means a calm trip; going during it means seeing something genuinely communal, with the crowds that implies.

Hung Kings Temple Festival, on the tenth day of the third lunar month, is a public holiday honouring Vietnam's legendary founders, centred on Phu Tho province north of Hanoi. It adds a day off to the domestic calendar.

Mid-Autumn Festival, on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, usually September, is the one most visitors enjoy most. Lanterns, mooncakes, lion dances and children in the streets. Hoi An is spectacular for it, and Hanoi's Old Quarter fills with lantern sellers in the run-up.

Hoi An's monthly lantern night

Separately from any festival, Hoi An turns off its electric lights on the fourteenth day of each lunar month and lights the old town with lanterns. It happens every month, it is beautiful, and it is easy to catch by accident or to plan for with a calendar check.

Regional and seasonal events

Hue hosts a biennial festival of royal arts and performance in its citadel, typically in spring, which transforms the city when it runs. Da Nang's international fireworks competition brings weekend displays over the Han River across several months in summer, and fills hotels on those weekends.

In the far north, the ethnic-minority markets have their own rhythm — Bac Ha's Sunday market being the best known and the most worth building a Sapa itinerary around, since it only happens on Sundays. Harvest in the northern terraces falls around September and October and is the reason those months are the photographic peak for Sapa and Ha Giang.

Dates most visitors never hear about

Vu Lan, the Wandering Souls festival on the fifteenth day of the seventh lunar month, is the second most important family occasion after Tet. Pagodas fill, offerings are burned in the street, and roses are pinned to clothing — red for those whose mother is living, white for those whose mother has died. It is quieter than Tet and does not disrupt travel, but it is deeply felt.

The Lim Festival in Bac Ninh, shortly after Tet, is where quan ho call-and-response folk singing is performed in its home province, now recognised by UNESCO. In fishing communities along the central and southern coast, whale worship festivals honour the animal as a protector of fishermen, with dates varying village by village.

Lunar or solar — check which

Reunification Day, Labour Day and National Day are fixed solar dates and land on the same day every year. Almost everything else here is lunar and moves. When you read a date in any article, including this one, confirm whether it is fixed or floating before you plan around it.

How to use the calendar

How to use the calendar

Two passes. First check whether your dates collide with Tet, the April–May pair or National Day, because those affect whether you can travel at all as planned. Then, separately, see whether anything you would actively enjoy happens to fall inside your window, and treat that as a bonus rather than the organising principle.

The one case for inverting that order is Mid-Autumn in Hoi An or the Sapa harvest, both of which are good enough to build a trip around. The Sapa harvest sits in a window when northern weather is at its best; Mid-Autumn in Hoi An does not, because September is storm season on that coast, so it is a festival worth a gamble rather than a safe fixture. Weighing a festival against the season it falls in is one of the things the complete Vietnam decision manual works through in sequence.
excerpt: Tet dominates the calendar, but a dozen other dates will shape what you see — and two of them will fill every beach and flight you wanted.
author: Editorial

title: What to Pack for Vietnam
content:
Packing for Vietnam is harder than packing for a single-climate country, because a two-week trip from Hanoi to the Mekong can cross a cold damp winter and a tropical dry season in the same suitcase. The list below is organised around the few things that actually go wrong rather than around completeness.

Start with which Vietnams you are visiting

If your trip is entirely in the south, pack as you would for Florida in summer and stop reading the cold-weather section.
