If it includes Hanoi or Sapa between roughly November and March, you need real layers: a fleece or light down, a waterproof shell, and something warm for your hands in the mountains. Sapa can approach freezing and visitors routinely arrive unprepared because they packed for Southeast Asia in the abstract.

For a trip spanning both, the workable approach is lightweight layers rather than bulky items — long-sleeve base layers, a packable insulated jacket, and a shell that handles both the northern drizzle and a southern downpour.

Rain, and what actually works

A compact umbrella beats a rain jacket for city use in the south, where the rain is warm and heavy and a sealed jacket turns into a sauna. In the north's fine winter drizzle the jacket wins. Carrying both is reasonable and neither takes much space.

Cheap plastic ponchos are sold on every street corner for less than a dollar and are the standard local solution for a sudden downpour on a motorbike. Buy one there rather than carrying one.

Shoes are the thing people get wrong

You will walk a great deal on uneven pavements and you will take your shoes off repeatedly — entering temples, homes, many homestays and some small shops. Slip-on or easily unlaced shoes save real friction. Bring one pair of comfortable walking shoes and one pair of sandals, and skip the third pair you are considering.

Clothing for temples and the mausoleum

Day-to-day dress in Vietnamese cities is relaxed and Western, and shorts and t-shirts are unremarkable. Two exceptions need packing for. Temples and pagodas require shoulders and knees covered, so bring one lightweight long-sleeve layer and trousers or a long skirt that you can put on over what you are wearing. A scarf doubles as a shoulder cover and is the single most useful item on this list.

The Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum in Hanoi enforces a stricter code than anywhere else you are likely to go — no shorts, no bare shoulders, no hats inside, and cameras and phones are not permitted in the viewing chamber. If it is on your itinerary, plan an outfit for it.

The small things that matter

Vietnam runs on 220V at 50Hz, and sockets commonly take both US flat two-pin and European round two-pin plugs, so a US charger usually fits without an adapter. The voltage is the part to check: almost all phone and laptop chargers handle 100–240V and are fine, but a 110V-only appliance such as an older hair dryer will be destroyed. Read the label before packing it.

Bring insect repellent with DEET or picaridin — dengue is daytime-biting and urban, so this is not only a jungle concern. Carry prescription medication in its original labelled packaging with a copy of the prescription — but note that packaging alone does not make a substance legal: ingredients in some common prescriptions, including for ADHD, may be illegal in Vietnam, so check anything you depend on before you fly rather than at the border. A small supply of rehydration salts and loperamide covers most of what goes wrong.

What not to bother with

Do not pack towels, basic toiletries, or large quantities of clothing. Laundry is cheap, fast and available everywhere, usually priced by the kilo and returned the same day, which makes a week's clothes sufficient for a month's trip. Do not bring a water filter bottle unless you are trekking; bottled water is universal and cheap. And do not bring much cash in US dollars beyond a modest emergency reserve — you will spend in dong.

If your trip has a motorbike or trekking leg

Riding pillion on the Ha Giang loop or trekking out of Sapa changes the list. Bring real closed shoes with grip rather than sandals, long trousers regardless of heat, and a windproof layer — mountain roads are markedly colder than the valley you left. Operators supply helmets, but the supplied ones are often token shells, and anyone riding for days should consider their own.

A dry bag or a few resealable plastic bags protect electronics from both rain and dust, and a power bank matters more here than in cities, because a day on the road is a day away from sockets while using your phone for photographs and navigation.

Connectivity

An eSIM bought before you leave is usually the lowest-friction option, provided your phone supports eSIM and you check the provider's Vietnam coverage; a physical tourist SIM bought at the airport requires passport registration and takes a few minutes. Check what your own US carrier charges for international data before relying on it — roaming add-ons are typically far more expensive per gigabyte than a local plan, though a few plans include Vietnam at no extra cost.

One thing to leave room for

One thing to leave room for

Hoi An's tailors are a genuine industry rather than a tourist gimmick, and a lot of visitors leave with more clothing than they arrived with. If that is likely, arrive with space or plan on a cheap extra bag bought locally.
excerpt: Pack for three climates, two dress codes and a lot of walking. The list that matters is short, and most of it is about rain, feet and temples.
author: Editorial

title: Getting to Vietnam: Flights from the US
content:
Vietnam is a long way from the United States, and the flight is the part of the trip most people underestimate. The headline numbers matter less than two structural facts: there is only one nonstop, and the arrival date on your ticket is almost never the day you left.

The nonstop options, and who they serve

Vietnam Airlines flies nonstop from San Francisco to Ho Chi Minh City, at roughly sixteen to seventeen hours westbound. That single route is the entire nonstop map between the United States and Vietnam. If you are starting from the West Coast and your trip begins in the south, this is the simplest way to do it.

From anywhere else — New York, Newark, Washington, Chicago, Dallas, Seattle — you will connect at least once. There is no nonstop to Hanoi from the United States at all, which is worth knowing before you plan a north-to-south route.

Where you connect, and why it matters

The realistic hubs are Seoul Incheon, Tokyo Narita or Haneda, Taipei, Hong Kong, Singapore, and the Gulf airports at Doha and Dubai. North Asian hubs are usually the shortest total routing from the East Coast and the West. Gulf routings are often cheaper and almost always longer, sometimes adding six or more hours of total journey.

Door to door, plan on twenty-two to twenty-six hours from the East Coast with one stop. That total elapsed figure is the number to plan around, not the flight time, because it determines what state you arrive in and whether the first day of your itinerary is real.

The calendar day you lose

Vietnam has a single time zone and does not observe daylight saving, so the gap to the United States shifts by an hour twice a year rather than staying fixed — twelve hours ahead of the East Coast during Eastern Standard Time, eleven during Eastern Daylight Time. Combined with the westbound flight time, a departure on Monday evening typically lands on Wednesday morning. You lose a calendar day going out and nominally gain it coming back.

The practical consequence is that two weeks on the ground is not two weeks away from home: the outbound crossing eats a calendar day and the return takes most of another, so count the travel days separately when you work out how much leave you need. Build the arrival day in as a write-off rather than scheduling anything into it.

Which city to fly into

The default assumption is to fly into one end and out of the other, which avoids backtracking the length of the country. Open-jaw tickets into Hanoi and out of Ho Chi Minh City, or the reverse, are widely available and usually cost little or nothing more than a return.

If the nonstop from the West Coast is what makes the trip affordable, that points you to starting in Ho Chi Minh City and travelling north. If you are connecting anyway, the direction is open and should be decided on other grounds — season, Tet, and what you want to see first.

Da Nang as a third option

Da Nang now has a reasonable number of international connections through the Asian hubs and sits in the middle of the country. For a trip focused on the central coast — Hoi An, Hue, the beaches — flying in and out of Da Nang removes two internal legs that would otherwise eat a day each.

When to book, and what moves the price

Fares to Vietnam move with the Asian holiday calendar more than the American one. The expensive windows are around Tet, which moves each year, and the mid-summer peak. The cheapest reliable period is the autumn shoulder outside the holidays.

Booking two to four months ahead is the usual sweet spot for long-haul to Asia, with the important exception of Tet, where the relevant window is much earlier. Fares move constantly and this page does not track them, so treat any number here as a planning bracket to check against a live search rather than a quote. The bracket people generally plan around is several hundred dollars for a West Coast round trip in shoulder season, with the East Coast and the peak summer and Tet windows running higher. Check live fares before you plan around any of that.

Arriving, and the jet lag nobody plans for

Eleven or twelve hours is close to the maximum possible time difference, which means there is no gentle version of this adjustment. Flying west is generally the easier direction, and the standard advice holds: get onto Vietnamese meal times immediately, get daylight on the first afternoon, and do not nap for more than half an hour on arrival day.

Plan the first forty-eight hours accordingly. A walking day in Hanoi's Old Quarter or a slow first morning in Ho Chi Minh City absorbs jet lag far better than a 6am domestic flight or a Ha Long cruise transfer. The temptation is to front-load the itinerary because the trip feels short; the result is usually two wasted days instead of one.

The connection that decides your first day

One thing worth weighing when you choose a routing: a connection that lands at dawn at least gives you the option of a slow first day, while one that lands near midnight costs you a hotel night and the morning after. Those two itineraries can cost the same and differ by the better part of a day — which is the sort of trade that only shows up once you line the route, the season and the internal legs against each other, and which the complete Vietnam decision manual works through in order.
excerpt: There are only two nonstop routes from the United States to Vietnam. Everything else connects, and where you connect shapes the whole first day.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Airport Guide: Hanoi, Saigon, Da Nang
content:
Vietnam's three main international airports are modern, busy and straightforward, and the things that slow people down are mostly knowable in advance. Here is what each one is actually like and what to have in hand before you join the queue.

Before any of them: the paperwork to have ready

Have your printed e-visa with your passport — the official instruction is to carry a paper copy, which is a cheap hedge against a dead phone in an immigration hall. Have the address of your first night's accommodation written down, because the arrival form and the officer may both ask for it.

Complete the online pre-arrival declaration before you fly, within the three days before arrival. It is free and takes about ten minutes. The two governments describe its status differently — the US State Department calls it required for air arrivals, Vietnam's own portal presents it as advice that shortens the queue — so the practical answer is simply to do it.

The gate-matching trap

Your e-visa names a port of entry, and that choice is binding: arriving at an airport other than the one you selected can mean being refused. Check the document against your ticket before you leave home, while it is still fixable.

Noi Bai, Hanoi (HAN)

International arrivals use Terminal 2, domestic flights Terminal 1, and the two are a short shuttle apart — allow for that on a connection. The airport sits about sixteen miles north of the city and the transfer takes forty-five minutes to an hour, longer in the morning and evening peaks.

Getting in: Grab is the simplest option and the pickup area is signposted, though it is a short walk from arrivals. Airport taxis are metered and legitimate but this is the classic place for an inflated fare, so agreeing the app price beforehand avoids the conversation entirely. The 86 express bus runs to the Old Quarter cheaply and takes about an hour.

Tan Son Nhat, Ho Chi Minh City (SGN)

Unusually close to the city — about four miles from District 1 — but the traffic means thirty to fifty minutes regardless. Terminal 2 handles international arrivals, Terminal 1 domestic, and the newer Terminal 3 has taken much of the domestic load.

Immigration here is the busiest in the country and queues at peak arrival times are long. Grab pickup is on the upper level rather than directly outside arrivals, which catches people out; follow the signs up rather than accepting the first offer at the kerb. Long Thanh, the planned replacement airport, is not yet operating, so do not plan around it.

If you are connecting to a domestic flight

You clear immigration and customs on arrival, collect your bags, and check in again at the domestic terminal. Budget three hours between an international arrival and a domestic departure at either Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City, and more during holidays.

Da Nang (DAD)

The easiest of the three. Small, modern, about two miles from the city centre, and roughly forty-five minutes from Hoi An by car. International and domestic terminals sit side by side.

Most Hoi An hotels will arrange a transfer, and at this distance a prearranged car is worth the small premium over sorting it on arrival after a long flight. Grab also operates normally here.

Practicalities on arrival

Airport exchange counters typically give poorer rates than banks or gold shops in town, so change only enough to reach your accommodation and handle the rest in the city. ATMs are available in all three arrival halls, and the flat-fee structure means one larger withdrawal beats several small ones.

Buy a SIM at the airport if you have not arranged an eSIM; counters are in the arrivals halls and registration needs your passport. Free wifi is available in all three airports, which is enough to call a Grab if you would rather sort connectivity in town.

The smaller international airports

Four others take international flights and are worth knowing if they suit your route. Cam Ranh serves Nha Trang and is about forty minutes from the town. Phu Quoc takes direct flights from several Asian hubs and is the arrival point for the island's thirty-day visa exemption. Cat Bi at Hai Phong is the closest airport to Cat Ba and Ha Long. Phu Bai serves Hue, mostly domestically.

All of them are small, quick to clear and far less stressful than Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City. If your itinerary is regional rather than country-wide, routing through one of these instead of the big two can save a couple of hours and a lot of queueing.

Leaving the country

Arrive three hours before an international departure. Vietnam requires valid status to exit as well as to enter, so an overstayed visa is a departure problem rather than something to apologise for at the gate. Duty-free purchases on the way out are unrestricted in quantity by Vietnam, but your destination's allowances still apply.
excerpt: What to expect at Noi Bai, Tan Son Nhat and Da Nang — immigration, getting into town, and the one form to have ready.
author: Editorial

title: How to Ride the Reunification Express Train
content:
The Reunification Express runs the length of Vietnam, from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City, and it is the most romanticised transport in the country. It is also slow. Understanding why people ride it anyway — and which part they ride — is most of what you need.

What the route actually is

A single line of roughly a thousand miles connects Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, taking somewhere in the region of thirty-two to thirty-six hours end to end depending on the service. Trains stop at Ninh Binh, Hue, Da Nang, Nha Trang and a long list of smaller towns along the way.

Almost nobody rides it end to end, and there is no particular reason to. The train is used in segments, and the segments are what make it worthwhile.

The one leg worth planning around

Hue to Da Nang, about two and a half to three hours, runs along the coast and over the Hai Van Pass with the sea on one side and mountains on the other. It costs very little, it is one of the most scenic rail stretches in Southeast Asia, and it replaces a road transfer you would otherwise make anyway. If you take one train in Vietnam, take this one, and sit on the right-hand side heading south.

Classes, and which to book

Four broad options, in ascending order of comfort: hard seat, soft seat, hard sleeper in a six-berth compartment, and soft sleeper in a four-berth compartment. Air conditioning is standard on the better services and worth confirming when booking.

For an overnight leg, the four-berth soft sleeper is the one most visitors want. Berths are sold individually, so a couple booking two berths shares with two strangers unless they buy the compartment out — which is possible and, split between two, often still reasonable. Lower berths cost a little more and are worth it for the headroom and the window.

Private operators

Several companies attach their own refurbished carriages to the regular trains, particularly on the Hanoi to Lao Cai route for Sapa and on the central legs. They are more comfortable and more expensive, and they run on the same timetable as the train they are attached to.

The Sapa branch

The other railway worth knowing is the overnight branch from Hanoi to Lao Cai, the jumping-off point for Sapa. It leaves Hanoi in the evening and arrives around dawn, followed by an hour's road transfer up the hill. For years this was the standard way to reach Sapa.

The expressway has changed that calculation. A day bus or limousine van now covers the same ground in five to six hours, and most travellers take it. The train survives as the choice for people who would rather sleep through the journey than lose a daylight half-day to it, and the private sleeper carriages on this route are the most comfortable rail travel in the country.

Booking

Tickets are sold through Vietnam Railways and at station counters, and a number of agencies resell them with a markup for the convenience of an English-language interface. Book ahead for overnight sleepers in high season and well ahead around Tet, when the whole network fills.

Bring your passport; tickets are issued against it. Arrive at the station twenty to thirty minutes early, as platforms are announced late and the trains do not wait.

What riding it is actually like

Comfortable rather than luxurious, and sociable. Vendors come through with food and the dining options are basic, so bring snacks and water. Bathrooms are serviceable at the start of a journey and less so by the end. The ride is noisier and bumpier than European rail, and sleeping through an overnight leg is easier with earplugs.

The compensation is the window. The coastal stretches in the centre are genuinely beautiful, and the train passes through rice paddies, fishing villages and backyards that no road route shows you.

Food, and what to bring

Trolleys come through with rice boxes, instant noodles and drinks, and there is hot water on board for the noodles. It is edible rather than good. Stations on the longer stops sell better food from platform vendors, though you need to judge the stop length before getting off.

Bring water, snacks, and something to eat that does not need heating. Bring toilet paper. Bring a power bank — sockets exist in the sleeper compartments but are shared and not always working.

Train versus the alternatives

For the long hops the train loses badly on elapsed time — Hanoi to Da Nang is roughly fifteen to seventeen hours by rail against about an hour and a quarter in the air. Against the sleeper bus the train wins on comfort and loses on price. The honest summary is that the train is mostly a choice about how you want to spend the hours rather than a way to save them, with two qualifications: an overnight service converts some of those hours into sleep you would have spent in a hotel anyway, and on the Hue to Da Nang leg the train is roughly as quick as the road and far more enjoyable.

Which legs to fly, ride or sleep through is one of the decisions that shapes a Vietnam itinerary most, and the complete Vietnam decision manual works that sequence through in order.
excerpt: Vietnam's north–south railway is slower than the bus and far slower than flying. People ride it for one stretch in particular.
author: Editorial

title: Domestic Flights in Vietnam: Routes and Airlines
content:
Vietnam's domestic air network is dense and cheap by American standards, and it is what makes a short trip through a long country comfortable rather than rushed. One flight can replace fourteen hours on the ground — though plenty of people cover the same route by train or bus and treat the journey as part of the trip.

The airlines

Vietnam Airlines is the full-service national carrier and a SkyTeam member, so Delta miles earn and burn on it. VietJet Air and Bamboo Airways are the low-cost operators, with Vietravel Airlines a smaller fourth. Between them they cover essentially every pairing a visitor would want.

The trade is the familiar one. Vietnam Airlines includes checked baggage and has the better on-time record; VietJet is usually the cheapest and sells baggage, seats and everything else separately. On a short hop with hand luggage the low-cost option is often genuinely fine. On a connection where a delay would cost you something, the premium is worth it.

What the fares look like

Low. Internal hops on the main routes are cheap by American standards — the kind of fare that makes flying the obvious choice over a long overland leg — but the actual number moves with the date, how far ahead you book, and the holiday calendar. Check a live search rather than planning against a figure on a page. Treat that as an order of magnitude rather than a quote. The useful shape is that the gap between the cheapest and most expensive carrier on the same route is often smaller than the baggage fee that separates them.

The routes that matter

Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City is one of the busiest air corridors in the world and runs many times a day, taking a little over two hours against more than thirty by rail. Hanoi to Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City to Da Nang are the next tier, both around an hour and a quarter, and both replace a very long ground journey.

Beyond the big three, useful services run to Phu Quoc, Nha Trang via Cam Ranh, Hue via Phu Bai, Da Lat via Lien Khuong, and Con Dao. Flights also reach Dien Bien and Con Dao on smaller aircraft, which are the only practical way to reach either.

The route that is not worth flying

Hue to Da Nang. The two cities are about two and a half to three hours apart by rail, and the airports are close enough together that flying makes no sense once you add two transfers, check-in and security. The train is cheaper and is one of the best rides in the country.

Booking and baggage

Book directly with the airlines where you can. Fares rise closer to departure in the usual way, and the holiday periods — Tet above all, then the April–May pair and National Day — book out and spike well in advance.

Check the baggage allowance before you book a low-cost fare, because the headline price frequently excludes checked bags and adding one at the airport costs considerably more than adding it online. Weigh your bag: enforcement is real and consistent.

When the train or bus is the better call

Flying is not automatically right just because it is fast. On the shorter corridors the door-to-door maths closes up: a one-hour flight between Hue and Nha Trang becomes four hours once you add two airport transfers, check-in and security, against a train that leaves from the middle of town.

The rule of thumb that holds is that flying wins decisively above roughly five hundred miles, loses below about a hundred and fifty, and is a genuine toss-up in between — decided by what time of day each option runs and whether you would rather sleep through the journey or see it.

Airports and timing

Domestic terminals are separate from international ones at both Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, so a same-day international-to-domestic connection means clearing immigration, collecting bags and moving terminals. Allow three hours, more at holidays.

For a purely domestic flight, ninety minutes at the airport is comfortable. Vietnamese domestic airports are efficient and the security queues are short by US standards.

Delays

Delays are common on the low-cost carriers, particularly late in the day as the schedule accumulates slippage. If a flight has to connect with something else — an international departure, a cruise check-in, a prepaid transfer — book it early in the day and leave a buffer rather than relying on the schedule.

The island and remote routes

Some places are effectively only reachable by air. Con Dao, the former prison islands off the southern coast, has no practical alternative. Phu Quoc is served by ferry from the Mekong Delta, but the flight from Ho Chi Minh City takes an hour against most of a day by road and boat. Dien Bien Phu in the far northwest is a long mountain drive otherwise.

These routes often use smaller aircraft with tighter baggage limits and thinner schedules — sometimes one or two flights a day — so a cancellation can leave you waiting until the next one rather than catching a later service the same afternoon. Build a spare day around any of them rather than connecting straight onto an international departure.

How flights change the shape of a trip

The real effect of cheap internal flights is that they decouple your route from geography. Without them, a two-week trip is a forced march down a single line; with them, you can skip the middle, double back, or treat Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City as two separate bases. Which legs to fly and which to take slowly is one of the first decisions worth making deliberately rather than by default, and the complete Vietnam decision manual lays that sequence out.
excerpt: Internal flights are cheap and frequent, and they are what makes a two-week Vietnam itinerary possible. Here is how the network works.
author: Editorial

title: Sleeper Bus vs Sleeper Train in Vietnam
content:
Vietnam's long distances and cheap overnight transport make the sleeper a genuine planning tool: on the right leg you cover the distance and the night's accommodation at once. The choice between bus and train is not really about money, because both are inexpensive. It is about what each one costs you in comfort and risk.

What each one is

The sleeper bus is a coach fitted with reclining berths rather than seats, usually in two tiers down three aisles. You lie down, more or less flat, in a space built to a Vietnamese frame. Shoes come off at the door and go in a bag. Routes cover essentially the whole country, including places the railway does not reach.

The sleeper train is a four or six-berth compartment on the Reunification line, air-conditioned on the better services, with a door you can close. It runs only where the single north–south railway runs, plus the Hanoi to Lao Cai branch for Sapa.

The honest comfort comparison

The train wins, and it is not close if you are tall. Sleeper bus berths are short, and anyone around six feet will spend the night with their knees bent. The train also gives you a flat berth you can sit up in, a door, and the ability to walk about. The bus is cheaper and goes more places.

The safety question

This is where the two genuinely diverge, and it is worth being plain about. Road safety is the hazard the State Department warns about at greatest length in Vietnam, and an overnight coach on mountain roads sits inside that risk in a way a train on rails does not. Operator quality varies widely, and unlike comfort it is not something you can assess from the seat.

That does not make sleeper buses unreasonable — millions of journeys happen uneventfully, and most travellers who take them are fine. It does mean the choice is not purely about comfort. Reviews will tell you about legroom and punctuality rather than maintenance or driving, so they are a weak proxy for safety; the honest position is that you cannot easily verify an operator, which is itself a reason some travellers prefer the train.

Where each makes sense

Take the train for Hanoi to Hue or Da Nang, and for Hanoi to Lao Cai if you are going to Sapa by rail. These are the legs where the railway goes exactly where you want and the overnight timing works.

Take the bus where the train does not go — Da Lat, Mui Ne, the Mekong towns, Phong Nha, Cat Ba — or where the bus is dramatically more direct. Many of these are daytime journeys, which sidesteps the overnight question entirely.

And sometimes, take neither

For the longest hops, a cheap internal flight usually beats both. Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh City by sleeper bus is over thirty hours; the same trip is a little over two hours in the air for a fare that is often not much higher than the bus. Spending a day and a half horizontal to save a modest amount is a trade worth making consciously rather than by habit.

Practical notes for either

Book ahead in high season and well ahead around Tet. Bring a layer: both buses and trains run the air conditioning hard. Bring earplugs and an eye mask. Keep your passport, cards and phone on your body rather than in a bag in the luggage hold or on a shelf. On buses, pick a berth in the middle of the vehicle, away from the wheels and the door.

Choosing a bus operator

If you are taking the bus, the operator is the decision, not the price. Look for recent reviews rather than a brand name, because quality on a given route changes as companies rotate vehicles. Book through your accommodation or a reputable agency rather than the cheapest aggregator, and be wary of a fare that undercuts everything else on the route by a wide margin.

Two specifics worth asking about: whether the service is a cabin bus with individual pods rather than open berths, which is markedly more comfortable and increasingly common on the main routes, and whether the ticket includes a transfer to the central drop-off point. Long-distance buses often terminate on the edge of a city rather than downtown, and arriving there before dawn without an onward plan is a well-known way for an otherwise fine journey to end badly.

What you are really choosing

Look at what this decision quietly settles. An overnight leg can save a hotel night and shift a journey out of daylight hours, which is the main reason it is tempting on a two-week trip — but it also fixes where you wake up, which fixes the next day's plan, and it trades a comfortable arrival for an early one. Two overnight legs might free up two daytime journeys; how much of that you actually get back depends on how well you sleep sitting up in a moving vehicle, which for most people is not very well.

How many overnight legs a trip can absorb, and which ones to spend them on, is the sort of thing that only resolves when you look at the whole route at once — which is what the complete Vietnam decision manual is for.
excerpt: Both can save a hotel night and move a long journey out of your daylight hours. They differ on comfort, on risk, and on how well you actually sleep.
author: Editorial

title: North to South or South to North: Which Way to Travel Vietnam
content:
Almost every first Vietnam trip runs the length of the country in one direction, and most people pick that direction by instinct. It is worth a few minutes of thought instead, because three separate forces pull on the answer and they do not always pull the same way.

The short version

North to south — Hanoi first, Ho Chi Minh City last — is the more common choice and the one that suits most American itineraries. South to north works better if the nonstop from the West Coast is what makes your trip affordable, or if you are travelling in a season that favours finishing in the north.

Neither is wrong. What makes the decision real is that it is effectively locked the moment you buy your international tickets, which is usually before you have finished planning anything else.

Why most people go north first

Hanoi is the harder city, and arriving there with fresh energy rather than two weeks of travel fatigue tends to work better. The north also carries the trip's most weather-sensitive items — Ha Long Bay, Sapa — so doing them early leaves room to adjust if conditions are poor. And finishing in Ho Chi Minh City means ending somewhere with the widest choice of onward flights.

What your flights decide for you

There is no nonstop from the United States to Hanoi. The only nonstop route is Vietnam Airlines from San Francisco to Ho Chi Minh City, which means a West Coast traveller who wants to avoid a connection is starting in the south whether they intended to or not.

If you are connecting anyway — which anyone flying from the East Coast or the Midwest will be — the direction is genuinely open. Open-jaw tickets into one city and out of the other are widely available and usually cost little more than a return, so there is rarely a price penalty for not backtracking.

Da Nang as a third door

If your trip is centred on Hoi An, Hue and the central beaches rather than the whole country, flying in and out of Da Nang removes the direction question entirely. It has a reasonable set of connections through the Asian hubs and sits in the middle, which turns a country-length march into a regional trip with far less transit.

Backtracking is the thing to avoid

Flying into and out of the same city on a country-length trip means either a long internal flight at the end or a rushed return up the spine. An open-jaw booking removes that entirely, and it is the single most useful thing to get right early.

What the season decides

The regions do not share a calendar, so a long trip will sit in more than one weather window whichever way it runs. An autumn trip meets the central coast's storm season at some point in either direction, so the useful response is slack around the central leg rather than a particular direction. A trip in the northern winter faces cool, grey, drizzly weather in Hanoi and Sapa, which some people would rather take at the start while they are fresh and others would rather skip entirely.

March and April are forgiving in every region, which is one reason they make the direction question much less consequential. Outside that window the season has an opinion.

What jet lag decides

Arriving from the US East Coast means landing twelve hours out of step during Eastern Standard Time and eleven during Eastern Daylight Time, after a journey that commonly runs twenty-two to twenty-six hours door to door. Whatever city you land in, the first day is largely a write-off.

That argues for starting somewhere you are happy to spend a slow day. Hanoi's Old Quarter absorbs a jet-lagged wander well. Ho Chi Minh City is hotter and harder going in that state. It is a modest consideration, but it is the one most people ignore entirely and then regret on day two.

What the two ends are actually like

They are different cities in temperament, not just geography. Hanoi is older, denser and cooler in winter, with a street plan that rewards walking and a food culture built on a handful of dishes done exactly. Ho Chi Minh City is bigger, hotter, flatter and more commercial, with wider boulevards, better nightlife and the country's most significant war museums.

Ending in Ho Chi Minh City means finishing on the easier city with the most flights out. Ending in Hanoi means finishing on the one most people find more atmospheric. Neither is a strong argument on its own, but if the other three factors cancel out, this is a reasonable tiebreaker.

What this actually settles

Look at what has just happened. Direction feels like the first creative decision of the trip, and it is mostly not a decision at all — it is the residue of things settled elsewhere. Which airports you can reach is set by the airline map. Which month you travel is usually set by work. Whether an open-jaw ticket is available at a sensible price is set by the fare market on the week you look.

By the time anyone asks themselves which way to go, those three have normally answered it. The useful move is to notice that earlier, and treat the international booking as the moment the route is chosen rather than a separate errand. Which commitments quietly foreclose which others is the subject of the complete Vietnam decision manual.
excerpt: The direction you travel Vietnam is decided by your flights, your season and your jet lag — not by preference. Here is how each one pulls.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Itinerary: One Week
content:
A week in Vietnam is a real trip, provided you accept the arithmetic early: the country is about a thousand miles long, and seven days on the ground is enough to do two regions properly. Trying for three is the mistake that turns a good week into a transit log.

What a week actually means from the US

Seven days in Vietnam is not seven days away from home. The outbound crossing eats a calendar day and the return takes most of another, so count the travel separately when you work out your leave. Door to door from the East Coast is commonly twenty-two to twenty-six hours each way with one connection.

The arrival day should be treated as a write-off. Plan a slow first afternoon and an early night rather than a sunrise departure the next morning.

The two-region rule

Pick north plus centre, or centre plus south. The north plus south combination skips the middle of the country, which is where Hoi An and Hue are, and tends to be the one people regret. Within a week, each additional region costs most of a day in transfers.

The week that works: north and centre

Day 1 — Land in Hanoi. Transfer to the Old Quarter, stay awake, walk Hoan Kiem slowly, eat bun cha, sleep early.

Day 2 — Hanoi properly. Temple of Literature, the Ho Chi Minh complex in the morning while it is open, and one of the museums in the afternoon. Egg coffee somewhere with a balcony.

Day 3 — Transfer to Ha Long or Lan Ha for an overnight cruise. Kayaking, a cave, dinner on the water.

Day 4 — Cruise morning, disembark, return to Hanoi, and fly to Da Nang on the last useful departure of the day. Transfer to Hoi An, about forty-five minutes. This is the one leg where a late flight is unavoidable, so build in the possibility of a delay rather than booking anything in Hoi An that evening.

Day 5 — Hoi An. The Ancient Town early before the crowds, a tailor fitting if you want one, An Bang beach or a cycle through the paddies in the afternoon, lanterns after nine.

Day 6 — My Son Sanctuary at opening, back to Hoi An for a second fitting, Marble Mountains if there is time.

Day 7 — A slow morning, then Da Nang airport and out.

What this version gives up

Ho Chi Minh City, the Mekong Delta and Sapa. That is a real loss and worth being honest about: you are not seeing the south at all. The compensation is that nothing in the week is rushed and only one internal flight is needed.

The alternative: centre and south

If you want Ho Chi Minh City and the war history, invert it. Two days in Ho Chi Minh City with the War Remnants Museum and Reunification Palace, a Cu Chi or Cho Lon day, then fly to Da Nang for three days in Hoi An and Hue. Same shape, same single internal flight, different half of the country. The Mekong is deliberately not in this version; see below.

This version is warmer year-round and less weather-dependent, which makes it the safer choice for a trip in the northern winter.

The internal flight is not optional

Hanoi to Da Nang is about an hour and a quarter in the air against fifteen to seventeen hours by rail. On a seven-day trip the train is a day you do not have. Book the flight early in the day rather than late, because low-cost carriers accumulate delay as the schedule runs on.

Indicatively, as of October 2026, a one-way internal hop on a main route commonly falls somewhere around $30 to $80 booked a few weeks out. Check live fares rather than planning around that.

If you only have a week, what to skip

Sapa is the most commonly attempted and most commonly regretted addition. It is five to six hours each way from Hanoi, which on a seven-day trip means two travel days for one day in the mountains. Ninh Binh, two hours away, delivers a comparable landscape for a fraction of the time.

The Mekong Delta has the same problem from the other end. The packaged day trip out of Ho Chi Minh City is the weakest day most people have in Vietnam, and the version worth doing needs an overnight in Can Tho for the dawn floating market. On a week, leave it.

And what to protect

Keep the slow morning in Hoi An and the slow evening in Hanoi. The complaint people tend to have about a one-week Vietnam trip is rarely that it missed a city — it is that every day started with an alarm.

Why one week is the hardest itinerary to build

Notice what this week is actually made of. Almost none of the work was choosing what to see — the good things in Vietnam are not in dispute. All of it was choosing what to give up, and then giving it up early enough that the rest of the trip could be built properly around the gap.

That is the uncomfortable part. Most people plan by addition, fitting in one more place, and end up with a week where everything is present and nothing is enjoyed. Planning by subtraction is harder because it means deciding what this particular trip is not for. Working out what to cut, and in what order, is what the complete Vietnam decision manual is built around.
excerpt: Seven days on the ground is enough for two regions done well, or three done badly. Here is the week that works, and what it costs you to try for more.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Itinerary: Two Weeks
content:
Fourteen days on the ground is the length at which Vietnam stops feeling rushed. You can run the country north to south, spend real time in three regions, and still keep slack for the weather to misbehave. There are still trade-offs — they are just no longer brutal. Here is the shape that works and the decisions inside it.

The frame

Fly into Hanoi, out of Ho Chi Minh City, open-jaw. Two internal flights — Hanoi to Hue or Da Nang, then Da Nang to Ho Chi Minh City — with the Hue to Da Nang leg done by train. Count the travel days separately from the fourteen: the crossing eats a calendar day each way.

The direction matters less at this length than at seven days, because two weeks absorbs a mistake. If your flights point you south-to-north, run the same plan backwards.

Days 1 to 3 — Hanoi

Arrive, write off the afternoon, and give the city two full days. Hoan Kiem and the Old Quarter on foot, the Temple of Literature, the Ho Chi Minh complex in a morning, and one of the Vietnamese Women's Museum or Hoa Lo Prison. Eat bun cha at lunch and pho at breakfast, not the other way round.

Days 4 to 5 — the northern choice

This is the first real fork. Sapa, five to six hours by road, gives you terraced mountains and a valley homestay. Ninh Binh, two hours away, gives you the same karst landscape as Ha Long but on rivers, and costs you half the travel. Doing both inside two weeks is possible and leaves the rest of the trip tight.

Ninh Binh is the better choice for most first visits: two hours each way against five or six, for a landscape that is extraordinary in its own right rather than a lesser version of anything. Sapa is the better choice if mountains and trekking are why you are coming, and it is worth the travel if they are.

Days 6 to 7 — Ha Long or Lan Ha

An overnight cruise from Hanoi, back the following afternoon. Lan Ha Bay, reached via Cat Ba, has the same karst scenery with a fraction of the boats and is worth asking for by name. Then an evening flight south.

Days 8 to 9 — Hue

Fly Hanoi to Hue, or to Da Nang and transfer. The Imperial City takes a morning, two of the royal tombs take an afternoon, and the DMZ — Vinh Moc tunnels, Khe Sanh, the Ben Hai river — takes a full and sobering day. Hue is also where the food changes: bun bo Hue, and the steamed rice-cake plates.

Day 10 — the Hai Van Pass

Hue to Da Nang by train, about two and a half to three hours along the coast and over the pass. It is one of the best rail stretches in Southeast Asia, costs very little, and replaces a transfer you would make anyway. Sit on the right heading south.

Days 11 to 12 — Hoi An

The Ancient Town before eight and after nine, My Son Sanctuary at opening, An Bang beach in between, and a tailor if you want one — allow two fittings, which means arriving with time.

Days 13 to 14 — Ho Chi Minh City

Fly down. The War Remnants Museum first and early; it will shape the rest of the day. Reunification Palace, Cho Lon in the late afternoon, street seafood in District 4 at night. Use the last morning for Cu Chi or the markets, then fly out.

The two things people cut that they should not

The Mekong Delta usually gets dropped, and the version that survives — a packaged day trip from Ho Chi Minh City — is widely reported as a disappointment. If the Delta matters to you, it needs an overnight in Can Tho for the dawn floating market, which means taking two days from somewhere else. That is a real trade, and worth making consciously rather than discovering on day twelve.

The DMZ day out of Hue is the other. Alongside Cu Chi in the south, it is one of the few places the war is on the ground rather than in a museum, and it is the less crowded and more sobering of the two.

Where the slack lives

Keep a spare half-day in the centre if you are travelling between September and November, because that is the central coast's storm season and boat trips and beach days are the first things cancelled. Keep the last night near your departure airport rather than two hours from it.

What makes this plan hold together

Look at the joints rather than the days. The cruise's return time decides whether the flight south is that evening or the next morning, which decides whether day eight starts in Hue or in an airport. Putting Hue before Hoi An turns the Hai Van crossing into a scenic train ride; putting it after turns the same journey into backtracking. Each choice is small, and each one sets the terms of the next.

That is what distinguishes a two-week plan that works from one with the same list of places in a different order. The days are easy. The joints are where a trip is won or lost, and the complete Vietnam decision manual is organised around them.
excerpt: Two weeks is the length Vietnam is built for. Here is the north-to-south run, what it includes, and the two places most people wrongly cut.
author: Editorial

title: Crossing the Street in Vietnam (Hanoi/HCMC Traffic)
content:
The first time you stand at a kerb in Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City and look at an unbroken river of motorbikes, the gap you are waiting for is never going to come. That is the first thing to understand: you are not waiting for a gap. You are joining the flow.

The technique

Step off at a slow, steady, predictable pace and keep going, watching the traffic as you move. The system works because riders who have seen you can steer around a path they can predict; what breaks it is unpredictability, since stopping halfway or darting forward forces anyone who had already adjusted to re-solve the problem at close range. It is a technique for improving your odds, not a guarantee that every rider has noticed you — which is why you keep looking.

Keep watching the traffic as you go. Predictability is the technique, not a guarantee, and the point of watching is to see the one rider who has not seen you.

What does not apply

Cars, buses and trucks do not flow around you the way scooters do. They are heavier, slower to change line, and often cannot see you. Wait those out. The technique is for the two-wheeled river, not for everything on the road.

Learning it in the first hour

Cross alongside a local. Stand near someone who is about to cross, go when they go, and stay on their downstream side. Two or three crossings of that and the rhythm makes sense. It is the fastest way to acquire the nerve, and nobody minds.

Pick your first crossing deliberately: a wide street with a median gives you a halfway refuge, and a quieter side street in the morning is gentler than a six-lane junction at six in the evening.

Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are not the same problem

Hanoi's Old Quarter has narrow streets, slower speeds and a very high density of two-wheelers, which makes it intimidating but forgiving: everything is moving at a pace you can read. Crossing there is mostly a question of nerve.

Ho Chi Minh City's boulevards are wider and faster, with more cars mixed into the flow and longer distances to cover in the open. The technique is the same but the margin for error is smaller, and a median refuge is worth walking to find. If you are nervous, learn the skill in Hanoi and arrive in the south already fluent.

Where the rules differ from home

Green pedestrian signals exist and are not a guarantee of an empty road — right-turning traffic generally continues, and motorbikes may cross regardless. Treat a green light as improved odds rather than permission.

Pavements are frequently parked solid with motorbikes, so pedestrians walk in the road as a matter of course. Walk with the traffic beside you rather than against it where you can, and expect scooters on the pavement too; this is normal rather than aggressive.

Phones

Do not cross reading your phone, and more importantly do not stand near the kerb reading it. Petty theft is the common crime against visitors in Vietnamese cities, and snatching a phone from a moving motorbike is its signature form — a stationary person holding one at the roadside is an easy mark. Stop with your back to a wall if you need to look at a map.

Grab, and when walking is the wrong answer

Distances in both cities are longer than a map suggests, and the heat makes a two-mile walk in July considerably less pleasant than the same walk in a temperate climate. Ride-hailing fares are low enough that taking a car or a motorbike taxi for anything over about a mile is a sensible default rather than a luxury, particularly in the middle of the day.

A GrabBike — riding pillion behind a driver — is also the fastest way across a congested city and the cheapest. You are handed a helmet, and the driver is navigating traffic he reads fluently. It feels alarming for about four minutes and then becomes the obvious way to get around.

At night, and in the rain

Both make you harder to see and make riders less willing to slow. Wet roads mean longer stopping distances on bald tyres, and a tropical downpour cuts visibility to very little. Wear something light-coloured at night if you can, and be more conservative about which crossings you take on.

Walking with children or limited mobility

The flow technique assumes you can maintain a steady pace and change nothing. With a small child, hold them on the downstream side and cross with a group rather than alone. With limited mobility or anything that makes your pace unpredictable, use signalled crossings where they exist, cross with locals, and do not be shy about using a taxi or Grab for a distance you would otherwise walk — fares are low enough that it is a reasonable default rather than an indulgence.

The wider point

Traffic is the part of Vietnam that most alarms American visitors on arrival and the part they adapt to fastest. Within three days the river stops looking like chaos and starts looking like a system, because it is one.

What is worth keeping in proportion is which road risks actually matter. Crossing on foot, done sensibly, is a skill you acquire in a day. Riding a motorbike yourself is a different question entirely — a US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, and that has consequences for your insurance as well as your legality.
excerpt: Vietnamese traffic looks impassable and is not. The technique is simple, and the mistakes that cause accidents are the instinctive ones.
author: Editorial

title: Overland Border Crossings: Vietnam to Cambodia and Laos
content:
Vietnam shares long land borders with Cambodia, Laos and China, and the crossings into the first two are a normal part of a Southeast Asia trip. The thing that goes wrong is almost never the journey. It is the paperwork, and specifically which gate your visa is valid at.

The rule that decides everything

A Vietnamese e-visa works only at designated border gates. There are 83 of them since December 2025 — 17 airports, 27 land crossings and 39 seaports — and that covers every international airport in Vietnam. Gate eligibility is therefore never the obstacle when you fly, though your visa still has to be valid and name the port you actually use.

Land is different. Only some land crossings are on the list, so a crossing that exists and is open to foreigners is not necessarily one your e-visa works at. Check the specific gate before you commit to a route.

And a second rule people miss

Separately from gate eligibility, your e-visa names the entry point you selected on the application, and that selection is binding. If you intend to come back to Vietnam after Cambodia or Laos, you need entry permission that covers the return — either a multiple-entry visa, or a fresh single-entry one — and it has to name the gate you will actually use. Both rules have to be satisfied, not just one.

Vietnam to Cambodia

Moc Bai, between Ho Chi Minh City and Phnom Penh, is the busiest and easiest. Direct buses run the route in roughly six to seven hours including the border formalities, and the bus company walks passengers through the process. Cambodia issues visas on arrival to most nationalities including Americans, or you can obtain an e-visa in advance.

In the Mekong Delta, Ha Tien and the Chau Doc river route are the scenic alternatives, with the Chau Doc to Phnom Penh boat a genuinely pleasant way to travel. Both are smaller and slower.

Vietnam to Laos

The Lao Bao crossing on the old Route 9 from Dong Ha, and Nam Can from Vinh, are the usual options. These are long journeys on mountain roads, and the bus services across them have a mixed reputation for comfort and timekeeping. Laos issues visas on arrival at the main international crossings.

Be realistic about the time. Hanoi or Hue to Vientiane or Luang Prabang overland is a full day and often more, against a short flight. People do it for the scenery and the cost, not the convenience.

What the crossing itself is like

You exit one country and enter the next at two separate windows with a walk in between. Have your passport, your Vietnamese exit documentation and your onward visa or the fee for a visa on arrival. Keep small denominations of US dollars for the Cambodian and Lao fees.

Informal fees are sometimes requested at the smaller crossings. The official position is that the posted fee is the fee; asking for a receipt usually resolves it, and the organised bus services generally handle the process in a way that avoids the question.

Timing the crossing

Land borders keep their own hours and they are shorter than you expect — most close in the early evening and some take a long lunch. Arriving at a remote crossing an hour after it shuts means a night in a border town with very little in it.

Build the crossing into the middle of a day rather than the end of one, and confirm the current hours locally rather than from an article, because they change and the smaller gates change most. The organised through-buses are scheduled around the hours, which is one of the better arguments for taking one instead of assembling the journey yourself.

Leaving Vietnam needs valid status too

Vietnam requires a valid visa, a residence card or Immigration Department approval to exit as well as to enter. An overstayed visa is therefore a departure problem at a land border just as much as at an airport, and it is harder to resolve from a remote crossing.

The China border

Crossings into China exist, at Huu Nghi near Lang Son and at Lao Cai, and they are used by travellers continuing north. They are a different proposition from Cambodia and Laos: China requires a visa arranged well in advance for most nationalities including Americans, with no visa on arrival at these crossings, and the paperwork needs to be in place before you travel to the border.

If China is part of the plan, treat it as a separate project rather than an extension of a Vietnam trip, and confirm both the Chinese visa and the Vietnamese gate eligibility before fixing any dates.

Whether to do it at all

For Cambodia from Ho Chi Minh City, the overland route is genuinely competitive: six or seven hours door to door against a flight that, with two airport transfers, is not much quicker and costs more. For Laos, the flight usually wins unless the journey itself is the point.

The reason this matters beyond the day itself is that a loop out of Vietnam and back changes what you need from your Vietnamese visa — multiple entry, or a second application, named for the gate you will return through. A one-way exit into Cambodia at the end of a trip needs none of that. Which shape your trip has is therefore worth settling before you apply rather than after, and that ordering problem is what the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: Crossing into Cambodia or Laos by land is straightforward if your visa is valid at that gate — and impossible if it is not.
author: Editorial

title: Hanoi Travel Guide for First-Timers
content:
Hanoi is the harder of Vietnam's two big cities and the one most visitors end up preferring. It is older, denser, cooler in winter, and organised around a lake and a tangle of trading streets that have been doing the same jobs for centuries. Three days is enough to stop feeling lost.

How the city is laid out

Hoan Kiem Lake is the centre of gravity and the thing to orient yourself by. North of it is the Old Quarter, a dense grid of narrow streets historically organised by trade — one street for tin, one for silk, one for votive paper — and still partly organised that way. South and east is the French Quarter, with wider boulevards, the Opera House and the grander hotels.

West of that sits Ba Dinh, the political district, where the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum complex and the embassies are. Further northwest, around West Lake, is Tay Ho, a leafier expat-and-cafe neighbourhood that is genuinely pleasant and genuinely far from everything else.

The first thing to understand

Distances look walkable on a map and are, but the pavements are frequently parked solid with motorbikes, so pedestrians walk in the road. That is ordinary here rather than reckless, and traffic generally flows around people who move predictably — though it is a technique for improving your odds, not a guarantee. Give yourself a day to acquire the rhythm.

Three days, loosely

Day one: walk. Hoan Kiem at six in the morning, when the lakeside fills with exercise classes and badminton, is a different city from Hoan Kiem at noon. Then the Old Quarter on foot with no particular destination. Egg coffee somewhere with a balcony.

Day two: the Ho Chi Minh complex in the morning, because the mausoleum keeps short hours and closes for a period each year — check the current schedule before going, as the rest of the complex does not always follow it. Then the Temple of Literature, Vietnam's first university, founded in 1070 and the calmest half-hour in the city.

Day three: one museum and one escape. The Vietnamese Women's Museum is the best-curated in the city. Hoa Lo Prison, the so-called Hanoi Hilton, presents its American POW period from the Vietnamese side, and going in knowing that is part of why it is worth seeing.

Eating

Hanoi's food is its real argument. Pho here is the plainer northern original — clear broth, no basil plate, no hoisin — and it is a breakfast dish eaten at shops that sell nothing else. Bun cha, grilled pork in a bowl of dressed broth with cold noodles, is the lunchtime dish and the one Hanoi is proudest of.

Beyond those: cha ca, turmeric-and-dill fish cooked at your table; banh cuon, steamed rice rolls; and egg coffee, a Hanoi invention that is far better than it sounds. Eat where there is a queue of locals and high turnover.

Practicalities

Grab is the default for any distance, and a GrabBike through traffic is both the fastest way across the city and the most memorable. The metro exists but serves commuter corridors rather than the sights. Carry cash: street food, markets and small cafes are cash-only.

The weather nobody warns Americans about

Hanoi has four real seasons, including a genuinely cold winter. December to February runs in the 50s and 60s Fahrenheit with a persistent grey drizzle, and visitors who packed for Southeast Asia in the abstract arrive badly dressed. Summer is the opposite — 90s with high humidity and the heaviest rain of the year.

One more consideration: the State Department notes that air pollution is a significant problem in Vietnam’s major cities, especially Hanoi, If you are asthmatic or travelling with someone who is, check a live air-quality reading for your dates rather than any figure printed in an article.

What Hanoi is like compared with Ho Chi Minh City

Worth knowing if you are doing both. Hanoi is older, denser and more reserved; Ho Chi Minh City is bigger, hotter, flatter and more openly commercial. Hanoi's food culture is narrower and deeper — a handful of dishes done exactly — while the south is sweeter, more varied and more influenced by the Mekong.

Plenty of visitors arrive expecting to prefer the south and leave preferring the north. The reason usually offered is that Hanoi is a city you walk and Ho Chi Minh City is a city you ride through.

Safety, in proportion

Hanoi is a safe city by any ordinary measure. Petty theft is the common risk, with phone snatching from passing motorbikes its signature form, so do not walk and scroll. Emergency numbers are 113 for traffic police, 115 for an ambulance, though be aware they are frequently answered only in Vietnamese. For anything serious, Hanoi's international hospitals are the route most visitors are advised to take.

The scams that exist are mostly price-ambiguity rather than theft: an unsolicited shoe repair, a cyclo quoted per person rather than per trip. Agreeing the number before anything begins removes the ambiguity these rely on.
excerpt: Hanoi is a thousand-year-old street plan still working as one. Here is how to read it on a first visit, and what to expect.
author: Editorial

title: Best Things to Do in Hanoi
content:
Hanoi rewards wandering more than ticking off, but there is a real short list underneath the wandering. These are the things worth building a day around, with a plain note on each about what you are actually getting.

Hoan Kiem Lake and the Old Quarter

Not an attraction so much as the city's organising principle, and the single best use of a first morning. The lake at six is full of exercise classes, badminton and tai chi; by evening it is couples and ice cream. Ngoc Son Temple sits on an island reached by a red bridge and takes twenty minutes.

At weekends the streets around the lake close to traffic and the whole district changes character — street games, music, families. If your dates include a weekend, keep an evening for it.

Temple of Literature

Vietnam's first university, founded in 1070, and the best place in the city to see pre-colonial Vietnamese architecture in a sequence of courtyards. It is calm in a way almost nothing else in central Hanoi is. An hour is enough.

The Ho Chi Minh complex

The mausoleum, the stilt house where he actually lived, the Presidential Palace grounds and the One Pillar Pagoda sit together and are done as one walk. The mausoleum has limited morning hours, closes one or two days a week, and shuts entirely for a period each year for maintenance — check before going.

A strict dress code applies — shorts and bare shoulders are not accepted, hats come off, and phones and cameras are not permitted inside the viewing chamber. Rules are enforced and have changed before, so check the current ones rather than relying on this paragraph. The queue generally moves quickly and the room itself takes a minute or two.

The two museums that matter

The Vietnamese Women's Museum is consistently the best-curated museum in the city and the one that most reframes the country for a visitor — it covers marriage customs, street vendors and the role of women in the war with real depth. Two hours.

Hoa Lo Prison, the Hanoi Hilton, is the other. Its account of the French colonial period is harrowing and its account of the American POW period is partisan. Both halves are worth your time, and knowing which is which going in is the point.

Train Street, with a caveat

The narrow residential stretch where the railway runs within arm's reach of cafe tables is genuinely striking. Access has been restricted and reopened repeatedly on safety grounds, and the current rules change — check locally rather than planning around it.

Water puppets, and whether to bother

The Thang Long Water Puppet Theatre runs a short show of an art form that originated in the villages of the northern delta, performed by puppeteers standing waist-deep behind a screen. It is squarely aimed at visitors and it is also very old. An hour, and worth it once.

Getting out onto the water and the hills

Two half-days inside the city limits are easy to miss. West Lake is large enough to cycle around in a leisurely couple of hours, passing Tran Quoc Pagoda — the oldest in Hanoi, on a causeway over the water — and a string of lakeside cafes that make a good late-afternoon stop.

The Long Bien Bridge, a French-built steel span from the turn of the twentieth century that was bombed repeatedly during the war, is still in use and can be walked. Underneath it, on the sandbanks in the middle of the Red River, there are banana plantations and market gardens that feel a very long way from the Old Quarter ten minutes behind you.

A cooking class, if you have four days

Most start at a market, which is the useful half — someone explaining what the herbs are and why northern cooking uses fewer of them than southern does changes how you eat for the rest of the trip. The cooking itself is secondary.

Eat as an activity

Eat as an activity

The most memorable thing most people do in Hanoi is not on a list of sights. Bun cha at lunch, pho at breakfast, bia hoi — the fresh draught beer poured on street corners in the late afternoon — and egg coffee in a room above the street. A guided street-food walk on a first evening is one of the few organised activities that reliably pays for itself.

The quieter alternatives

If the main list feels crowded, three places tend to be much quieter. Quan Thanh Temple, near West Lake, is a Taoist temple with a large bronze statue and far fewer visitors than the lakeside sites. The Fine Arts Museum has an excellent collection of lacquer and silk painting in a colonial building, and is usually near-empty. And the Long Bien Bridge, a French-built span repeatedly bombed during the war and patched ever since, can be walked across for a view of the river and the banana fields below it.

Day trips

Ninh Binh, two hours away, is the strongest: karst landscape on rivers rather than sea, reached by rowed boat. Ha Long Bay as a day trip means a long road transfer in each direction for a few hours afloat, which is why most people who have done both recommend the overnight cruise. The Perfume Pagoda is a boat ride and a climb, and it draws very large crowds during its spring pilgrimage festival in the months after Tet. Outside that period it is far quieter.
excerpt: The short list that earns its place in two or three days, with the honest note on which ones are worth the queue.
author: Editorial

title: Where to Stay in Hanoi
content:
Where you sleep in Hanoi changes the trip more than it does in most cities, because the Old Quarter is both the best-located neighbourhood and the loudest. Here are the four areas worth considering and who each one actually suits.

The Old Quarter

The default, and the right default for a first visit of two or three nights. The central sights are on foot: Hoan Kiem is a few minutes away, the street food is at the door, and you are inside the thing you came to see. Accommodation runs from hostel dorms to small boutique hotels, and the value is remarkable by American standards.

The cost is noise. Scooters start before six, the streets are commercial all day, and the bar strip around Ta Hien runs loud until late. Ask for a room at the back and above the second floor, and look at where the hotel sits relative to Ta Hien before booking, since the bar corner carries further than its footprint suggests.

Who it suits

First-timers, short stays, anyone who wants to walk everywhere, and anyone who would rather be woken at six than take a taxi to dinner.

The French Quarter

South and east of the lake: wider streets, colonial architecture, the Opera House, and the city's grander hotels including the Metropole. Ten to fifteen minutes on foot from Hoan Kiem, which is close enough to walk in and far enough to sleep.

This is the right answer for a second visit, for anyone noise-sensitive, and for travellers who want a more comfortable base without losing walkability. The trade is that the immediate streets are quieter in the evening — you walk to the life rather than opening a window onto it.

Tay Ho and West Lake

Northwest of the centre, around a large lake: leafy, low-rise, full of cafes and expatriates, and the most pleasant place in Hanoi to spend an unhurried day. The air feels better and the pace is slower.

It is also genuinely far. Each outing to the Old Quarter means a Grab ride of fifteen minutes or more, and considerably longer in peak traffic, which adds up across a short trip. Tay Ho makes sense for stays of a week or more, for families, and for anyone working while travelling. It is the wrong choice for three nights of sightseeing.

Ba Dinh

The embassy and government district, west of the Old Quarter around the Ho Chi Minh complex. Calm, green, wide pavements that are actually walkable, and noticeably fewer tourists. Hotels here are often better value for the standard than their equivalents near the lake.

It is a reasonable compromise if the Old Quarter is full or if quiet matters more than immediacy, and it puts the mausoleum complex on your doorstep for its early opening hours.

Two areas worth ruling out

Anywhere out by the airport. Noi Bai is forty-five minutes to an hour from the centre and the surrounding area has little to offer a visitor. For most early departures a pre-dawn Grab from the city is the better trade; a genuinely pre-6am flight is the exception worth reconsidering.

And the far side of the Red River, in Long Bien district. Listings there look central on a map and are cheap, but you are across a bridge from everything and the crossings are congested at exactly the hours you will want to use them.

How many nights

Three is the number most itineraries land on and it works: one to arrive and acclimatise, two to see the city. Two nights is workable if you have been to Vietnam before. Four or more makes Tay Ho a genuine option and gives room for a Ninh Binh day trip without cutting anything.

What to check before booking

What to check before booking

Ask which floor the room is on and whether there is a lift, because many Old Quarter buildings are tall, narrow and stair-only. Ask whether the room has a window — a surprising number of cheap rooms in the Old Quarter do not, and the price often does not signal it.

Check the walking distance to Hoan Kiem on a map rather than trusting a listing that says central, and look at where the nearest bar street is. In winter, check that the room has heating as well as air conditioning; Hanoi's damp cold catches both travellers and hotels out.

The registration point

Under Vietnamese rules every visitor must have their overnight address registered with the local police. Hotels do this automatically from your passport at check-in, which is why they ask for it and sometimes keep it briefly. In an Airbnb or a private homestay the host is responsible, and it is worth confirming when you book that they handle it.

Prices, in rough terms

Hanoi is inexpensive by American standards at every tier: a dorm bed costs a few dollars, a clean private room in a small Old Quarter hotel is a modest two-figure sum, and even a well-reviewed four-star in the French Quarter sits far below the equivalent US rate. Rates rise around Tet and the April–May holiday pair. Check live rates for your own dates rather than planning around any figure in an article.
excerpt: Four neighbourhoods, four different trips. The Old Quarter is the obvious answer and not always the right one.
author: Editorial

title: Hanoi Old Quarter Guide
content:
The Old Quarter is the reason most people remember Hanoi. It is a thousand-year-old commercial district that never stopped being commercial, and understanding its underlying logic turns an overwhelming tangle into something you can navigate.

The thirty-six streets

The district grew as a cluster of craft guilds, each occupying its own street and each named for what it sold. The prefix Hang means merchandise, and what follows is the product: Hang Bac is silver, Hang Gai silk, Hang Ma votive paper and festival decorations, Hang Thiec tin.

Much of that survives. Walk Hang Thiec and you will pass a row of metalworkers hammering; Hang Ma is still a street of red and gold paper goods and becomes spectacular before Tet and Mid-Autumn. Others have turned over to tourism, but the pattern holds often enough to be useful: if you see one shop selling something, the next six will sell it too.

Navigating

Street names change every block, which makes the district feel larger and more confusing than its actual footprint. Use the lake as your southern anchor and St Joseph's Cathedral as a western one. Beyond that, being briefly lost here is the point rather than a problem.

What to actually see

Dong Xuan Market at the northern edge is the district's wholesale heart, three floors of fabric, household goods and dried everything. It is a working market rather than a souvenir one, which is what makes it worth an hour.

Bach Ma Temple, the oldest in the quarter, is a small dark hall on Hang Buom that most people walk past. The Heritage House at 87 Ma May is a restored merchant's home that shows how these narrow tube houses actually worked — deep, thin plots with internal courtyards, built to a shape that made the most of very narrow street frontage.

St Joseph's Cathedral, neo-Gothic and weathered almost black, anchors a square that has become one of the better places in the city to sit with a drink in the late afternoon.

The tube houses

Look at the shape of the buildings and the district's history becomes legible. Frontage onto the street was taxed, so merchants built narrow and deep — plots two or three metres wide running twenty or more metres back, with internal light wells and courtyards to keep the far end habitable. The usual explanation offered locally is that street frontage was taxed.

You can still walk through several. The restored house at 87 Ma May is the obvious one, but many shops are tube houses with a family living behind and above the business, which is why a cafe entrance sometimes looks like somebody's corridor. It usually is.

The rhythm of the day

The quarter runs on a schedule worth knowing. Before seven it belongs to pho shops and exercise; mid-morning the shops open and the deliveries clog the lanes; the early afternoon is the quietest it gets; from five the bia hoi corners fill and the night market sets up at weekends; after ten the shutters come down street by street.

Seeing it twice — once at six in the morning and once at nine at night — tells you more about Hanoi than any museum.

Bia hoi corner

The junction of Ta Hien and Luong Ngoc Quyen is the famous one: fresh draught beer brewed that morning, served on plastic stools on the pavement for less than a dollar. It is crowded, loud and genuinely good fun early in the evening, and it is why you do not want a bedroom window directly above it.

Eating your way through

The Old Quarter packs an extraordinary amount of good cheap food into a small area. Bun cha at lunch, banh cuon in the morning, cha ca on the street named after it, and egg coffee in an upstairs room reached through what looks like somebody's hallway — several of the best cafes are hidden behind shops.

The selection rule is turnover: a queue of locals and food cooked in front of you. Tidiness is a weaker signal than throughput.

Where the quarter ends

The Old Quarter is smaller than it feels — roughly a kilometre across — and knowing its edges helps. Dong Xuan Market marks the north, the lake the south, Hang Da and the cathedral the west, and the river embankment the east. Step over any of those and the streets tend to widen and the density to drop, often with prices following.

That matters practically: walk five minutes east towards the river and you are in an ordinary residential Hanoi with ordinary Hanoi prices, which is often where the better pho is.

Staying here, briefly

Sleeping in the quarter puts everything at the door and the noise in the room. Scooters start before six and the bar corner runs late. Ask for a room at the back, above the second floor, and check how many streets separate you from Ta Hien before you book.

Shopping, and the price question

Shopping, and the price question

Hang Gai sells silk and tailoring, Hang Bac silver, and the streets around Dong Xuan sell everything else. Bargaining is expected in markets and with street vendors, not in shops with marked prices.

The common complaint is not dishonesty but ambiguity — a service performed before a price is agreed, then an aggressive number. Settling the price first, in dong, removes the ambiguity that makes it possible.
excerpt: Thirty-six streets, each once dedicated to a trade, still largely doing the same jobs. Here is how to read the district rather than get lost in it.
author: Editorial

title: Getting Around Hanoi
content:
Hanoi is more walkable than it first looks and more congested than any map suggests. The short version: walk the central district, use Grab for everything beyond it, and do not plan around the metro.

Walking

The Old Quarter, Hoan Kiem and the French Quarter form a compact area you can cross on foot in twenty minutes, and walking is the only way to see any of it properly. The complication is that pavements are routinely parked solid with motorbikes, so pedestrians walk in the road as a matter of course.

That sounds alarming and is normal. Traffic flows around people who move at a steady, predictable pace. Walk with the traffic beside you where you can, and expect scooters on the pavement too.

Crossing

Step out at a slow constant pace, keep going, keep watching. Riders who have seen you can steer around a path they can predict, which is why stopping halfway causes problems — but you keep watching because not every rider has seen you.
