Carry a small bag on your front rather than your back, and do not take a GrabBike with a large suitcase — that is what GrabCar is for. In rain, the driver will usually produce a poncho that covers you both.

Airport runs

Grab works from all the main airports, with designated pickup zones. For a very early departure, consider booking a car through your hotel the night before instead — at four in the morning the app can be thin, and a prearranged car waiting outside is worth the small premium.

One thing it does not solve

Renting a motorbike to ride yourself is a different matter entirely: a US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, and riding without a Vietnamese licence is illegal. GrabBike puts you on two wheels with a local at the handlebars, which is the legal version of the same experience.
excerpt: Grab is probably the most useful app to install before you land. Here is how it works, what it costs and where it does not.
author: Editorial

title: Ho Chi Minh City Travel Guide for First-Timers
content:
Ho Chi Minh City is Vietnam's largest city and its commercial engine, and it makes a very different impression from Hanoi. It is hotter, flatter, louder and more openly modern, and for an American visitor it is also where the war is least avoidable. Two or three days covers the essentials.

Saigon or Ho Chi Minh City

Both names are in everyday use. The official name has been Ho Chi Minh City since 1976; Saigon survives in ordinary speech, in the airport code SGN, in business names, and as the common shorthand for District 1 specifically. Using either is unremarkable.

How the city is organised

Districts are numbered, and District 1 is the centre: the Opera House, Ben Thanh Market, the main hotels, Dong Khoi's shops and most of what a short visit covers. District 3 sits immediately northwest, quieter and leafier. District 5 is Cho Lon, the historic Chinese quarter. Across the river in what was District 2 is Thao Dien, long established as the main expatriate neighbourhood. District 4, small and central, has a reputation for street food.

Almost everything a first visit wants is in District 1 and walkable within it, though the heat and the distances make a Grab the sensible default for anything over a few blocks.

The three days that work

Day one: the War Remnants Museum in the morning, early, while you have the energy for it. Then Reunification Palace, ten minutes away, which is the same history from inside the government that lost. Finish somewhere with air conditioning.

Day two: Cu Chi Tunnels as a half or full day, or Cho Lon if you would rather stay in the city. Cho Lon is the better choice for anyone who has had enough of the war by then — Thien Hau temple, the herb streets and Binh Tay market make a good slow afternoon.

Day three: the Mekong Delta, or a slower city day — the Central Post Office, Notre-Dame Cathedral, the Fine Arts Museum, and a rooftop at dusk.

Eating

Southern food is sweeter and more herb-heavy than northern. Pho here is usually served with a plate of bean sprouts, basil, lime and sauces on the side, which is not the northern style. Com tam, broken rice with grilled pork, is the city's workhorse lunch. Banh mi has a strong claim to being at its best here, and hu tieu, the southern noodle soup, is the one to order in Cho Lon.

The eating happens on the street, on low plastic stools, and the best of it is in Districts 4 and 5 rather than the tourist streets of District 1.

The heat

Ho Chi Minh City is warm year round, typically in the 80s and 90s Fahrenheit with high humidity, and there is no cool season — only a dry one from December to April and a wet one from May to November. Wet season rain is usually a heavy afternoon hour rather than an all-day event.

Adopt the local rhythm: start early, take the middle of the day slowly and indoors, and go out again after four.

Safety and the city's one real annoyance

The State Department notes that petty crime is common, especially in popular tourist locations, and in Ho Chi Minh City the signature form is bag and phone snatching from a moving motorbike. It is the single thing worth adjusting your habits for: do not walk while looking at your phone, keep bags on the traffic-away side, and stop with your back to a wall if you need to check a map.

Beyond that, the usual big-city precautions apply. Grab at least removes the taxi-fare question, since the price is agreed before you get in.

Getting in from the airport

Tan Son Nhat is unusually close — about four miles from District 1 — and still takes thirty to fifty minutes in traffic. Grab pickup is on the upper level rather than outside arrivals, which catches people out; follow the signs up rather than accepting the first offer at the kerb.

A day out of the city

Two options dominate. Cu Chi Tunnels, an hour and a half to two hours northwest, is the war site most visitors add. The Mekong Delta is the other, though the packaged day trip from the city is widely described as thin — the version worth doing is an overnight to Can Tho for the dawn floating market.

If you have one spare day and want neither, Cho Lon fills it better than most people expect, and it costs you a Grab fare rather than a coach.

How it compares with Hanoi

Most itineraries include both, and they are worth approaching differently. Hanoi is older, denser and best walked; Ho Chi Minh City is bigger, hotter and best ridden through. Hanoi's food culture is narrower and deeper, the south's broader and sweeter. Hanoi's sights are mostly pre-colonial and colonial; Ho Chi Minh City's are mostly twentieth-century and about the war.

Visitors often expect to prefer the south and leave preferring the north, which says more about what a short visit shows you than about either city.
excerpt: Bigger, hotter and more commercial than Hanoi, and the place the war is hardest to look away from. How to read Saigon on a first visit.
author: Editorial

title: Best Things to Do in Ho Chi Minh City
content:
Ho Chi Minh City's sights are concentrated and mostly twentieth-century. Two of them are more affecting than anything else in Vietnam for an American visitor, and the rest of this list is what to do with the days around them.

War Remnants Museum

The site most frequently singled out by visitors afterwards. It documents the war from the Vietnamese side, with photography, military hardware in the courtyard, and rooms on Agent Orange and on photographers killed covering the conflict. Allow around two hours; the Requiem photography exhibition is the part many people mention.

It presents a national account and makes no attempt at American balance, which is worth knowing going in rather than discovering halfway round. Go early, go first, and do not schedule anything demanding afterwards.

Reunification Palace

The former South Vietnamese presidential palace, left largely as it was in April 1975 — the cabinet room, the president's quarters, and the command bunker in the basement with its maps and radio equipment. The gates that a tank crashed through are the image that ended the war on television.

It is the counterpart to the museum: the same event from inside the government that lost. The two together in one morning are a lot, and worth it.

Cho Lon, the Chinese quarter

District 5, and a part of the city many short visits skip. Thien Hau Temple, hung with spiral incense coils, is the one to see. Around it are the herbal medicine streets, the lantern makers, and Binh Tay Market, which is a working wholesale market rather than a souvenir one.

It is a slow, unstaged afternoon and a complete change of register from District 1.

The colonial centre

The Central Post Office, with its vaulted iron roof, still operates as a post office. Notre-Dame Cathedral stands opposite, built with materials shipped from France, and has been under long-running restoration — check whether it is open before making a trip of it. The Opera House and the Hotel de Ville complete the set, all within a short walk.

Ben Thanh Market sits at the end of it. As a shopping destination it is tourist-priced and hard work; as an orientation point and a place to eat, it earns an hour.

A rooftop at dusk

The city is unreadable from street level and makes sense from above. The bars on the upper floors of the riverside towers are expensive by Vietnamese standards and cheap by American ones, and the view at sunset over a city of eight million scooters is the thing people photograph.

Ben Thanh after dark

The market building closes in the evening and stalls set up in the surrounding streets. It is squarely aimed at visitors, and it is also where a lot of Saigon eats late. Treat the stalls as the attraction rather than the merchandise.

Cu Chi Tunnels

A half or full day northwest of the city: the tunnel network used during the war, with sections widened for visitors. Ben Duoc is the quieter of the two sites. The tunnel sections are genuinely confined, and claustrophobia is not something to test here.

Opinions divide. Some find it the most vivid war site in the country; others find the firing range and the souvenir presentation jarring. Both reactions are common.

The Mekong Delta

The standard day trip from the city is heavily packaged — a boat, a coconut-candy workshop, a sampan through a canal — and frequently described as the weakest day of a Vietnam trip. The version worth doing is an overnight to Can Tho for the Cai Rang floating market at dawn.

Eating as the main event

The most memorable afternoon many visitors have here is not on a list of sights. District 4, a short Grab across the canal, is where the city eats seafood on plastic stools; the alleys off Vo Van Tan and the area around Ben Thanh at night do the same for everything else.

A guided street-food walk on a first evening is one of the few organised activities that reliably pays for itself, mostly because somebody is telling you what you are eating and where the next one is.

Coffee

Vietnam is the world's second-largest coffee producer and Ho Chi Minh City takes it seriously. Ca phe sua da, iced with condensed milk, is the standard; the apartment-block cafes on Nguyen Hue, stacked in a converted residential tower, are the ones worth seeking out for the setting as much as the drink.

Two quieter ones

The Fine Arts Museum occupies a colonial mansion and holds a strong collection of lacquer and silk painting, with almost nobody in it. The Jade Emperor Pagoda, small and dark and thick with incense, is the most atmospheric temple in the city centre and takes twenty minutes.

Both are a short Grab from District 1 and both reward an hour that would otherwise go on another market.
excerpt: The short list, led by the two places that will shape the rest of your trip, plus the quieter half of the city most visitors skip.
author: Editorial

title: Where to Stay in Ho Chi Minh City
content:
Ho Chi Minh City is large and its districts are genuinely different, so where you book changes your days more than it would in a smaller city. For a short first visit the answer is usually District 1 — but which part of District 1 matters too.

District 1

The centre, and the default. Dong Khoi and the streets around the Opera House hold the grander hotels; Ben Thanh is busier and better connected to the street food. From here the War Remnants Museum, Reunification Palace and the colonial buildings are all walkable, and everything else is a short Grab.

The trade is price and noise: District 1 costs more than the surrounding districts and the traffic is constant. A room on a higher floor, away from the main boulevards, makes a noticeable difference.

Pham Ngu Lao and Bui Vien

The backpacker quarter, inside District 1 at its western end. Cheap, central, and loud — Bui Vien runs as a pedestrianised bar street at weekends and the noise carries well past midnight.

Choose it deliberately if that is what you want, and check how many streets separate your hotel from Bui Vien if it is not. Booking here on price alone and expecting a quiet night is the mismatch to avoid.

District 3

Immediately northwest of District 1, leafier, quieter, and with a concentration of local cafes and restaurants. It is a short Grab ride from the main sights and generally better value for the standard of room.

This is the sensible choice for a second visit, for anyone staying four nights or more, and for travellers who would rather eat where Saigon eats than where visitors do.

Thao Dien, District 2

Across the river: riverside, low-rise, full of international schools, Western groceries and expat cafes. Genuinely pleasant and a completely different pace.

It is also a long way from the sights — twenty to thirty minutes each way depending on traffic, across bridges that congest at peak. It suits families, long stays and anyone working while travelling. For three nights of sightseeing the commute will eat into the trip.

District 4

Small, central, just across a canal from District 1, and known for street food. It was once a rough reputation and is now largely a food destination. Accommodation is thinner here but the location is good and the eating is better than District 1's.

What a room costs

Ho Chi Minh City is inexpensive by American standards across every tier, and the gap between a basic private room and a genuinely good hotel is smaller than it would be at home. District 1 carries a premium over Districts 3 and 4 for the same standard, and Thao Dien sits somewhere in between.

Rates climb around Tet and the April-May holiday pair. Check live rates for your dates rather than planning around any figure in an article.

Pools and rooftops

More relevant here than in Hanoi. The heat is constant rather than seasonal, and a hotel with a pool changes what you can do with the middle of the day. Several mid-range hotels in District 1 have small rooftop pools, which is often the difference between resting in the afternoon and losing it.

What to check before booking

How far it actually is from District 1, measured on a map rather than from the listing's description of itself. Which floor the room is on and whether the windows face a main road. Whether there is a pool, which matters more here than it would in a cooler city.

And the Bui Vien question, for anything in the Pham Ngu Lao area: two or three streets of separation is the difference between hearing the bass and not.

Airport proximity

Tan Son Nhat is about four miles from District 1 and thirty to fifty minutes in traffic, so there is little reason to stay near it. The area around the airport is cheaper and has little a short-stay visitor would go there for. For a very early flight, a pre-dawn Grab from the centre is usually the simpler answer.

Noise, generally

Ho Chi Minh City is loud in a way that is not confined to the bar streets. Construction starts early, traffic is constant, and karaoke carries. A room facing an internal courtyard rather than a boulevard is worth asking for anywhere in the centre, and earplugs are not an unreasonable thing to pack.

How many nights

Two nights is enough for the museums and the colonial centre at a reasonable pace. Three leaves room for Cu Chi or Cho Lon. Four or more makes District 3 or Thao Dien worth considering and allows a Mekong overnight.

Most north-to-south itineraries end here, which argues for booking somewhere comfortable: it is the last stop, and a good room at the end of two weeks of travel is worth more than the same room at the start.
excerpt: District 1 for a first visit, District 3 for value, Thao Dien for a longer stay. And one area to choose deliberately rather than by accident.
author: Editorial

title: Getting Around Ho Chi Minh City
content:
Ho Chi Minh City is flatter and more spread out than Hanoi, and hotter. Those two facts determine most of how you move around it: distances that look walkable are longer than they appear and considerably less pleasant at midday.

Grab, first and mostly

Ride-hailing is the default. GrabCar for air conditioning and luggage, GrabBike for speed and price. In a city this congested, a motorbike taxi will often beat a car across the centre at peak, and it costs a fraction as much.

The fare is fixed before you accept, which removes the meter conversation entirely. Be and Xanh SM are the main alternatives and worth having installed for when Grab surges in the evening or in rain.

Taxis

Metered taxis from the established companies are legitimate and widely used. The reason to prefer an app is price certainty rather than safety. If you do flag one, make sure the meter is running.

The metro

Line 1 runs from Ben Thanh in the centre out to the northeast, and it is clean, air-conditioned and cheap. It is useful if your journey happens to lie along it — Ben Thanh, the Opera House, the zoo, Thao Dien, and on towards Suoi Tien.

For most visitor itineraries it does not replace a Grab, because the sights cluster in District 1 within a few blocks of each other and the line runs outward rather than between them. Ride it to Thao Dien if you are going there; otherwise treat it as a bonus rather than a plan.

Walking

The colonial centre is genuinely walkable — the Post Office, Cathedral, Opera House, Reunification Palace and the War Remnants Museum sit within a compact area. Beyond that the blocks get long and the shade runs out.

Pavements are often parked with motorbikes, as in Hanoi, so you will sometimes walk in the road. Crossing is the same technique: a slow, steady, predictable pace, keep going, keep watching, and wait out anything with four wheels.

The heat, as a transport factor

A mile on foot at two in the afternoon in June is a different proposition from the same mile in a temperate climate. Fares are low enough that taking a Grab for a short distance is sensible rather than indulgent, and most people adjust to doing exactly that within a day.

Cyclos

The three-wheeled pedal rickshaws still operate in the centre and are a tourist ride rather than transport, priced accordingly. They are also the classic setting for a price misunderstanding — a figure agreed as the fare turning out to be per person, per hour, or in dollars. Settle the number, the currency and the duration before you sit down.

Buses

Extensive and extremely cheap, with the 109 between the airport and the centre the route visitors most often use. Beyond that, the network takes some deciphering without Vietnamese, and for short city hops a Grab is usually quicker door to door.

Renting a motorbike

Not advisable here, and not legal. A US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, so riding without a Vietnamese licence is illegal and your travel insurance may decline a claim after an accident. Ho Chi Minh City's traffic is also faster and more car-heavy than Hanoi's, with less margin for a first-timer.

A GrabBike puts you in the same traffic as a passenger, with a local riding, for a couple of dollars.

The river

Water buses run along the Saigon River between District 1 and Thu Duc, and a hop-on boat is a pleasant and slightly slow way to see the city from the water. It is sightseeing rather than transport, which is the right way to approach it.

Traffic, and when it bites

Congestion follows a predictable pattern: roughly seven to nine in the morning and five to seven in the evening, when a short journey can take considerably longer. The river bridges and the roads around the airport are among the worst affected.

Add half an hour to any app estimate during those windows if you have something fixed at the other end. A GrabBike slips through congestion that stops cars, which is the argument for it beyond price.

Rain

Wet-season downpours flood some streets within minutes, empty the pavements and send app wait times and prices up sharply. The local solution is a one-dollar poncho and carrying on; the visitor solution is usually a cafe and an hour, which is also pleasant.

Getting to and from the airport

Tan Son Nhat sits about four miles from District 1 and takes thirty to fifty minutes depending on traffic. Grab pickup is on the upper departures level rather than directly outside arrivals — follow the signs up rather than taking the first offer at the kerb.

For an international departure, allow three hours at the airport, and more around holidays. This is Vietnam's busiest airport and the queues reflect it.
excerpt: Grab for nearly everything, a new metro line that helps less than you would hope, and a heat that decides more than the map does.
author: Editorial

title: War Remnants Museum and Cu Chi Tunnels: What to Expect
content:
For most American travellers these are the two places in Vietnam where the war stops being history and becomes a room you are standing in. They are very different experiences and they ask different things of you.

The War Remnants Museum

A museum in District 1 documenting the war from the Vietnamese perspective. The courtyard displays American military aircraft, tanks and artillery. Inside, the exhibits cover the conduct of the war, the effects of Agent Orange and international opposition to it, largely through photography.

The Requiem exhibition, drawn from the work of photographers killed covering the conflict, is the part visitors most often single out. The Agent Orange material is the most distressing in the building.

What to know going in

It presents a national account of a national trauma and does not attempt American balance. The museum was for years called the Museum of American War Crimes, and the framing remains direct. Knowing that beforehand is not a reason to discount what is on the walls — most of it is photographic — but it does let you read it as one country's account rather than being ambushed by the tone.

Allow around two hours. Going early and leaving the rest of the day loose is the usual advice. Parents should know that some of the photography is graphic.

Cu Chi Tunnels

A network of tunnels northwest of the city, used during the war for shelter, supply and movement. Two sites are open to visitors: Ben Dinh, closer and busier, and Ben Duoc, further out and generally quieter.

A visit usually includes a documentary film of a certain vintage, a walk through the forest past displays of trapdoors and booby traps, and a chance to go down a section of tunnel that has been widened for visitors. Even widened, it is tight, low and hot.

The claustrophobia question

Take it seriously. The tunnel sections are genuinely confined and there are limited exit points once you are in. There is no obligation to go down, and plenty of people walk the site without doing so.

The firing range

There is a range at the site where visitors can pay to fire period weapons, and the sound carries. Some find it an incongruous addition to a war memorial; others treat it as part of the visit. It is worth knowing in advance, because the gunfire is audible while you are walking round.

Practical notes for the tunnels

Wear clothes you do not mind getting dirty and shoes you can crouch in; the tunnel sections are earth and the forest paths are dusty in the dry season and muddy in the wet. Bring water and insect repellent. Entry fees are modest and usually separate from the tour price.

Getting there

Cu Chi is roughly an hour and a half to two hours from District 1 by road, so a group tour is a half day at minimum and often a full one. Ben Duoc is further out and generally reported as quieter, and is worth asking for if the operator offers a choice.

Some operators run a boat along the Saigon River instead, which takes longer and is a more pleasant journey than the coach.

Reunification Palace, the third piece

Ten minutes from the museum and often overlooked next to it. The palace is preserved roughly as it was in April 1975 — the cabinet room, the president's quarters, and the basement command bunker with its maps and radio sets.

It completes the picture the museum starts. The museum shows the war as it was experienced; the palace shows the government that was conducting it, and the rooms where that ended. An hour is enough, and taken together with the museum it makes a coherent morning.

Doing both in one day

Possible and not recommended. Cu Chi in the morning and the museum in the afternoon is a standard tour combination, and it compresses a great deal of difficult material into one day with a long drive in the middle. Splitting them across two days gives each one room.

If you only have time for one, the museum is the one that leaves the deeper impression for most people, and it is in the city.

How Americans are received at these places

Worth saying plainly, because it is the thing people worry about. American visitors commonly report being treated with ordinary courtesy at both sites. The material is pointed; the reception, by most accounts, is not.

Most Vietnamese people were born long after 1975, the war is called the American War there, and the national posture towards American visitors is welcoming. If the subject comes up in conversation afterwards, listening tends to serve better than explaining, and nobody is expecting an apology.

And the third site, if you go north

The DMZ day out of Hue — Vinh Moc tunnels, Khe Sanh, the Ben Hai river — is the other place the war is on the ground rather than in a museum. Vinh Moc, where a village lived underground for years, is unaltered for visitors in a way Cu Chi is not, and it is far less crowded.
excerpt: Two war sites that affect American visitors more than anything else in Vietnam. What each one is, and how to approach them.
author: Editorial

title: Hoi An, An Bang or Da Nang: Where to Base Yourself
content:
Three of central Vietnam's main destinations sit close together. Hoi An's Ancient Town, An Bang beach and the city of Da Nang are all within about an hour of each other by road, which makes it easy to treat them as one stop. Which one you sleep in shapes the trip more than those distances suggest.

Hoi An Ancient Town

Sleeping inside or on the edge of the old town means walking to most of what you came for: the lanterns at night, the tailors, breakfast, the riverside. The trade is that the Ancient Town is heavily visited, and the central streets are at their busiest through the middle of the day and into the evening.

It suits short stays and first visits, and anyone whose main reason for coming is the town itself. The town is quietest early and late, and those hours are considerably easier to use if you are already inside it.

An Bang and the beach

A short ride from the Ancient Town — ten to fifteen minutes by bicycle, less in a Grab — and a different pace entirely: low-rise guesthouses and small resorts, a wide beach, beach restaurants. You get the old town as a destination you ride to rather than a place you live in.

It suits stays of three nights or more, and families who want the beach at the door rather than a city around them. The cost is that an evening in the Ancient Town means arranging transport back.

Da Nang

A city rather than a town: a long beachfront, high-rise hotels, the Han River, a city's range of bars and restaurants, and an airport close to the centre. Hoi An is around forty-five minutes south by car.

It suits travellers who want a city, anyone arriving late or leaving early by air, families who want more than a beach to fill a week, and longer stays generally. It is a poor base for a two-night trip built around the Ancient Town, because the round trip eats into a short stay.

What each base costs you in travel

The distances are the whole argument, so it is worth being concrete. Hoi An to An Bang is a few kilometres of flat road — ten to fifteen minutes by bicycle, less in a Grab. Hoi An to central Da Nang is roughly thirty kilometres and about forty-five minutes by car. Da Nang's airport sits close to its own city centre, and around forty-five minutes to an hour from Hoi An depending on traffic.

On those figures, a Da Nang base puts about an hour and a half on the road each time you go into the Ancient Town and come back. From An Bang the same return trip is twenty to thirty minutes by bicycle, less by Grab. From Hoi An the town is a walk, and the beach is that same twenty to thirty minutes there and back. Which of those you would rather pay is the choice.

How to choose, practically

Two nights and the old town is the point: stay in Hoi An. Three or four nights with beach time: An Bang, and ride in. A week, a family, or an early flight: Da Nang, or split between Da Nang and Hoi An.

Season matters too. Between roughly September and November the central coast is in its storm season, and a beach base loses much of its advantage when the sea is rough and the sky is grey. The Ancient Town is less dependent on the weather, though it is not immune to it — the streets nearest the river flood in some years.

The split option

Two nights in Hoi An and two in Da Nang is a workable shape for four nights, and it costs you one transfer. It gives you the town at its quiet hours and a city with an airport at the end.

What is nearby from each

From Hoi An: the Ancient Town, Tra Que vegetable village, the Thu Bon river, and My Son Sanctuary roughly an hour west. From An Bang: the same list, plus the beach itself and the quieter coast north of it. From Da Nang: the Marble Mountains, the Son Tra peninsula and Linh Ung Pagoda, My Khe beach, the Ba Na Hills complex with the Golden Bridge, and the Hai Van Pass heading north.

The list from Da Nang is the longer of the three, which is the honest case for it on a longer stay. The Hoi An list is shorter, and most of it other than My Son is within a short ride.

Getting between them

Grab operates in all three. Hoi An to An Bang is flat enough to cycle. Some hotels in Hoi An and An Bang run shuttles to the Ancient Town — worth asking about before booking, since it changes how easily you get to dinner.

What this choice is actually setting

Look at what follows from it. Your base shapes how easily you can be in the Ancient Town early or late, which is the difference between the lantern-lit streets in the photographs and the middle of a busy day. It sets whether the beach is somewhere you stay or somewhere you visit. And it shapes how much travelling you need to do when the weather changes your plans.

Those consequences are easy to miss when the three are three dots close together on a map. Where the base question gets harder is when it meets the rest of the trip — which nights you have in the region at all, and what you have committed to before and after. That wider ordering is what the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: Three bases inside an hour of each other that produce three different trips. The choice is less about the places than about what your days look like.
author: Editorial

title: Hoi An Travel Guide
content:
Hoi An was an international trading port for several centuries, dealing with Japanese, Chinese, Dutch and Portuguese merchants, before its river silted and the trade moved elsewhere. The old town survived largely intact. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the most visited places in Vietnam.

The ticket system

Entry to the Ancient Town area is managed by a ticket that admits you to a set number of heritage sites chosen from a longer list — old merchant houses, assembly halls, the Japanese Covered Bridge, a museum or two. It is sold at booths around the perimeter of the old town.

Two things are worth asking at the booth, because both are reported differently by different visitors: how many sites your ticket covers, and how long it stays valid. Enforcement at the entrances also varies, which is the source of most of the confusion you will read online. The ticket is inexpensive, it funds conservation, and the heritage houses are worth going into.

What to see with it

Tan Ky House and Phung Hung House are two merchant homes that show how these buildings worked — deep, narrow plots, internal courtyards, and Japanese, Chinese and Vietnamese elements in the same structure. The Fujian Assembly Hall is a Chinese community hall with elaborate decoration. The Japanese Covered Bridge is the town's emblem.

The hours that matter

Early in the morning the Ancient Town belongs to people sweeping, setting up and buying breakfast. Through the middle of the day and into the evening it is busy. Late at night the day visitors have thinned out and the lanterns are lit.

If you remember one thing from this page, make it that. Hoi An gets described both as magical and as a tourist trap, and those descriptions are of the same streets at different hours.

The lantern nights

On the fourteenth day of the lunar month the old quarter dims its electric lighting and is lit by lanterns instead. It is beautiful and it draws a crowd. Check which date it falls on for your trip.

Eating

Hoi An has dishes strongly associated with the town and hard to find elsewhere. Cao lau is the signature — thick noodles, pork, greens and very little broth, said locally to require water from particular wells in the town. White rose dumplings are the other. Banh mi is everywhere here and cheap.

Com ga Hoi An, turmeric chicken rice, completes the set. All four are sold within a few streets of each other.

Shopping, and the pressure

Hoi An sells lanterns, leather, tailoring and art, and the central streets are a near-continuous retail frontage. Shops with prices marked on the goods generally hold to them; in the market and with street vendors, bargaining is expected.

The practical advice is the same as anywhere in Vietnam: settle the number before anything begins, and in dong rather than dollars. That is how you avoid an argument at the end.

Beyond the old town

An Bang beach is ten to fifteen minutes by bicycle. The rice paddies and vegetable village at Tra Que sit between the two and make a pleasant cycle. My Son Sanctuary, the Cham temple complex, is roughly an hour away by road and is the usual half-day trip.

For the beach and Tra Que, a bicycle is the right way to do it — the land is flat and the distances are short. Accommodation often lends them; ask. My Son is a car or tour trip, not a cycle.

Tailoring

Hoi An's tailors are a real industry rather than a gimmick. It needs time: allow for two fittings, which in practice means not leaving the order to your last day.

When to go, and the flooding

Roughly February to August is the drier stretch and the period the beaches work best. September to November is the central coast's storm season, and the streets of Hoi An nearest the river flood in some years — in a bad one they can be navigable by boat.

That is worth planning around rather than fearing. The town carries on through most of it, but a trip built on beach days in October is a gamble.

Getting there

Hoi An has no airport and no railway station. Most arrivals come via Da Nang, which has both — the airport is around forty-five minutes to an hour away by car, the train station a little further. Grab runs between the two, as do hotel transfers and a local bus.

From Hue, the two usual approaches are the coastal train to Da Nang and a car from there, or a private car the whole way over the Hai Van Pass. From Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City it is a flight to Da Nang; trains run too, and take far longer.
excerpt: An intact trading port, best seen at its quietest hours. What to do, when to do it, and what to ask about the ticket.
author: Editorial

title: Hoi An Tailors: How to Order Clothes That Actually Fit
content:
Hoi An's old town is full of tailoring shops, and clothes are made here fast. The results range from genuinely excellent to disappointing. Time, fabric and how clearly you communicate are the parts of that you can influence.

Allow enough time

This is the part most within your control. Overnight turnarounds are advertised and shops can produce them, but rushing leaves no room for the fittings that correct the fit.

Plan on a minimum of two full days in town, ordering on the first morning. Three is better. If your itinerary gives you one night in Hoi An, this is not the trip to have clothes made on.

What two fittings actually do

The first garment off the machine is usually close rather than right — a shoulder sits oddly, a sleeve is long, a waist needs taking in. The fitting is where that gets corrected, and a second fitting catches what the first one introduced. A shop that does not offer a fitting has no way to fix what the first attempt gets wrong.

Bring a reference garment

A useful thing to do. A jacket, a pair of trousers or a dress that already fits you well gives the tailor a physical specification rather than a verbal one, and removes a lot of the ambiguity about cut and fit.

Photographs help for style, less for fit. Bring both if you can: the garment for how it should sit, the picture for how it should look.

Fabric is where the price sits

Two quotes for a suit are not comparable until you know what cloth each one is for. Ask what the fabric is — wool, wool blend, linen, synthetic — and ask to see and feel the bolt rather than a swatch card.

Synthetic blends are cheaper and warmer to wear, which matters in the Vietnamese climate. Natural fibres cost more.

Questions worth asking

What is the fabric and where is it from? Is the jacket fused, half canvassed or fully canvassed — that is, is the front held in shape by glued interlining or by a stitched-in layer, the second being more durable and more expensive? How many fittings are included? Is the work done on site or sent out? What happens if it still does not fit at the final fitting?

A shop that answers those plainly is telling you something useful. A shop that deflects to how quickly it can be done is telling you something too.

Agreeing the price and the terms

Settle the full price before any measuring happens, in dong, and establish what it covers: the fabric, the lining, the fittings, any alterations after the first fitting. A deposit now and the balance on collection is a normal arrangement; if you pay the whole amount up front you have less leverage should the result be wrong.

Get the collection date alongside the price. A shop that is vague about when the garment will be ready is a shop you may be chasing on your last morning.

Choosing a shop

Read recent reviews rather than relying on how long a shop has been there — a reputation from five years ago is not evidence about the work being done this week. Walk in and look at the work in progress rather than the finished display pieces. Ask who will actually be sewing your garment.

If your accommodation recommends a tailor, ask whether they receive a commission. That does not make it a bad shop; it does mean the recommendation may not be disinterested.

What to do at the fitting

Stand normally rather than holding yourself straight, and move — sit down in the trousers, raise your arms in the jacket, reach forward. Fit problems show up in motion.

Say precisely what is wrong rather than that something feels off: the sleeve covers my knuckles, the waistband sits above my hip, the shoulder pulls when I reach. A tailor can act on that. "It doesn't look right" gives them nothing to change. And if it is still wrong at the second fitting, say so then, not after you have paid and left.

What travels well

Suits, shirts, dresses and coats are all made here. Lightweight linen and cotton suits are a Hoi An staple and genuinely useful if you live somewhere warm. Heavy winter coats are made too, and are harder to judge in the heat.

Shoes are also made to order. The same rules apply, with the added caution that leather needs breaking in and a single fitting may not reveal a fit problem.

Getting it home

Many shops offer shipping and will quote for it. Factor in that your own country's customs rules apply when the clothes arrive, and that a large order may be dutiable at your end.

Managing expectations

What is on offer is made-to-measure at a low price, produced fast, with quality that varies by shop. It is not Savile Row. Going in expecting the latter is the way to be disappointed; expecting a well-fitting linen suit for a good deal less than the equivalent would cost at home is realistic.
excerpt: The industry is real and so is the variance. What to bring, how long it takes, and the questions that separate a good result from a bad one.
author: Editorial

title: My Son Sanctuary: What to Know Before You Go
content:
My Son is a complex of Hindu temple ruins in a valley roughly an hour west of Hoi An, built by the Cham over many centuries. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and the Cham temple complex most visitors to central Vietnam see.

What you are looking at

The Cham kingdom held much of central Vietnam for a long period and was Hindu rather than Buddhist, and the architecture reflects that — the towers read closer to Indian and Khmer temple building than to a Vietnamese pagoda. They are built of fired brick, laid with almost no visible mortar, and the complex was dedicated largely to Shiva.

Groups of towers are labelled by letter. The groups usually pointed out to visitors are B, C and D, which are the better preserved; Group A is largely gone.

The war

The valley was used militarily during the war and was bombed, and a number of towers were destroyed. Craters remain visible on the site. Restoration has been partial, so much of what you see is ruin rather than reconstruction.

Go early

This is the practical heart of it. The site opens early, the coaches from Hoi An and Da Nang arrive through the morning, and the valley is hot and busy by the middle of the day. An early arrival gives you cooler air, better light and fewer people.

Sunrise departures are offered for exactly that reason. The alternative is late afternoon, once the coaches have gone. The middle of the day is the part to avoid.

Getting there

Roughly an hour from Hoi An by road. Options are a group tour, a private car with a driver, or riding — though a US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, driving without a Vietnamese licence can mean a fine, arrest, or jail, and your insurer may decline a claim after an accident.

Some tours return by boat along the Thu Bon river, which adds time. Entry is often ticketed separately from the tour price; ask which applies before you book.

What a visit involves

An electric buggy runs from the ticket area towards the temple groups, and from there it is walking on uneven ground between them. Allow two to three hours including the moving around. There is a small museum near the entrance worth ten minutes before you walk in.

Reading the site without a guide

Unguided, My Son is a set of brick towers with limited signage, and a good deal of what makes it interesting is not self-evident. A guide, hired at the entrance or included in a tour, is more worthwhile here than at sites that explain themselves.

If you go without one, the things to look for are the brickwork, laid with almost no mortar line; the sandstone lintels and pedestals, many of them carved; the kalan, or main sanctuary tower, at the centre of each group; and the linga and yoni stones that were the focus of worship. The Cham sculpture museum in Da Nang holds a large part of the statuary removed from here, and visiting it before or after changes what you see.

Practicalities

There is little shade in the valley and it gets hot. Bring water, a hat and sunscreen, and wear shoes you can walk on broken ground in. Insect repellent is sensible.

A Cham dance performance is staged near the entrance at set times. It is short and clearly presented for visitors; check the schedule if you want it.

When to go in the year

The valley is in the open and the ground between the groups is uneven, so the weather shapes a visit more than it does in a town. The drier stretch, roughly February to August, is hot but straightforward. September to November is the central coast's storm season, when the paths are muddy and a downpour can shorten the visit.

Is it worth it

My Son is far smaller than Angkor, and much of it is rubble, so if you have been to Cambodia it will feel modest. If you have not, it is an atmospheric and genuinely ancient site in a beautiful valley, and the damage is part of what it has to say.

Either way the early start is what makes the difference. My Son first thing and My Son in the middle of the day are different experiences.

Tour or private car

Group tours from Hoi An run on a fixed schedule, which usually means arriving when the other coaches do unless you specifically book the sunrise departure. A private car costs more and lets you set the hour, which on this site is the thing most worth paying for.

If you book a group tour, ask two questions: what time it leaves Hoi An, and whether the entry ticket is included. The departure time is what decides whether you arrive before or after the coaches.

Combining it

It pairs naturally with a slow afternoon back in Hoi An rather than with anything else demanding. Tours that bundle My Son with the Marble Mountains and a Da Nang city tour move you constantly and leave little time at each stop.
excerpt: Cham temple ruins in a jungle valley, bombed during the war and never fully restored. Go early or late — the middle of the day is the problem.
author: Editorial

title: Hai Van Pass: How to Cross It
content:
The Hai Van Pass climbs over a spur of mountains between Hue and Da Nang, with the sea on one side. It is among the best-known stretches of road in Vietnam, and if you are travelling between those two cities you will cross it one way or another — so the question is how.

What is actually up there

The road tops out at the Hai Van Gate, an old stone fortification that guarded the route, with later military structures around it. The view back along the coast on a clear day is why people stop.

Weather matters more here than the height suggests. The pass makes its own weather and can be sitting in cloud when both cities are clear.

The tunnel

A road tunnel runs beneath the pass. It is faster, motorbikes are not permitted through it, and it sees none of the view. Much through traffic uses it by default — so if you want the pass, say so when you book.

By train

The railway runs along the coast below the road between Hue and Da Nang; allow around three hours. It costs very little, it goes where the road cannot, and it is one of the best rail stretches in Southeast Asia. Ask for a seat on the sea side when you book.

This is the simplest answer for most itineraries: it replaces a transfer you were likely making anyway, and the views from the track are arguably better than from the road.

By car with a driver

A private car over the pass, with stops, is a half day rather than a hop, and it lets you get out at the top and at the beaches on either side. Many drivers will carry your luggage directly between hotels, which makes it a transfer and a day out at once.

It is the option that gives you the most control over the day, and the one that suits families, groups, and anyone who wants the photographs without riding.

By motorbike, and the legal problem

The pass is well known as a ride, and the easy-rider model — riding pillion behind an experienced local while your bag goes by van — is a common way to do it. Riding pillion removes the licence problem. It does not remove the road risk: this is a demanding road with switchbacks, trucks, sudden cloud and wet surfaces, and road traffic is the main hazard for visitors to Vietnam.

Riding it yourself is the other problem. A US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, driving without a Vietnamese licence can mean a fine, arrest, or jail, and your travel insurance may decline a claim after an accident.

If you ride pillion

Easy-rider operators run the route in both directions. Agree in advance what is included — the bag transfer, lunch, the stops — and expect the day to be longer than the distance suggests, because the stopping is the point.

How long it takes

Da Nang to Hue is about 100 kilometres. Through the tunnel, allow around two hours by car. Over the pass without stopping, allow a little more. With stops at the summit and a beach it becomes a half day, and an easy-rider trip takes most of one.

The train runs to a timetable and is not held up by road traffic. Plan the day around whichever you pick rather than treating any of them as a quick hop.

What to stop for

The summit is the main stop: the old gate, the bunkers, the stalls selling drinks, and the view in both directions when the cloud allows. Heading south, Lang Co beach and its lagoon sit at the northern foot of the pass and are worth stopping for. Heading north out of Da Nang, the Son Tra peninsula and Linh Ung Pagoda are a detour before the climb begins.

Expect to be approached by vendors at the summit. Expect also that the view may simply not be there — a grey crossing is a real possibility rather than bad luck.

Timing and weather

September to November is the central coast's storm season, and it is the worst stretch for this crossing — cloud on the pass, wet and slick road surfaces, and a view that may not appear at all.

Which to choose

Train if you want the cheapest and easiest version, and the one least affected by the road sitting in cloud. Car with driver if you want to stop, or have luggage and company. Easy-rider if the road itself is why you came. The tunnel if you are in a hurry and do not mind missing it.

Booking it

Train tickets for this stretch are sold at the stations and through the national railway's own booking site, and the carriage classes vary by service. Private cars and easy-rider trips are arranged through hotels and local operators in both cities, usually a day or two ahead. Whichever you book, say explicitly whether you want the pass or the tunnel.

The rest of Vietnam's long legs are a separate question, and one the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: The coastal mountain road between Hue and Da Nang, and the four ways to travel it. One of them you cannot legally do yourself.
author: Editorial

title: Where to Stay in Hoi An and Da Nang
content:
Hoi An and Da Nang are usually booked as one leg of a trip, which makes the accommodation question more complicated than it looks: you are choosing not just a hotel but which of six quite different areas you wake up in. This page describes each one and who it suits.

Hoi An: inside the Ancient Town

Small hotels and converted houses on and immediately around the old streets. You walk to the restaurants, the tailors, the riverside and the lantern-lit streets at night, and you can be out in the town at the hours when it is quietest.

The trade is noise and traffic. The old town is busy through the middle of the day, and some streets carry bar noise late. Ask for a room at the back, and look at where the hotel sits relative to the main nightlife street before booking.

Hoi An: the edge of town and the paddies

A ring of mid-size resorts and guesthouses sits in the rice fields a few minutes out, between the Ancient Town and the beach. Prices tend to be lower than in the centre for more space, and many have pools.

You will use a bicycle or a Grab for everything. That is a mild inconvenience in daylight and a decision to make each evening.

An Bang and the Hoi An beaches

Low-rise guesthouses, villas and small resorts behind a wide beach, roughly ten to fifteen minutes from the Ancient Town by bicycle. Beach restaurants, a slower pace, and sand at the door.

It suits longer stays and families. The limitation is the same one that makes it pleasant: you are not in the old town, so evenings there take planning. During the September-to-November storm season the beach is the part of the proposition that fails first.

Da Nang: My Khe and the beachfront

A long strip of beachfront hotels, from budget rooms a block back to the large international resorts on the sand. It is the largest concentration of accommodation in the city.

You get a proper beach, a lot of choice at every price, and the city behind you. You also get a strip that is genuinely built up, with the character that implies. The Ancient Town is around forty-five minutes away by car, so this is a base for Da Nang rather than a base for Hoi An.

Da Nang: the city centre and the Han River

Across the river from the beach: business hotels, apartment blocks, the Han Market, the riverfront and the bridges. Cheaper than the beachfront, and closer to where the city actually eats.

It suits short stops, early flights, and travellers who would rather be in a working city than on a resort strip. The beach is a short Grab ride when you want it.

Da Nang: An Thuong

The grid of streets a block or two back from My Khe beach, with small hotels, hostels, cafes and western-facing restaurants. Cheaper than the beachfront, walkable to the sand, and where a good deal of the longer-stay and remote-working crowd ends up.

It suits anyone who wants the beach without resort prices, and anyone staying more than a few nights. It is less suitable if you want a quiet residential street or a view.

What the choice turns on

Three questions settle most of it. How many nights do you have in the region? Is the Ancient Town the point of the stay, or one thing among several? And are you travelling in the dry stretch or the storm season?

Two nights with the old town as the reason: stay in it. Four or more with beach time: An Bang, or split. A week, a family, or a flight at either end: Da Nang, and treat Hoi An as a day and an evening out.

The split

Two nights in each is a common shape and costs one transfer. It is the version that gets you the Ancient Town early and late, and a city with an airport at the end of the leg.

Practical points before you book

Ask whether the property runs a shuttle to the Ancient Town and at what times — it changes how easily you get to dinner from anywhere outside the centre. Check the walking distance from the hotel to the old town rather than the stated distance to "Hoi An", which can mean the district.

In Hoi An, check how close the property is to the river if you are travelling between September and November; the streets nearest the water flood in some years. In Da Nang, check which side of the river you are on, because the bridges add time at busy hours.

What you are paying for

The pattern across both places is that the premium sits on position rather than on the room. Put a central Ancient Town room next to a larger room with a pool ten minutes out at the same price, and what separates them is whether you walk home from dinner. On the Da Nang beachfront the premium is the sand, and a block back it disappears quickly.

That makes the useful question not "how much" but "what does this position save me each day", which is answerable before you book.

Booking

Both places are heavily supplied with accommodation at every level, and outside the main holiday periods there is usually availability. The exception is the lunar new year period and the local holiday weeks, when the domestic travel market fills the coast.

For deciding how many nights this region gets within the wider trip, the complete Vietnam decision manual works through the itinerary order.
excerpt: Six distinct areas across two places forty-five minutes apart, and what each one is actually like to wake up in.
author: Editorial

title: Hue to Hoi An: Train, Car, or the Hai Van Pass
content:
Hue to Hoi An is one of the shorter journeys on a Vietnam itinerary and one of the more interesting. The two places are separated by a mountain spur that drops to the sea, and how you cross it changes the day considerably.

The geography, briefly

Hue sits north of the Hai Van Pass, Da Nang immediately south of it, and Hoi An about forty-five minutes further south again. There is no airport or railway station at Hoi An, so every version of this journey goes through or past Da Nang.

That means the real choice is how you get from Hue to Da Nang. If you take the train, you continue from Da Nang to Hoi An by car.

By train to Da Nang, then car

The railway runs along the coast below the road, and the Hue to Da Nang run is widely regarded as one of the best rail stretches in Southeast Asia. Allow around three hours. Tickets cost very little and are sold at the stations and through the national railway's booking site.

At Da Nang you take a Grab or a pre-booked car for the last leg to Hoi An. The whole thing is cheap, the scenery is the point, and it replaces a transfer you were making anyway. Ask for a seat on the sea side when you book.

By private car over the pass

A car with a driver, the whole way, over the Hai Van Pass rather than through the tunnel beneath it. With stops at the summit and perhaps a beach, it is a half day rather than a transfer.

This is the flexible version: your luggage goes door to door, you stop where you want, and you can add the Marble Mountains or Lang Co on the way. Say explicitly when booking that you want the pass and not the tunnel, because the tunnel is the default for much traffic.

By car through the tunnel

Faster and cheaper than the pass, and it sees none of the view. This is what a standard hotel transfer will usually do unless you ask otherwise. Reasonable if you are short of time or the weather has closed the view anyway.

By motorbike

The pass is well known as a ride, and the easy-rider arrangement — riding pillion behind an experienced local while your bag travels by van — is a common way to do this leg. It turns the transfer into the day's activity.

Riding it yourself is a different matter. A US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, driving without a Vietnamese licence can mean a fine, arrest, or jail, and your insurer may decline a claim after an accident. The road is also demanding: switchbacks, trucks, sudden cloud and wet surfaces, and road traffic is the main hazard for visitors to Vietnam.

By bus

Tourist buses and sleeper buses run the route and are the budget option. They generally take the tunnel. They are a reasonable choice if the budget is the constraint and the view is not the point.

What is worth stopping for

If you are going by road, the stops are what justify the version. The summit of the pass, with the old gate and the view back along the coast when the cloud allows. Lang Co, a long beach and lagoon at the northern foot of the pass. The Marble Mountains, a cluster of limestone hills with caves and pagodas just south of Da Nang, which sit almost exactly on the route.

A car doing all three turns the transfer into a full day out. A car doing none of them is just a transfer, and the train does that better.

How long each takes

Hue to Da Nang is about 100 kilometres. The train runs to a timetable; allow around three hours plus the last leg to Hoi An. A car through the tunnel is a straightforward morning. A car over the pass with stops is a half day. An easy-rider trip takes most of a day, because the stopping is what you are paying for.

None of these is a quick hop, and the mistake is treating this leg as dead time to be minimised rather than as something worth building the day around.

Weather and the view

The pass makes its own weather and can be sitting in cloud when both Hue and Da Nang are clear. September to November is the central coast's storm season and the worst stretch for a road crossing — cloud on the top, wet surfaces, and a view that may not appear.

The railway runs lower and closer to the sea, which is why it is the version least affected by cloud sitting on the pass. Check the forecast the evening before if you are deciding between the two.

Which to pick

Train if you want the best of it for the least money and effort, and it is also the version least affected by cloud sitting on the pass. Private car over the pass if you have luggage, company, or want to stop. Easy-rider if the road itself is the reason. Tunnel or bus if you are simply moving.

Booking it

Train tickets are sold at Hue station and online through the railway's own site; book a day or two ahead for the better carriages. Cars and easy-rider trips are arranged through hotels and local operators in Hue, usually the day before. Agree in advance what is included — the stops, the luggage, whether the price covers the run from Da Nang to Hoi An.

Vietnam's other long legs raise the same question in harder form, and that is something the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: A short leg with several quite different versions, and the cheapest of them is also the best.
author: Editorial

title: Hue Travel Guide
content:
Hue was the capital of Vietnam under the Nguyen dynasty, the country's last ruling house, and the seat of its emperors until the middle of the twentieth century. What remains is a walled citadel on the north bank of the Perfume River, a scatter of royal tombs in the hills outside, and a distinct court cuisine.

The shape of the city

The Perfume River divides Hue. On the north bank is the Citadel — a walled and moated enclosure holding the Imperial City, which held the Forbidden Purple City at its centre. On the south bank is the modern town: most of the hotels, the restaurants, the backpacker streets and the riverside promenade.

The two are connected by bridges and the distances are walkable in good weather; a Grab is the easy way across.

What to see

The Imperial City is the main event and needs a half day on its own. Beyond it, the royal tombs are what distinguish Hue from anywhere else in Vietnam — each emperor built his own, and they are spread through the countryside south and west of the city, set in gardens, lakes and pine.

The three usually included on a tour circuit are Minh Mang, Tu Duc and Khai Dinh, and they are deliberately unalike: Minh Mang formal and symmetrical, Tu Duc rambling and overgrown, Khai Dinh a dark concrete hybrid of Vietnamese and European styles. Seeing two or three is better than trying to see them all.

Thien Mu Pagoda

A seven-tiered tower on a rise above the river, a few kilometres upstream from the Citadel, and one of the images associated with the city. It can be reached by road or by dragon boat along the Perfume River, and the boat is the pleasanter approach.

Getting around the tombs

The tombs are not walkable from the centre and not close to each other. The usual options are a hired car with a driver for a half or full day, a motorbike taxi arrangement, a bicycle for the nearer ones if you are fit and the weather allows, or a boat trip that combines a pagoda with one or two tombs.

A car with a driver is the straightforward version. Agree the list of stops and the price before setting off, and expect each tomb to need thirty to sixty minutes.

The Perfume River

Dragon boats run upstream from the city towards Thien Mu and, on the longer trips, on to one or two of the tombs. The boats are slow and the commentary is limited, but the river is the thread the whole city was laid out along, and seeing it from the water reorders the map in your head.

Shorter evening cruises also run from the south bank. Agree the route and price before boarding, and be clear whether tomb entry fees are included.

The food

Hue has a culinary reputation within Vietnam that is out of proportion to its size, a legacy of the court. Bun bo Hue, a beef and lemongrass noodle soup, is the dish that travelled; it is spicier and more robust than northern pho and is eaten here at breakfast.

Beyond it the city is known for a family of small steamed and savoury cakes — banh beo, banh nam, banh loc — usually served as a set of little dishes. Com hen, rice with baby clams, is the local speciality that is easiest to overlook.

Where to eat it

The south bank has the restaurants aimed at visitors; the better bun bo Hue is generally found at small specialist places that sell one dish and open early. The Dong Ba market on the north bank near the Citadel is the other place to eat, and is the city's main market besides.

When to go

Hue sits on the central coast and shares its weather pattern. September to November is the storm season, and Hue has a reputation for rain that extends beyond it — the city is wetter than Da Nang and Hoi An through much of the cool season. The drier, hotter stretch runs roughly from February to August.

Plan indoor-tolerant days if you are there in the wet months. The Imperial City is largely open ground and is a much better visit in dry weather.

How long to stay

One full day covers the Imperial City and one or two tombs at a brisk pace. Two days lets you do that without rushing and add the pagoda, the market and an evening on the river. More than two is for people with a specific interest in the dynasty or the food.

Many itineraries give Hue a single night on the way between Hanoi and Hoi An. That works, but it means choosing between the Citadel and the tombs rather than seeing both properly.

Getting there and away

Hue has its own airport with domestic flights, and a station on the north-south railway. The coastal train south to Da Nang is one of the best rail stretches in Southeast Asia. North, the overnight train and the flights both run to Hanoi.

The DMZ and the Vinh Moc tunnels are a day trip north of the city, and they are the reason some visitors give Hue an extra night.
excerpt: The imperial capital, a river, royal tombs spread across the countryside, and the food Vietnamese people travel for.
author: Editorial

title: Hue Imperial City Guide
content:
The Imperial City at Hue is the walled palace complex of the Nguyen emperors, built from the early nineteenth century inside the larger Citadel. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and much of it is ruin, open ground and ongoing restoration rather than intact building.

Three walls, not one

The structure is easier to follow once you know it is concentric. The outermost is the Citadel, a large fortified enclosure with a moat, containing a working district of the city as well as the palace. Inside it is the Imperial City, the ceremonial and administrative enclosure. Inside that was the Forbidden Purple City, the emperor's private residence.

What you buy a ticket for is the Imperial City. The Forbidden Purple City is largely gone.

What happened to it

The complex was badly damaged during the Battle of Hue in 1968, which was among the longest and most destructive urban battles of the war. A large part of the Forbidden Purple City was destroyed. Restoration has been continuous since the site's UNESCO listing, and you will see scaffolding and rebuilt sections alongside original fabric and empty foundations.

The walk through

Enter through the Ngo Mon gate, the main southern gate with the pavilion on top from which the last emperor abdicated in 1945. Beyond it a bridge and courtyard lead to the Thai Hoa Palace, the throne hall, which is among the best-preserved major buildings in the complex and the one that shows what the rest looked like.

Behind that the ground opens out. The halls of the mandarins face each other across a courtyard; further back are the Forbidden Purple City's foundations, the Royal Theatre, the reading pavilion, and the temple complexes on the western side.

The Mieu temples

The To Mieu temple compound on the west side holds the dynastic altars and the Nine Dynastic Urns, large bronze vessels cast in the 1830s, each dedicated to an emperor and decorated with scenes and objects from around the country. This corner is among the most intact and is often the quietest part of the site.

The Citadel outside the ticket

The enclosure around the Imperial City is a living district, not a monument: houses, shops, schools and streets inside the fortified walls and moat. Walking or cycling a stretch of those public streets before or after the palace gives the scale of the thing, which is hard to read from inside the ceremonial enclosure.

The flag tower on the southern wall faces the river and is visible from the far bank; it is part of this outer ring rather than of the ticketed site.

Practical notes

Allow two to three hours. The site is large, largely unshaded, and the walking is on stone and gravel; in the hot months go early. There is a combined ticket covering the Imperial City together with several of the royal tombs, which is worth asking about at the gate if you plan to see them.

Dress is not formally restricted across the site, but the temple buildings are active places of commemoration and covered shoulders are appropriate inside them.

Getting the most out of it

This is a site that rewards knowing what you are looking at, because a great deal of it is absence — foundations, gateways to nothing, lawns where buildings stood. An audio guide or a hired guide fills that in, and the difference is larger here than at a site whose buildings are standing.

If you go without one, read the dynastic sequence first. The Nguyen emperors are the thread tying the Imperial City to the tombs outside the city, and the two make much more sense seen as one story than as two attractions.

What the restoration means for a visit

Expect a mixture. Some halls have been rebuilt to a high standard with lacquer, gilding and reconstructed roofs; others are stabilised shells; others are marked foundations in grass. Work is ongoing, so a building that was closed on one visit may be open on the next, and the reverse.

That unevenness is worth knowing in advance because it shapes expectations. This is not an intact palace complex, and visitors who arrive expecting one tend to be the ones who leave disappointed.

Combining it with the tombs

The Imperial City in the morning and one or two tombs in the afternoon is the standard full day in Hue, and it works. The tombs are in the countryside and need a car or a boat; the Imperial City is in town and is walked.

If you only have half a day, take the Imperial City. It is the centre of the story, and it is the part of that story specific to Hue.

Photography and timing

The complex opens early and the light in the first hour is both better and cooler than later. Groups tend to arrive later in the morning and to concentrate around Ngo Mon and the throne hall; the western temple compounds are generally quieter.
excerpt: A walled city inside a walled city, heavily damaged in 1968 and under restoration since. What survives, and how to walk it.
author: Editorial

title: DMZ and Vinh Moc Tunnels Tour from Hue
content:
The Demilitarised Zone was the strip either side of the seventeenth parallel that divided Vietnam from 1954 until 1975. It is about two hours north of Hue, and the day trip out to it is the main reason visitors give Hue an extra night.

What the day covers

Most tours run a circuit of several sites spread over a wide area. The usual stops are the Ben Hai river and the bridge at the old border, the Vinh Moc tunnels on the coast, the Khe Sanh combat base inland, and sometimes the Rockpile, the Dakrong bridge or a roadside memorial along Route 9.

The sites are far apart. A full-day tour out of Hue is a long one, often ten to twelve hours door to door, and a good part of that is in the vehicle.

Vinh Moc

The stop the day is usually built around. Vinh Moc is a tunnel system on the coast where a village lived underground through years of bombardment — living chambers off the main passages, a maternity room, a well, and exits onto the beach.

What distinguishes it from the better-known tunnels near Ho Chi Minh City is that it was dug for civilians to live in rather than for fighters to move through, and the passages are reported to be close to their original dimensions rather than widened for visitors. There is a small museum at the entrance.

Going underground

The tunnels are confined, humid and dark, with lighting and a guided route. Anyone uneasy in enclosed spaces should know that before arriving; there is no obligation to go in, and the site above ground and the museum are worth the stop on their own.

Khe Sanh

Inland, towards the Laos border, the former US Marine combat base. There is a museum, a stretch of airstrip, and military equipment on display in the open. The surrounding hills are the landscape the siege of 1968 was fought over.

Khe Sanh divides opinion. Some visitors find the setting and the emptiness powerful; others find a small museum and a field. If the base is specifically why you are going, say so when booking, because some itineraries allow very little time there.

The Ben Hai river

The old dividing line, with a reconstructed bridge, flag tower and museum on the northern bank. It is a short stop and mostly a marker — the significance is in the line itself rather than in what stands there now.

The Rockpile and Route 9

Route 9 runs west from the coast towards the Laos border and was the axis of much of the fighting in this area. The Rockpile, a steep outcrop used as an observation post, is a roadside stop rather than a site you enter. The Dakrong bridge marks a crossing point on one of the routes south.

These are short stops and their interest is almost entirely in what the ground was used for, which is why the guide matters.

Tours and guides

These sites are spread out, poorly served by public transport and thin on explanation. A guided tour is the practical way to do it, and the guide matters more here than at most places, because much of what you are looking at is terrain.

Options range from large group buses to private cars with a guide. A private car costs considerably more and lets you set the stops and the pace, which on a day with this much driving is worth weighing. Ask in advance which sites are included and how long is allowed at each.

What to bring and expect

A long day, a lot of road, and sites that are mostly outdoors. Bring water, sun protection and shoes for uneven ground, and a light layer for the tunnels. Lunch is usually included or stopped for; check which.

The subject matter is war and civilian casualties, and the presentation at these sites is Vietnamese and reflects that perspective. Visitors commonly report being received with ordinary courtesy.

Timing in the year

Most of the day is outdoors and much of the ground is unsurfaced. The storm season from September to November makes the tunnels wetter and the inland stops muddier, and a heavy day can cut the itinerary short. The hot dry months are easier underfoot but the Khe Sanh site in particular has very little shade.

Is it worth the day

It depends on what you want from it. If the war is a specific interest, this is the part of the country where it is on the ground rather than in a museum, and Vinh Moc in particular is unlike anything else you will see. If it is a general interest, the War Remnants Museum in Ho Chi Minh City covers the subject in a morning without devoting a full day to an excursion.

The common compromise is a half-day trip to Vinh Moc and the Ben Hai river only, skipping Khe Sanh and the inland stops. It cuts the driving substantially and keeps Vinh Moc.
excerpt: A long day north of Hue through the old demilitarised zone. What the stops are, and what the day actually asks of you.
author: Editorial

title: Da Nang Travel Guide
content:
Da Nang is one of Vietnam's largest cities and the gateway to the central coast. It has an international airport, a station on the north-south railway, a long city beach and a river running through the middle. Most visitors arrive here for somewhere else — Hoi An to the south, Hue to the north — and the question is how much of the city itself to use.

The shape of the city

The Han River divides Da Nang. The west bank is the older city: the market, the cathedral, the museum, the business district. The east bank is the beach side: My Khe and the hotel strip, the An Thuong grid of cafes and small hotels behind it, and the Son Tra peninsula rising at the northern end.

Several bridges connect the two, the best known being the Dragon Bridge. Distances across the city are short, and Grab is cheap and everywhere.

The beach

My Khe runs for several kilometres along the eastern side of the city — wide, sandy, and lined with hotels from budget to international resort. It is a genuine city beach rather than a resort strip in isolation, with local swimmers early in the morning and in the evening.

Swimming conditions change with the season. From roughly September to November the central coast is in its storm season, the sea gets rough and flags go up; the drier months are when the beach works.

What to see

The Museum of Cham Sculpture holds a large collection of Cham art, much of it removed from My Son and the other temple sites. It is, to my mind, the most rewarding indoor hour in the city, particularly before or after a trip to My Son.

The Son Tra peninsula, north-east of the centre, is a forested headland with viewpoints, a long coast road and the Linh Ung Pagoda with its tall Lady Buddha statue facing the sea. The Marble Mountains, south towards Hoi An, are a cluster of limestone hills with caves and shrines inside them.

The Dragon Bridge

A steel bridge in the form of a dragon, lit at night, which breathes fire and sprays water at set times on weekend evenings. It is unapologetically a spectacle, it is free, and the crowds on the embankments are part of it. Check the current schedule locally, because the timing changes.

Eating

Da Nang is a seafood city. The restaurants along the beach road and on the river sell fish, crab and shellfish chosen from tanks and priced by weight — agree the weight and the price before it is cooked.

The local dish to look for is mi quang, a turmeric-yellow noodle dish from this province with pork, shrimp, herbs and only a small amount of broth. Banh xeo, the crisp folded rice-flour pancake, is a Da Nang staple too, eaten wrapped in rice paper and herbs.

Where to stay

Three broad choices. The My Khe beachfront, where the international resorts and the sea view are. An Thuong, the grid of streets a block or two back, with smaller hotels, hostels and cafes at lower prices. Or the west bank near the river and the market, which is cheaper again and closer to where the city eats.

The bridges add time at busy hours, so which side of the river you are on matters more than the map suggests.

Day trips

Hoi An is around forty-five minutes south by car and is the most common day trip, though most people stay there rather than visit. The Marble Mountains sit on the same road and take an hour or two. Ba Na Hills, with its cable car and the Golden Bridge, is west of the city and takes a full day. The Hai Van Pass heads north towards Hue.

My Son Sanctuary is roughly ninety minutes south-west, and is usually combined with Hoi An rather than done from Da Nang.

How long to stay

Da Nang rewards a stay in proportion to what else you want. Two nights covers the Cham museum, the beach, Son Tra and an evening on the river. A week works if you want a beach base with a city attached and day trips in several directions. One night is an airport stopover, which is a legitimate use of it.

What Da Nang is not is a substitute for Hoi An. The two are different propositions forty-five minutes apart, and treating one as a day trip from the other costs real time each way.

An evening on the river

The riverfront between the Dragon Bridge and the Han River Bridge is where the city walks in the evening. Bridges and buildings are lit, there are cafes along the embankment, and the Han River Bridge swings open late at night to let boats through.

Getting there and around

The airport sits close to the city centre and takes domestic flights from Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City as well as regional international routes. The railway runs north to Hue along the coast and south towards Nha Trang and Ho Chi Minh City.
