Within the city, Grab covers everything; renting a motorbike yourself is not an option for most visitors, because a US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam and driving without a Vietnamese licence can mean a fine, arrest, or jail.

Which of Vietnam's airports you fly into and out of shapes the whole route, and that is a question the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: A working coastal city with a long beach, an airport and a bridge that breathes fire. What it is for, and what it is not.
author: Editorial

title: Ba Na Hills and the Golden Bridge
content:
Ba Na Hills sits on a mountain west of Da Nang, about an hour from the city. It was a French hill station in the colonial period, abandoned, and redeveloped from the 2000s into a resort and entertainment complex at the top of a very long cable car. The Golden Bridge, held up by two enormous stone hands, is the image that made it famous.

The cable car

The cable car is the main piece of infrastructure and, for a lot of visitors, the best part of the visit. It climbs more than a kilometre of vertical height over forested mountainside, and the ride takes a substantial part of the journey time. Several lines run at different points; the one you take depends on which station the operator uses.

The cabins are enclosed and the ride is long. Anyone uncomfortable with heights should know that in advance.

The Golden Bridge

A curved pedestrian walkway held up by two giant weathered stone hands, standing out from the mountainside with the valley below. It is short, it is busy, and it was designed to be photographed.

The experience depends almost entirely on two things: cloud and crowds. On a clear morning the bridge appears to float above the valley. In cloud you see the hands and the walkway and very little else. Arriving at opening is the single most useful thing you can do.

What else is up there

A full French village reconstruction — streets, a square, a church facade, hotels and restaurants — built in European style at the summit. A large indoor games and amusement area. Gardens, a wine cellar, a pagoda complex and a large seated Buddha. Shows and parades at set times.

It is a theme park, and it does not pretend otherwise. Visitors who arrive expecting a mountain beauty spot are the ones who find it strange; visitors who arrive expecting a theme park with an extraordinary cable car generally do not.

Tickets and what they cover

Entry is a single ticket that includes the cable car and access to most of the attractions at the top, with some activities and the food charged separately. Buy it online in advance or at the base station. Children are priced by height rather than age, which is worth knowing if you are travelling with a tall child.

Transport from Da Nang is separate: a hired car, a Grab, or a bus included in a packaged tour. A car with a driver waiting is the straightforward version, since the base station is not somewhere you want to be looking for a ride at the end of the day.

Timing the day

Go early. The first cable cars run before the coach groups arrive, the bridge is at its emptiest in the first hour, and the cloud tends to build through the day. Going up in the afternoon on a clear day is the second-best option; going up in the middle of the day in cloud is the worst.

Allow a full day from Da Nang: an hour each way on the road, a long cable car at each end, and three to five hours at the top depending on how much of the park you use.

Weather

The summit is noticeably cooler than the coast and has its own weather. A warm layer is worth carrying even in the hot months, and a rain layer in the wet ones. Check a mountain forecast rather than Da Nang's before committing to the day.

Getting there from Da Nang

The base station is about an hour west of the city. The options are a car with a driver for the day, a Grab each way, or a seat on a packaged tour bus that includes the ticket. A car waiting at the base saves you looking for a ride at the end of the day.

Shuttle buses also run from Da Nang on a fixed schedule; check the last return time before you commit to it, because the site empties quickly once the afternoon shows finish.

Is it worth it

It divides people sharply, and the division is predictable. If you want authenticity, a quiet mountain or a historical site, this is the wrong day out. If you are travelling with children, or you want the cable car and the photograph and are relaxed about the rest, it is likely to be a good day.

The cable car and the view from the bridge on a clear morning are genuinely remarkable. The French village is a film set. Both of those things are true at once, and knowing that before you buy the ticket is most of the battle.

With children

Of the day trips around Da Nang, this is the one built for children — the cable car, the indoor games area, the shows and the parades. If the rest of the itinerary is temples and old towns, it is the obvious day to break that up.

Practical notes

Wear comfortable shoes; there is more walking and more staircase than the photographs suggest. Food at the top is plentiful and priced accordingly. The site is busy at weekends and during Vietnamese holiday periods, when the queues for the cable car are the constraint on the day.
excerpt: A French hill station turned mountain-top theme park, reached by a very long cable car. What is actually up there.
author: Editorial

title: Marble Mountains Guide
content:
The Marble Mountains are a cluster of five limestone and marble outcrops rising out of flat coastal ground between Da Nang and Hoi An. Inside them are caves, Buddhist shrines, tunnels and viewpoints, and the whole thing sits directly on the road you will be travelling anyway.

What is there

The five hills are named for the classical elements. Only one, Thuy Son — the water mountain — is developed for visitors, and it is the one all the photographs come from.

Thuy Son holds a network of caves and grottoes with Buddhist and Hindu shrines inside them, pagodas on the surface, stone staircases cut into the rock, and viewpoints looking over the coast and back towards Da Nang. The best-known chamber is Huyen Khong cave, a tall grotto with daylight falling through openings in the roof onto an altar.

The lift

There is a lift up one side of Thuy Son, sold separately from the entry ticket, which saves a long staircase. It only goes up to the first level; there is still climbing inside. Taking the lift up and the steps down is a reasonable compromise.

How long it takes

An hour is enough for the main caves and one viewpoint. Two hours covers the site properly. It fits naturally as a stop on a Da Nang to Hoi An transfer, which is how a lot of visitors do it, and it works equally well as a half-morning out of either place.

There is a second, much less visited cave complex at Am Phu — the "hell cave" — with sculpted depictions of the Buddhist underworld, entered separately near the main entrance.

Timing it

Go early or late. The site is largely stone, it is exposed, and the middle of the day in the hot months is genuinely uncomfortable. The caves themselves are cool, which makes the contrast worse when you come back out.

Coach groups work the site through the middle of the day. Early morning is when the caves are at their emptiest.

Practical notes

Wear shoes with grip. The stone steps are worn smooth in places and are slippery when wet, and there is more scrambling inside the caves than the entrance suggests. Bring water.

The shrines are in use. Covered shoulders and knees are appropriate, and the usual temple courtesies apply inside the caves as much as in the pagodas above them.

The stone carving village

The settlement at the foot of the mountains, Non Nuoc, is a marble carving village, and the road in is lined with workshops producing everything from small figures to pieces several metres high. The carving is genuine and worth looking at.

The marble used is now largely brought in from elsewhere, since quarrying the mountains themselves was stopped to protect them. If you are buying, be clear about shipping before you commit to anything you cannot carry.

What to see inside Thuy Son

From the top of the staircase or the lift, the route runs past Tam Thai Pagoda, the main temple on the summit plateau, then through a series of openings into the caves below. Linh Ung Pagoda and its tower sit on the eastern side, with the viewpoint over the coast behind it.

Huyen Khong is the chamber to find: a high grotto with shrines around the walls, statues set into the rock, and shafts of daylight coming through holes in the roof. The shafts of light are at their strongest once the sun is higher, which is the one argument for not going at opening — the choice is between fewer people and better light.

The war

The caves were used by Viet Cong fighters during the war, within sight of an American airbase on the coast below, and there are markers at several points in the complex noting what happened there. It is a quiet layer under what is otherwise a pleasant climb, and it is easy to walk past the plaques without reading them.

Getting there

About twenty minutes from central Da Nang and twenty-five from Hoi An, directly on the main road between them. A Grab in either direction is straightforward, and most drivers doing the transfer will stop here if you ask when you book.

Parking, ticket booths and the lift entrance are all at the base on the main road side. Entry is inexpensive, with the lift and the Am Phu cave ticketed separately.

The second viewpoint

Most visitors climb to one viewpoint and leave. There are two, on opposite sides of the summit, and the second one — reached by a short unmarked scramble up bare rock — looks inland over the other four mountains rather than out to sea. It is a short detour and is usually quiet.

Combining it

The natural pairing is with the transfer between Da Nang and Hoi An, or with a Son Tra and Linh Ung morning out of Da Nang. It does not combine well with Ba Na Hills, which is a full day in the opposite direction.
excerpt: Five limestone hills with caves, shrines and a lift, on the road between Da Nang and Hoi An. An hour well spent if you time it.
author: Editorial

title: Cat Ba Island Guide
content:
Cat Ba is the largest island in the Ha Long Bay archipelago and the only one with a substantial permanent population. It has a town, a national park, beaches, and direct access to Lan Ha Bay — the southern section of the same karst seascape, with far fewer boats on it.

Why it exists as an option

Most visitors see Ha Long Bay from an overnight cruise booked out of Hanoi. Cat Ba is the alternative: you base yourself on the island, sleep on land, and go out on the water by day boat or kayak from there.

What you gain is flexibility, lower cost, a national park, and Lan Ha Bay, which is the same limestone landscape with a fraction of the cruise traffic. What a land-based stay gives up is the thing the cruises sell — waking up anchored among the karsts.

Getting there

From Hanoi, the usual routes are a direct bus-and-ferry combination ticket, or a bus to Hai Phong and a ferry from there. Allow most of a morning either way. A number of operators sell the whole journey as one ticket, which puts the connection on them rather than on you.

Once on the island, the town is small enough to walk and the rest is reached by taxi, rented bicycle or the local bus towards the national park.

Lan Ha Bay

The reason to come. Day boats run from Cat Ba town and from Beo pier into Lan Ha, usually combining a cruise through the karsts with kayaking, a swim, a floating fishing village and sometimes a cave. A full day on the water costs a fraction of an overnight cruise out of Hanoi.

Kayaking is the part people remember, because the scale of the limestone only registers at water level. Boats will drop kayaks in the quieter inlets.

Choosing a boat

Ask how many people are on the boat, what the route is, whether kayaking is included or extra, and whether the price covers the national park and bay fees. Smaller boats get into places the large ones cannot.

Overnight on the water

Operators out of Cat Ba also run one-night and two-night cruises into Lan Ha, which is the middle option between a day boat and a Hanoi cruise. The boats are generally smaller and the routes less crowded, and the price sits between the two.

Cat Ba National Park

Most of the island's interior is protected forest, with hiking trails of varying difficulty. The short climb to the Ngu Lam viewpoint takes an hour or so and gives the view out over the forested karst interior; the longer traverse to Viet Hai village is a half-day walk and can be combined with a boat back to town.

The park is home to the Cat Ba langur, a critically endangered primate found nowhere else. Sightings are a matter of luck and are not something to plan a day around.

The town and the beaches

Cat Ba town is a working harbour with a strip of hotels along the waterfront, restaurants, and a floating fishing village offshore. It is not a pretty town, and the high-rise hotel development along the front has changed it considerably in recent years.

Cat Co 1, 2 and 3 are small beaches cut into the cliffs a short walk or ride from town, connected by a cliff path. They are pleasant rather than remarkable; the water is the point, not the sand.

Getting around the island

The island is bigger than it looks and the road from the ferry to the town crosses the park. Taxis and the local bus cover the main route. Bicycles are available in town and are fine for the beaches and the coast road, less so for the park road, which climbs.

Renting a motorbike yourself is not a practical option for most visitors, because a US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam.

When to go

The northern coast has a cool, often grey and drizzly winter and a hot summer. The clearest water and best boat weather is generally in the shoulder months. Summer is also when the domestic holiday market fills the island, and the town is at its busiest.

Typhoon season affects the north through the late summer and autumn, and boats do not sail when the bay is closed. If the water is the whole reason for the trip, build in a spare day.

Booking

Accommodation on the island ranges from hostels in town to resorts on the quieter side, and outside the summer peak it is usually available at short notice. Day boats are booked through hotels and agencies in town the day before, and that is also where to confirm what the price includes.

Which of the north's big excursions — the bay, Sapa, Ninh Binh — actually fit into the days you have is a question the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: The largest island in the Ha Long archipelago, with a national park, a bay of its own and a way of seeing the karsts that is not a cruise.
author: Editorial

title: The Best Time to Trek in Sapa
content:
Sapa sits at around 1,500 metres in the far north of Vietnam, which gives it a climate unlike anywhere else in the country. The trekking is through terraced rice valleys between villages, and the year divides very clearly into periods that suit that and periods that do not.

The short answer

September and October are the best trekking months. The rice terraces are gold and ready for harvest, the heavy rain has eased, the air is clearer, and the temperature is comfortable for walking all day.

March to May is the second window: cooler, greener, with the terraces being prepared and planted, and far fewer visitors than the autumn peak.

September to November

The harvest season and the reason most people come. The terraces turn from green to gold through September, and the cut happens through late September and October. The paths are drying out from the summer rain, and visibility over the valleys is at its best.

The trade is that this is the busiest period and accommodation books up. November turns colder and the terraces are cut and bare, but the walking is still good and the crowds thin.

December to February

Genuinely cold. Sapa can drop close to freezing, mist sits in the valleys for days, and snow falls on the highest ground in some years. The views are frequently gone entirely.

It is not a write-off — the mist has its own quality and the villages are quiet — but it is the wrong time to come if walking in the terraces with a view is the point. Pack for actual winter if you do go.

March to May

The other good window. The weather warms through spring, the valleys green up, and the terraces are flooded and planted — which gives the mirrored-water effect that photographs well in a different way from the gold.

Rain increases through May as the summer pattern sets in. Early in this window is drier and cooler; later is warmer and wetter.

June to August

The wet season. This is the hottest and by far the wettest part of the year, with heavy afternoon rain, leeches on the trails, and paths that turn to deep mud. The terraces are at their most intensely green.

Landslides close roads in this period, and the drive or train up from Hanoi can be disrupted. If this is when you can travel, go with flexible plans and lower expectations about the longer treks.

Month by month, briefly

January and February: cold, misty, often no view. March: cool and clearing, terraces bare or being prepared. April and May: green, warming, flooded terraces, rain building. June to August: hot, very wet, mud and leeches, the deepest green. September: the terraces turn gold, the rain eases. October: harvest, the clearest air, the busiest month. November: cut terraces, cold air, quiet trails. December: winter sets in.

The festivals and markets

The weekly markets in the surrounding valleys are a reason to time a visit to a particular day rather than a particular season. Bac Ha, a few hours away, runs on Sundays and is the largest. Several smaller valley markets run on fixed weekdays.

The lunar new year period in late January or February shuts a good deal down and fills the transport, and it is the one date worth actively planning around.

What the weather means for the walking

The trails between villages are earth, rock and terrace edge, and they are a different proposition wet and dry. In the dry months they are a walk; in the wet months they are a scramble, and a guide earns their fee.

Sturdy shoes matter more here than almost anywhere else in Vietnam. Several guesthouses and agencies lend rubber boots in the wet season, which is a better solution than trainers.

Hiring a guide

Local guides, many of them women from the surrounding Hmong and Dao villages, run treks of a half day to several days with homestays. This is the standard way to do it and the money goes to the valley.

Agree the route, the duration, what is included and the price before setting off, and be realistic about your own fitness — the elevation changes between villages are larger than the distances suggest.

How many days to give it

A single day of walking out of Sapa town covers one valley and gets you back for dinner. Two days with a village homestay is the version most people do and is where the trek stops feeling like a day trip. Three or more gets you into valleys the day walkers do not reach.

Add the travel from Hanoi at each end. Budgeting four days for a two-day trek is a conservative allowance, and it is closer to what the leg actually costs than the trek length suggests.

Getting there

Allow five to six hours from Hanoi by road on the expressway, by sleeper bus or private car. The overnight train runs to Lao Cai, with a road transfer of about an hour on to Sapa; it is slower overall and more comfortable.

Whichever month you choose, book the accommodation before the transport in the autumn peak; the buses run constantly and the good guesthouses do not.
excerpt: The answer is September and October, with March to May a close second. Here is what each part of the year is actually like.
author: Editorial

title: Mekong Delta: Day Trip or Overnight?
content:
Almost everyone visiting Ho Chi Minh City is offered a Mekong Delta day trip, and a lot of people take it and come away unimpressed. The overnight version is a different experience, and the gap between the two is larger than the extra day suggests.

What the day trip is

A coach leaves Ho Chi Minh City in the morning for My Tho or Ben Tre, the nearest delta towns, roughly two hours away. The standard circuit is a boat across to an island, a horse cart, a coconut candy workshop, a bee farm with honey tea, a sampan paddle down a narrow palm-lined canal, lunch, and the coach back.

It is inexpensive, it is organised, and it delivers you back to the city for dinner. What it is not is the delta as a working place: the stops are built for coaches, the sampan stretch is short, and several of the activities are demonstrations rather than things happening anyway.

Why it disappoints people

Mostly because of what it is sold as. Marketed as "the Mekong Delta", it is a day of staged stops on the nearest fringe of it. Sold honestly as a day out of the city with boats, canals and coconut candy, it is reasonable value and a pleasant enough day.

What the overnight is

Can Tho is about three to four hours from Ho Chi Minh City, deeper into the delta and a proper city in its own right. You arrive in the afternoon, sleep there, and go out on the water before dawn.

The reason to do it is Cai Rang, the floating market, which operates in the early morning and is winding down by the middle of it. Wholesale boats moor with produce hung from a pole above the bow so buyers can see what they are selling; smaller boats work between them. By seven or eight it is thinning out.

The thing the standard day trip does not do

This is the whole argument. Cai Rang happens at dawn, and dawn in Can Tho is roughly four hours' drive from Ho Chi Minh City. The coach circuits sold out of Ho Chi Minh City leave in the morning and go to My Tho or Ben Tre, not Can Tho, so none of them is at Cai Rang while it is running. The "floating market" included in some day itineraries is a different and much smaller operation closer to the city.

So the choice is not between a short delta trip and a long one. It is between a day of staged stops on the near fringe and an early morning on a working wholesale market, several hours deeper into the delta, and those are not the same thing scaled differently.

What the overnight costs you

One extra day against the coach trip, and two days of the trip in total; on a short itinerary those days come out of somewhere else. A week in Vietnam that includes Hanoi, the centre and the south does not have two spare days for the delta without cutting something.

It also costs more, though not dramatically — the extra is a night's accommodation and the longer transport.

Doing the overnight independently

Can Tho is served by frequent buses from Ho Chi Minh City's western bus station and by private car. Accommodation in the city covers every level. Boats to Cai Rang are arranged through hotels or directly at the Ninh Kieu quay the evening before, and leave around five in the morning.

A private boat for two or three people is inexpensive by comparison with a tour seat, and lets you set the time and the route, which matters here because the market's best hour is early.

The middle options

Two-day packaged tours out of Ho Chi Minh City to Can Tho exist and solve the transport. They are a reasonable compromise if you would rather not arrange the pieces, though they put you on the water at the operator's hour rather than yours.

Ben Tre and Vinh Long homestays are the other middle route: closer than Can Tho, quieter than My Tho, with an overnight in a family home and a morning on smaller canals. They do not get you to Cai Rang, but they do get you off the coach circuit.

So which

If you have two weeks or more, do the overnight to Can Tho. If you have one week and the delta is a curiosity rather than a priority, skip it entirely rather than spend a day on the coach circuit — that day is better used in the city or the centre. If you have one week and you really want to see the delta, the day trip is the honest compromise, taken for what it is.

What makes this hard is that it is not a standalone decision. Two days for Can Tho come out of Hanoi, the centre or the coast, and which of those you can afford to shorten depends on what else is already fixed — the internal flights, the season, the airports at each end. Working out which commitments foreclose which is what the complete Vietnam decision manual is built around.
excerpt: The packaged day trip out of Ho Chi Minh City and the overnight to Can Tho are not two sizes of the same thing. They are different trips.
author: Editorial

title: Chau Doc to Cambodia: The Mekong Border Crossing
content:
From Chau Doc, in the far west of the Mekong Delta, boats run up the river to Phnom Penh. It is one of the more pleasant ways to leave Vietnam, and it turns a transfer into part of the trip. It also has a documentation requirement that catches people out.

The visa requirement

This is the part to get right before anything else. A Vietnamese e-visa names the port of entry and exit you selected when you applied, and a land or river border is not the same as an airport. If your visa does not name the crossing you intend to use, you have a problem at the border rather than a formality.

Check the crossing the boat uses against the gate you intend to name, and do that before you apply rather than after. An e-visa cannot be renewed or extended from inside Vietnam, and changing it means leaving and applying again from outside — so this is a thing to get right at the application stage, not on the day.

If you intend to come back

Leaving Vietnam for Cambodia does not by itself create a problem. Returning does: a single-entry visa is spent once you leave. If the plan is Vietnam, then Cambodia, then Vietnam again, you need either a valid multiple-entry visa covering the return, or a second visa approved before you come back — applied for from outside Vietnam, and naming the gate you will re-enter through. An application in progress is not permission to enter.

What the journey is

Operators run boats from Chau Doc up the Bassac and Mekong to Phnom Penh, with the border formalities handled at a riverside post on the way. The crossing takes most of a day. Faster speedboat services and slower, more comfortable river cruises both exist, and the price range between them is wide.

The scenery is river life rather than spectacle — stilt houses, fish farms, cargo barges, floating villages. It is a slow day and it is the point of taking the boat rather than the bus.

Getting to Chau Doc

Chau Doc is in An Giang province near the Cambodian border, around six hours from Ho Chi Minh City by bus and less by private car. Most people arrive the day before and stay the night, because the boats leave in the morning.

It can also be reached from Can Tho in a few hours, which makes a natural sequence: Ho Chi Minh City, Can Tho for the floating market, Chau Doc, then the boat to Cambodia.

Chau Doc itself

Worth the evening you will spend there. Sam Mountain outside the town has temples and a view over the floodplain into Cambodia. There is a large floating fish-farm community on the river, and a market that reflects the Khmer and Cham populations of the province as much as the Vietnamese.

Booking the boat

Tickets are sold by the operators and through hotels and agencies in Chau Doc and Can Tho, usually a day or two ahead. Confirm three things when you book: which border post the boat uses, whether the Cambodian visa is arranged on arrival at the post or must be obtained in advance, and what time the boat actually departs.

Carry passport photographs and small US dollar notes. Cambodian e-visa and visa-on-arrival rules are set by Cambodia and change independently of anything on the Vietnamese side, so check them with the Cambodian authorities rather than with the boat operator.

What to expect at the post

The boat stops at the Vietnamese post for exit formalities and again on the Cambodian side for entry. Passengers disembark, queue, and wait for the boat to be cleared. It is unhurried rather than difficult, and the operator's staff walk the group through it.

Have everything to hand before you arrive: passport, the printed e-visa, the Cambodian documentation, photographs and cash. Fishing a passport out of a packed bag at the window is how a straightforward crossing becomes a slow one for everybody.

Which direction the boat runs

The same route operates in reverse, Phnom Penh down to Chau Doc, and that direction has the same visa logic with the sides swapped: your Vietnamese e-visa must name the river crossing as its port of entry, not an airport. Arriving by boat on a visa issued for Tan Son Nhat is the version of this problem that strands people furthest from help.

The alternatives

Flying from Ho Chi Minh City to Phnom Penh takes about an hour in the air, plus the airports at each end. Buses run the direct road route from Ho Chi Minh City through the Moc Bai crossing in six to seven hours. Both of those start from Ho Chi Minh City; the boat starts from Chau Doc, six hours further west, so compare the whole journey from wherever you actually are rather than the legs.

The boat is the slowest and the most interesting of the three. If the journey is dead time to you, fly. If a day on the Mekong sounds like part of the holiday, take the boat.

On the day

Expect the border formalities to take a while and to involve waiting on the boat and at the post. Have your passport, your Vietnamese visa details and your Cambodian documentation accessible rather than packed. Bring water and something to eat; the stops are not catered.

Whether to run Vietnam north to south or south to north in the first place is a question the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: The boat from the delta up to Phnom Penh is a genuine alternative to flying, and it has one requirement people miss.
author: Editorial

title: Ben Thanh Market: What It Is Good For
content:
Ben Thanh is the market everyone in Ho Chi Minh City is sent to. It sits at the centre of District 1 under a clock tower that is one of the city's landmarks, and it has been there in some form since the French period. It is also, squarely, a market for visitors — and it works better once you accept that.

What is inside

The covered hall is divided roughly by trade. Clothing and fabric occupy a large share, then souvenirs — lacquerware, conical hats, embroidered linen, coffee, chopsticks, T-shirts. There is a jewellery and watch section, a dried goods and spice section, and a food court of small stalls towards the back.

The food is the part most worth your time. The stalls sell pho, bun, banh xeo, com tam and seafood at prices above street level but below restaurant level, and sitting at a stall counter is a pleasant way to spend an hour.

The coffee and spice stalls

Vietnamese coffee, dried fruit, cashews, pepper and cinnamon are among the better things to buy here, because they are compact, they travel, and the quality is reasonable. Check whether cashews and dried fruit are vacuum-sealed if you are flying with them.

Prices and bargaining

Prices are not marked on most stalls and the opening figure quoted to a foreign visitor is a starting point rather than a price. Bargaining is expected here and is conducted without hostility.

The useful habits: settle the number before anything is wrapped, agree it in dong rather than dollars, walk away if the gap is too wide — there are usually several stalls selling the identical item — and know roughly what the thing costs elsewhere before you start. A shop with marked prices nearby is a good calibration.

The night market

When the hall closes in the evening, stalls set up in the streets around it, concentrated along the two sides of the building. The night version is more food and souvenirs, less fabric and jewellery, and the atmosphere is better.

It is also busier and tighter. Keep your bag in front of you and your phone away; bag snatching and motorbike phone grabs are the common petty crimes in Vietnamese cities, and a crowded night market is exactly the setting.

What it is not good for

It is not where the city shops. Prices are higher than the neighbourhood markets, the goods are weighted towards souvenirs, and the pressure from stallholders is constant in a way it is not elsewhere.

If you want a market that serves local households, Binh Tay in Cholon is the wholesale market for the western half of the city, and the smaller district markets across town are where food is actually bought.

Tan Dinh and the fabric market

Tan Dinh market, north of the centre near the pink church, is the city's fabric market and is a different proposition entirely — rolls of cloth rather than finished clothing, and a local clientele.

The scams to know about

Nothing elaborate. The recurring ones are a price agreed in dollars then converted unfavourably, a quoted figure that turns out to be per item rather than for the set, and change counted back short in a crowd.

The same habits reduce all three: fix the number in dong, repeat it back, and count your change before you move off. None of that is a guarantee, but it removes most of the ambiguity a dispute grows out of.

Practical notes

The main hall opens early and closes in the evening; the street market runs after that. It is hot and closely packed inside, and the aisles are narrow. Go early in the day if you want to move around it comfortably.

The market sits above a metro station on the city's first line, which makes it easy to reach from the north of District 1. Grab drops and collects on the surrounding streets.

What is worth the money

Coffee, pepper, cinnamon, cashews and dried fruit are genuinely good value and travel well. Lacquerware and embroidered linen are reasonable if you look at the quality rather than the price. Silk, watches and branded clothing are where the gap between what you are told and what you are buying is widest.

How to use it well

Treat it as an hour rather than an afternoon. Eat at the food court, buy coffee and spices, look at the lacquerware, and go. The things worth buying here are the consumables and the small goods; the clothing and the branded items are where the price gap and the quality questions are widest.

And it is worth seeing once regardless of whether you buy anything, because the building and the scale of it are part of the city's fabric. Just do not plan the day around it.
excerpt: Saigon's best-known market is a tourist market, and knowing that is what makes it useful.
author: Editorial

title: Ho Chi Minh City Nightlife: Where to Go
content:
Ho Chi Minh City stays up later than anywhere else in Vietnam, and its nightlife divides into several quite separate worlds. Knowing which one you want helps you avoid an evening in the wrong district.

Bui Vien and the backpacker streets

A pedestrianised street in District 1 lined with bars, hostels and street kitchens, loud, lit in neon, and the single most concentrated nightlife in the city. Music competes from both sides of the street, plastic stools spill onto the road, and it runs late.

It is young, it is noisy and it is not subtle. People either enjoy it enormously or leave after twenty minutes, and both reactions are reasonable. Keep your phone and bag secure; crowded nightlife streets are where the city's petty crime concentrates.

Bia hoi and sidewalk beer

The cheapest and most characteristic drinking in Vietnam happens on plastic stools on the pavement. Bia hoi — fresh, light draught beer brewed daily — is a northern institution more than a southern one, but sidewalk beer culture is everywhere in Ho Chi Minh City.

Look for the streets where people are sitting out with Saigon or 333 and a plate of something fried. It costs very little, it starts early in the evening, and it generally finishes earlier than the bars.

The craft beer scene

Ho Chi Minh City has a well-established craft brewing scene, concentrated in a cluster of taprooms in District 1 and spreading into the surrounding districts. The beers are made in Vietnam, often with local ingredients — passion fruit, lemongrass, coffee, pepper.

It is a different evening entirely from Bui Vien: seated, conversational, more expensive than sidewalk beer and considerably cheaper than the rooftops. A taproom crawl through District 1 is one of the better nights out in the city.

Rooftops

The city has built upwards and the hotels and towers have put bars on top of it. Rooftop bars range from the very formal in the landmark towers to relaxed terraces on smaller buildings, and the view is what you are paying for.

Dress codes apply at the higher-end ones, and the prices are international rather than Vietnamese. Go for a drink at sunset rather than an evening; the view is the product and it does not improve after dark.

The apartment block bars

An old apartment building on Nguyen Hue has been converted floor by floor into small cafes, bars and shops, reached by a narrow staircase and a creaking lift. It is a genuine oddity and worth an hour. Similar conversions exist elsewhere in the centre.

Eating late

The city eats at every hour, and the late-night food is part of the night out rather than something preceding it. Com tam stalls, banh mi carts, oc restaurants selling snails and shellfish by the plate, and the hotpot places that fill up after ten all run well past midnight.

Oc in particular is worth seeking out: a street of small restaurants with tanks out front, where you order by the plate and the beer keeps coming. It is loud, cheap, and more characteristic of a Saigon night than any bar.

Live music and clubs

Live music runs from jazz clubs with a long history in the centre to rock bars and acoustic sets in the craft beer taprooms. The clubs cluster in District 1 and run very late at weekends.

The city also has a strong cafe-into-the-evening culture, which is worth knowing if you are not drinking — a lot of social life here happens over iced coffee at eleven at night.

Where the districts sit

District 1 holds most of it: Bui Vien, the rooftops, the taprooms and the clubs are within a short Grab ride of each other. Thao Dien, in District 2 across the river, is the expatriate neighbourhood and has a quieter, more residential bar scene. District 3 and Phu Nhuan have local bars and cafes with fewer visitors.

What it costs

The range between the ends of this is very wide. Sidewalk beer and street food is the cheapest evening in the city by a long way; a taproom night costs substantially more; a rooftop is priced like a bar in any major city. That gap is the single biggest decision you make about the evening, and it is worth checking current prices rather than assuming.

Getting home

Grab runs all night and is the sensible way back. Agree nothing with an unmetered taxi at three in the morning. Book through the app and check the fare and any extra charges it shows before you confirm.

Picking your evening

Sunset on a rooftop, dinner somewhere, and a taproom afterwards is the version that shows you the most of the city in one night. Bui Vien is better as a short visit than a destination unless that is specifically what you came for. And an evening on plastic stools with cheap beer and grilled food is the one most people remember, which is also the cheapest.
excerpt: Backpacker street, craft beer district, rooftops and sidewalk beer. Four different evenings, and they do not mix.
author: Editorial

title: The Best Rooftop Bars in Ho Chi Minh City
content:
Ho Chi Minh City's skyline has grown fast, and the bars on top of it are one of the few things in Vietnam priced internationally. They are worth it once, at the right hour, in the right place. Here is how to choose.

What you are paying for

The view, and nothing else. The drinks are competent rather than remarkable at most of them, the food is secondary, and a cocktail will cost several times what the same drink costs at street level. What justifies it is the city from above at the moment the lights come on.

Which means the single most important choice is the hour, not the bar. Arrive thirty to forty-five minutes before sunset, get a table at the rail, and watch the change. Arriving at ten at night buys you an expensive drink in the dark.

The landmark towers

Bitexco Financial Tower has the Saigon Skydeck observation level and a bar above it. The building's helipad disc makes it the most recognisable thing on the skyline, and the view from it covers the river and the centre. It is the most touristed option and it is priced accordingly.

Landmark 81, in Binh Thanh, is the tallest building in the city by a distance, with observation levels and bars near the top. It is further from the historic centre, so the view is of the river and the new city rather than the colonial core. The height is the draw.

The hotel rooftops

The Rex Hotel rooftop is the one with the history — it was where the daily American press briefings of the war were held, and the terrace overlooks the Nguyen Hue walking street and the People's Committee building. It is lower than the towers, which puts you in the city rather than above it. The crown and the topiary are unchanged and faintly absurd, in a good way.

The Caravelle's Saigon Saigon bar is the other wartime correspondents' rooftop, on the Opera House square, with live music most nights and a similar mid-height view across the old centre.

Chill Skybar, on the AB Tower, is the loud end of the category: a large open deck, DJs, a dress code, and a wide view over District 1. It is as much a club as a bar after dark.

The mid-height terraces

Below the headline names there is a tier of smaller rooftops on boutique hotels around District 1 — less view, far lower prices, no dress code, and often a better evening. The Nguyen Hue walking street and the streets around the Opera House have several.

Which to choose

For the classic skyline photograph and the river: Bitexco. For the sheer height: Landmark 81. For the history and the walking street below you: the Rex. For music and a crowd: Chill. For a quiet drink without an international bill: one of the smaller hotel terraces.

If you only do one, the Rex at sunset is the one that gives you the city rather than a panorama of it — you can see the street.

The riverside alternative

Not every elevated view in the city is a tower. The Thu Thiem side of the river and the bridges across it give you the District 1 skyline from the outside rather than from inside it, at no cost at all, and the walking street at Nguyen Hue is itself a good place to see the buildings lit.

If the photograph is the point, consider that the best picture of the skyline is taken from outside it, not from on top of it.

Practical notes

Dress codes at the larger venues generally rule out shorts, vests and open shoes for men; the smaller terraces do not care. Reservations are worth making at weekends and are essential if you want a rail table at sunset.

Many of the bars have a minimum spend or a cover at peak times rather than an entry fee. Ask when you book. And check the forecast — the rooftops close or move inside in heavy rain, which in the May-to-November wet season is a daily possibility in the late afternoon.

The cheaper version

The observation decks at Bitexco and Landmark 81 charge admission but no drinks minimum, and some bars let you spend the equivalent of the deck ticket on a drink instead and skip the deck. Doing the maths on that is worth two minutes before you buy either.

Going with children or not drinking

The observation decks work for both. They have no dress code, no minimum spend and no age restriction, and the view is the same one the bar above is charging for. The bars themselves vary — the hotel terraces are relaxed about it, the club-style rooftops are not.

When to go

Sunset, year round. In the dry months from December to April the air is clearer and the view goes further. In the wet season the late afternoon storms often clear just before dusk, which produces the better skies of the two.
excerpt: Which rooftops are worth the price, which view you are actually buying, and when to go up.
author: Editorial

title: Phu Quoc Travel Guide
content:
Phu Quoc sits in the Gulf of Thailand off Vietnam's south-western coast, closer to Cambodia than to Ho Chi Minh City. It is the country's largest island, and over the last fifteen years it has gone from a quiet fishing and pepper-farming place to a resort destination with an international airport.

The visa exception

This is the one genuinely unusual thing about Phu Quoc for an American traveller. Vietnam's visa requirement has a single exception for tourists, and it is a stay of 30 days or less on the island of Phu Quoc — arriving and leaving directly, without clearing immigration on the mainland.

The condition matters more than the exemption. If your flight routes through Ho Chi Minh City or Hanoi and you pass immigration there, you have entered Vietnam and need a visa like anyone else. The exemption covers arriving on the island and leaving it directly, without clearing immigration on the mainland.

The beaches

Long Beach, on the west coast running south from Duong Dong town, is the main strip and where most of the accommodation is. The sunsets face straight out to sea, which is the island's signature.

Sao Beach, in the south-east, is the postcard one — white sand, clear water, and crowded in the middle of the day. Ong Lang, north of Duong Dong, is quieter and more low-key. The far north has beaches that are still comparatively undeveloped, though that is changing.

What the island is now

Worth being direct about. The south of the island around An Thoi has been heavily developed, with a large resort and entertainment complex, a theme park, and a cable car running out to Hon Thom island. The north has a safari park and a second large resort development.

Some visitors want exactly that and are very happy. Others arrive expecting an undeveloped tropical island and find a construction site with beaches attached. Both descriptions are accurate about different parts of it, and which one you meet depends entirely on where you stay.

The cable car

The cable car from An Thoi out over the water to Hon Thom is extremely long and the ride over the fishing boats and islets is genuinely striking. It is also the gateway to a theme park, which is the thing at the other end.

Beyond the beaches

The island interior is largely national park, with forest, a few waterfalls that run in the wet season, and roads through it. Pepper farms and fish-sauce factories take visitors — Phu Quoc nuoc mam is a protected designation and the warehouses full of wooden vats are more interesting than they sound.

The An Thoi archipelago off the southern tip is where the snorkelling and diving trips go, on day boats out of An Thoi harbour. The night market in Duong Dong sells seafood by weight and is the main evening in town.

Eating

Seafood, sold by weight at the Duong Dong night market and at the restaurants along Long Beach. Squid, crab, prawns and the local herring salad, goi ca trich, which is raw herring dressed with coconut, onion and herbs and wrapped in rice paper.

The island's fish sauce is the thing to bring home, though check your airline's rules on carrying it — it is a liquid and it is pungent, and more than one bottle has ended a flight badly for its owner's luggage.

When to go

Phu Quoc's seasons run opposite to much of the rest of the country. The dry season is roughly November to April, which is the period the sea is calm and the sunsets are reliable. May to October is the wet season, with heavy afternoon rain and rougher water, and some boat trips do not run.

That makes Phu Quoc a good December-to-March destination at exactly the time the central coast has finished its storm season and the north is cold.

Getting there and around

Phu Quoc International Airport takes domestic flights from Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and Da Nang, and a growing number of direct international routes — the latter being what makes the visa exemption usable. Ferries run from Ha Tien and Rach Gia on the mainland, which is slower and only sensible if you are already in the delta.

On the island, Grab operates, taxis are plentiful, and most resorts run shuttles. Renting a motorbike is common among visitors but a US licence and an International Driving Permit are both invalid in Vietnam, so the legal position is the same here as everywhere else in the country.

How long to stay

Three or four nights is enough for the beaches, a boat trip and the night market. A week suits a holiday rather than a stop on a tour. One or two nights is not worth the flight.

What it costs relative to the mainland

Phu Quoc is more expensive than the Vietnamese average across accommodation, food and transport, and noticeably so at the resort end. Budget options exist around Duong Dong and the northern end of Long Beach. Taxi fares on the island are the other thing that adds up, because the distances are real.

Who it suits

Phu Quoc is a beach holiday rather than a cultural destination, and it works best treated as one — bolted onto the end of a Vietnam trip, or visited on its own using the visa exemption. If what you want from Vietnam is cities, food and history, this is not the part of it to spend a week on.
excerpt: Vietnam's largest island, developing fast, with the country's only visa exemption for Americans. What is good and what has been built over.
author: Editorial

title: Nha Trang Travel Guide
content:
Nha Trang is a coastal city in south-central Vietnam with a long curved bay, a wall of hotels along the seafront, and a reputation that divides visitors more sharply than almost anywhere else in the country.

What it actually is

A city of several hundred thousand people with a beach running down one side of it, not a beach resort with a town attached. The seafront is a boulevard of high-rise hotels; behind it is a working Vietnamese city with markets, traffic and ordinary streets.

It has also been a major destination for Russian and, more recently, Korean and Chinese package tourism, and the signage, menus and businesses along the front reflect that. Visitors who expected a Vietnamese fishing town are often surprised; visitors who wanted a city with a beach are not.

The beach

Six kilometres of sand along the bay, publicly accessible along its length, with a landscaped promenade behind it. The municipal beach is busy, clean, and used heavily by locals early in the morning and in the evening.

The water is clear through the dry months and the bay is sheltered by islands. In the wet season it can be rough and murky, and that difference is the single biggest factor in whether visitors enjoy the place.

Diving and the islands

Nha Trang is one of Vietnam's main diving centres, with operators running out to the islands in the bay and to Hon Mun marine protected area. Visibility and marine life are better than most of the Vietnamese coast, though divers who have been to Indonesia or the Philippines tend to find it modest.

Boat trips to the bay islands are the standard day out: Hon Mun for snorkelling, Hon Tam and Hon Mot for beaches, and the party-boat versions that are a different proposition entirely. Ask which kind you are booking.

Po Nagar and the Cham towers

On a rise above the Cai river at the northern edge of the city stand the Po Nagar Cham towers, built between roughly the eighth and eleventh centuries and still an active place of worship. They are the city's main historical site, and an hour is a reasonable allowance for them.

The Long Son Pagoda, with its large white seated Buddha on the hill behind, is the other main sight, and the view from the top covers the city and the bay.

The mud baths

Nha Trang's mineral mud baths are a local institution and a genuinely odd afternoon — communal or private tubs of warm mud, then mineral pools and showers. Several centres operate on the outskirts of the city. It is touristy and it is also fun.

Where to stay

The seafront strip has the hotels with the view and the highest prices. A block or two back the same standard costs considerably less and the beach is still a short walk. The northern end towards Po Nagar is quieter; the southern end towards the port has the newer high-rise developments.

Bai Dai, a long beach between the city and the airport, has its own resorts set well apart and little else along it. It is a different proposition: quiet, and dependent on the property you book.

Eating

Seafood, and a lot of it, sold by weight at restaurants along the front and in better value at the places a few streets back. Nem nuong Ninh Hoa — grilled pork skewers rolled at the table with rice paper, herbs and a thick dipping sauce — is the regional dish to look for.

The Dam market and the streets around it are where to eat away from the seafront, at a fraction of the price.

When to go

Nha Trang's dry season runs roughly January to August, which puts it out of step with the central coast immediately north of it. September to December is its wet period, with the heaviest rain and the roughest sea in October and November.

That makes it a useful summer beach when Hoi An and Da Nang are hot and humid, and a poor choice in late autumn.

Getting there

Cam Ranh International Airport is around forty minutes south of the city and takes domestic and regional flights. The north-south railway stops in the city centre, and the overnight train from Ho Chi Minh City is a reasonable way to arrive. Buses run everywhere.

Day trips

Inland from the city, the Ba Ho waterfalls and the Hon Ba nature reserve make half-day trips into the hills. The Thap Ba hot springs sit on the way to the Cham towers. Doc Let, a long white beach about an hour north, is where people go when the city beach is not what they wanted.

Is it worth a stop

If you want a beach day in the middle of a long overland route, and you are passing through anyway, yes. If you are choosing a Vietnamese beach destination deliberately and the surroundings matter, there are quieter options. And if the Cham towers or the diving are the draw, those are reasons to come in their own right.
excerpt: A city beach, a Russian-language resort economy, Cham towers and some of the best diving in Vietnam. Not everybody's idea of a beach town.
author: Editorial

title: Phu Quoc or Nha Trang: Which Beach?
content:
These are the two beach destinations most Vietnam itineraries end up choosing between, and they are not similar places. One is an island resort destination; the other is a city with a beach. Their wet seasons also fall at different times of year, which settles the question more often than any preference does.

Start with the month

This is the part people work out last and should work out first.

Phu Quoc's dry season is roughly November to April. Nha Trang's is roughly January to August. Four periods follow from that. November and December: Phu Quoc is dry and Nha Trang is at its wettest, so Phu Quoc. May to August: Nha Trang is dry and Phu Quoc is in its wet season, so Nha Trang. January to April: both are dry, and that is the only stretch when the question is genuinely about preference. September and October: both are wet, and neither is reliable.

Picking the wrong one for the month is how people end up on a grey beach wondering what the fuss was.

The character difference

Phu Quoc is an island with resorts strung along its coast and a small town in the middle. You stay at a property, you use its beach, and you take taxis to anything else. It is a holiday destination in the conventional sense, with the developed south and the quieter north offering genuinely different experiences.

Nha Trang is a city. The beach is public and runs along the front of it, there is street life behind, and you can walk to dinner. It is cheaper, busier, less polished and more Vietnamese in daily texture, with a large package-tourism layer on top.

Getting there

Phu Quoc is a flight. There is no sensible overland route — the ferries from the delta are slow and only make sense if you are already there. That means a dedicated leg of the itinerary, and an airport transfer at both ends.

Nha Trang is on the north-south railway and the main highway, so it drops into an overland route without a detour. If you are working your way down the country, it is on the way and Phu Quoc is not.

The visa point

Phu Quoc has one feature nowhere else in Vietnam does: the visa requirement has one exception for tourists, and it is a stay of 30 days or less on the island of Phu Quoc, arriving and leaving directly without clearing immigration on the mainland. That condition is the catch. It only helps if the island is the whole trip, which is not most people's Vietnam itinerary — but it does make Phu Quoc possible as a standalone holiday without a visa application, which nowhere else in the country is.

The beaches themselves

Phu Quoc's are better. The sand is whiter, the water is clearer in season, and Sao Beach in particular is the kind of beach people photograph. The trade is that the good ones are spread around the island and you travel to them.

Nha Trang's single long municipal beach is clean and perfectly pleasant, with a city behind it rather than palms. It is a good beach; it is not a beautiful one.

What else there is to do

Nha Trang has more: the Po Nagar Cham towers, the pagoda, the mud baths, the diving, the islands, and a real city to eat in. Phu Quoc has the beaches, boat trips to the An Thoi islands, a national park interior, pepper farms and fish-sauce warehouses, and a large theme park complex.

If you need the beach day to be one of several kinds of day, Nha Trang gives you more variety. If the beach is the point, Phu Quoc is the better beach.

Who each one disappoints

Phu Quoc disappoints people who booked an unspoilt tropical island and landed in the developed south, and people who wanted things to do in the evening beyond their own resort. Nha Trang disappoints people who expected a beach town and found a high-rise city, and anyone who arrives in October.

Both of those are expectation problems rather than problems with the places, and reading what each place actually is before booking is what prevents most of them.

Cost

Nha Trang is the cheaper of the two across accommodation, food and transport, in part because it is a city with a full range of options and in part because Phu Quoc's development has been weighted towards resorts. Both have budget and expensive ends; the midpoint sits lower in Nha Trang.

The third option

If neither fits the month or the route, Con Dao, Quy Nhon and Mui Ne each solve a different version of the problem — Con Dao for remoteness, Quy Nhon for an undeveloped coast on the north-south route, Mui Ne for wind and dunes rather than swimming.

So, which

Travelling November or December: Phu Quoc. Travelling May to August: Nha Trang. Travelling January to April, when both are dry: Phu Quoc if you want a beach holiday, Nha Trang if you want a beach day inside a wider trip. Travelling September or October: neither is reliable, and the real question is whether a beach belongs in that particular itinerary at all.
excerpt: They are opposite kinds of place with opposite weather. The answer usually comes down to which month you are travelling.
author: Editorial

title: Where to Stay on Phu Quoc: The Resort Areas
content:
Phu Quoc's accommodation is spread around an island roughly fifty kilometres long, in six distinct areas far enough apart that the one you pick decides the shape of the week. This is about the areas rather than individual properties, because the area is the decision that is hard to undo.

Long Beach

The main strip, running south from Duong Dong town down the west coast. Everything from hostels to large international resorts, restaurants and bars along the road behind, and the island's best sunsets straight off the beach.

It is the practical choice for a first visit: you can walk to food and a drink, you are near the town and the night market, and the range of prices is the widest on the island. The northern end near town is busiest; further south it thins out.

Duong Dong town

The island's main town, at the northern end of Long Beach. Cheaper accommodation, the night market, the fishing harbour and actual Vietnamese daily life. It is not a beach location, but it is a short ride from one and it is where the island's character is.

Ong Lang

North of Duong Dong, a stretch of coast with mid-size resorts and bungalow properties spaced out along it. Quieter than Long Beach, with coves rather than a continuous strip, and more trees.

It suits couples and anyone who wants the resort to be the evening. The trade is that there is very little within walking distance, so dinner means the property's restaurant or a taxi.

The far north

The northern tip has a large integrated resort development with its own beaches, a safari park and a casino, and separately some genuinely remote properties on undeveloped coast. These are two very different things in the same part of the island.

Either way you are a long way from Duong Dong — most of an hour — and the week is spent where you are staying. That suits some holidays exactly and strands others.

An Thoi and the south

The southern end of the island, around the An Thoi harbour and the entertainment complex. This is the most heavily developed part: a large themed resort town, the cable car to Hon Thom, a theme park, and the departure point for the island-hopping boats.

It suits families and anyone who wants things to do beyond the beach. It is also the part that least resembles the island people imagine when they book Phu Quoc, which is worth knowing in advance rather than discovering.

Sao Beach and the south-east

The island's most photographed beach is on the south-east coast, and there is comparatively little accommodation on it. Most people visit Sao for the day from elsewhere, which is why it is busy at midday and empty by late afternoon.

What the price buys

At the top end, Phu Quoc's resorts are genuinely international in standard and priced accordingly. In the middle, the island's rapid building means a lot of properties are new, which shows in the rooms and sometimes in the surroundings — a finished hotel next to an unfinished one is a common sight.

At the budget end, Duong Dong and the northern end of Long Beach have guesthouses and hostels at mainland prices. The gap between the ends here is wider than almost anywhere else in Vietnam.

How to choose

First visit, no car, want options: Long Beach. Couple, want quiet, happy to eat at the hotel: Ong Lang. Family with children who need entertaining: the south. Want the beach and nothing else and do not mind isolation: the far north. Travelling cheaply and want the island rather than the resort: Duong Dong.

The common mistake is booking on the property photographs without checking where on the island it is. A beautiful resort an hour from everything is a different holiday from the same resort ten minutes from a town.

Practical points before booking

Check the distance to Duong Dong and to the airport, in minutes by road rather than kilometres. Ask whether the property runs a shuttle and how often. Check whether the beach in front of it is swimmable in the month you are going — the west coast is calm in the dry season and considerably less so from May to October.

Check what is within walking distance, specifically. On much of this island the answer is nothing, and that is fine if you have decided it rather than discovered it.

Checking the construction

Development is continuous on parts of the island, and a beachfront property with building work next door is a real risk. Recent reviews are the only reliable guide to this, because it changes faster than any guide can track — look specifically for reviews from the last few months mentioning noise or site access.

When the island is full

Phu Quoc fills during the lunar new year period and the Vietnamese summer holidays, and prices move accordingly. Outside those, the dry season from November to April is high season for international visitors and the wet months are considerably cheaper.
excerpt: Six parts of the island with six different holidays. Choose the coast before you choose the hotel.
author: Editorial

title: Mui Ne Guide
content:
Mui Ne is a coastal strip in Binh Thuan province, about four to five hours east of Ho Chi Minh City. It is known for two things that have nothing to do with each other: sand dunes that look like a desert, and some of the most reliable wind in Southeast Asia.

The wind

This is what Mui Ne is actually for. From roughly November to April the wind blows consistently along this coast, and the bay has been a kitesurfing and windsurfing destination for two decades. Schools, rental shops and instructors line the main road, and the standard of teaching is high because the market is competitive.

The same wind that makes the sport work makes the sea choppy and the beach blustery. If you are coming to lie on sand and swim, you have picked the windy season at the windy beach.

The dunes

Two sets, and they are different. The white dunes, further out, are the large ones — a genuine expanse of pale sand with a lake in the middle, reached by jeep and usually visited at sunrise. The red dunes, closer to town, are smaller, orange, and busier, and are the sunset option.

The standard way to see them is the jeep tour: a pre-dawn pickup, the white dunes for sunrise, the fairy stream, the fishing village, and back for breakfast. It is a well-worn circuit and it works.

The fairy stream

A shallow warm stream running through a small canyon of red and white sandstone formations, walked barefoot in ankle-deep water. Allow half an hour for it, it is genuinely pretty, and it appears on the standard jeep itinerary.

The fishing village

Mui Ne is still a working fishing port, and the harbour full of round coracle boats and the morning market on the sand are the most photographed thing here after the dunes. Go early; the boats come in at dawn and the activity is over by mid-morning.

The beach, honestly

The main strip has lost a lot of sand to erosion in places, and several resorts have sea walls where there used to be beach. The eastern end towards the harbour and the western end towards Phan Thiet are better. In the windy season the water is choppy and swimming is unappealing along much of it.

In the calm months, roughly May to October, the sea is flat and the beach works — but that is also the wet season, with heavy afternoon rain. Mui Ne's wind and its swimming happen in opposite halves of the year.

Where to stay

The strip divides roughly in three. The western end towards Phan Thiet has the larger resorts and the better remaining beach. The middle is where most of the kite schools, guesthouses and restaurants are, and it is the practical base if the wind is why you came. The eastern end towards the harbour is quieter and closer to the fishing village and the dunes.

Because everything is on one road, the question is not which area has more but which end of the road you want to be walking along.

Getting there

Four to five hours from Ho Chi Minh City by bus or private car, and a similar time from Nha Trang in the other direction. Sleeper buses run the route frequently and cheaply. A railway station at Phan Thiet, about half an hour away, takes trains from Ho Chi Minh City.

Mui Ne is strung out along one long road, so getting around means a taxi, a Grab, or walking a long way. Check where on that road your accommodation sits.

How long to stay

Two nights covers the dunes, the fishing village and a day on the beach. If you are learning to kitesurf, a week is the minimum that makes sense. If you are simply breaking the journey between Ho Chi Minh City and Nha Trang, one night is enough.

Eating

Seafood at the harbour end is the cheapest and freshest. The main road has a long run of restaurants aimed at visitors, with Russian, Vietnamese and international menus side by side. The local speciality is banh canh cha ca, a thick noodle soup with fish cake, eaten at breakfast.

Who it suits

Kitesurfers, straightforwardly — this is one of the best places in the region to learn, in season. Photographers, for the dunes and the harbour. And anyone who wants a stop between the south and the central coast that is not another city.

It suits a conventional beach holiday considerably less well, and visitors who booked it as one are the ones who leave disappointed. The dunes and the wind are what you are coming for; the beach is incidental.

The Russian signage

Like Nha Trang, Mui Ne developed heavily around Russian package tourism, and the signage and menus along the main road reflect it. It is part of the character of the place now, and worth knowing if you were expecting something else.
excerpt: Sand dunes, kitesurfing and a fishing village four hours from Ho Chi Minh City. The beach is not the reason to come.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnamese Food: A Guide for First-Timers
content:
Vietnamese food is one of the main reasons people come, and it is easier to eat well here than almost anywhere. The difficulty is not quality, it is navigation: the country's regions cook differently, the best food is often sold by places that make one dish, and the menus are not written for you.

The three regions

The single most useful thing to understand. The north — Hanoi and the Red River delta — cooks with restraint: less sugar, less chilli, more black pepper and herbs, clear broths. This is where pho and bun cha come from.

The centre — Hue, Hoi An, Da Nang — is the spiciest and the most elaborate, with a court cuisine tradition behind it and a fondness for small, complicated dishes. Bun bo Hue, the little steamed cakes, cao lau.

The south — Ho Chi Minh City and the Mekong — is sweeter, uses coconut milk and more sugar, and has the greatest abundance of fresh herbs and produce. Southern pho is sweeter and comes with a plate of herbs that a northerner would find excessive.

How a meal is built

Most Vietnamese dishes are assembled by the eater rather than served finished. A bowl of noodles arrives with a plate of herbs, bean sprouts, lime and chilli beside it, and you add what you want. Grilled meat comes with rice paper, lettuce and herbs to wrap it in.

That is not a garnish you can skip. The herbs are a structural part of the dish, and a bowl eaten without them is a different and lesser thing.

The dipping sauce

Nuoc cham — fish sauce thinned with water, lime, sugar, garlic and chilli — is the thread running through the whole cuisine. Almost everything is dipped in it or dressed with it. The balance varies by region and by cook, and it is worth paying attention to how different it tastes in different places.

The dishes to know

Noodle soups: pho, the beef or chicken noodle soup; bun bo Hue, spicier and with lemongrass; hu tieu, the southern pork noodle soup with a clearer, sweeter broth; mi quang, the central turmeric noodle dish with almost no broth.

Rice dishes: com tam, broken rice with grilled pork chop, egg and pickles; com ga, chicken rice; com binh dan, the point-and-choose canteen rice with several dishes on one plate, which is how most Vietnamese people eat lunch.

Rolled and wrapped: goi cuon, the fresh summer roll; nem ran or cha gio, the fried spring roll; banh cuon, steamed rice sheets rolled around pork and mushroom.

Grilled: bun cha, grilled pork with noodles and dipping broth; nem nuong, pork sausage skewers; banh xeo, the crisp folded pancake you cut and wrap.

The sandwich: banh mi, which needs no introduction and varies enormously from cart to cart.

The things people find difficult

Three honest warnings. Fish sauce is in almost everything and its smell is stronger than its taste in a finished dish — most people who think they dislike it are reacting to the bottle rather than the food. Offal and less familiar cuts appear widely, particularly in noodle soups, and are usually listed, so ask if it matters. And coriander is everywhere; if you are one of the people for whom it tastes of soap, learn to say "khong rau mui".

Chilli is almost always served on the side rather than cooked in, outside the centre. You control the heat.

Where to eat

The general rule is that specialisation beats range. A place with one dish written on the sign, a queue at the right hour, and a cook who has made the same thing for years will almost always be better than a restaurant with a laminated menu of forty items.

Plastic stools on the pavement are not a lower tier of restaurant; they are often the top tier. The sit-down places with air conditioning and English menus are generally aimed at visitors and priced for them.

Timing

Many specialist places sell one meal and close. Pho is a breakfast dish and the good shops are out by mid-morning. Bun cha is lunch. Com tam is often late-night. Turning up at two in the afternoon expecting the famous place to be open is the most common way to miss it.

Vegetarian eating

Harder than it looks, because fish sauce is in almost everything, including dishes with no visible animal protein. The solution is the com chay places — Buddhist vegetarian canteens, common across the country and often near pagodas — which are entirely plant-based and inexpensive.

What a day of eating looks like

Breakfast is a hot savoury meal, usually a noodle soup or sticky rice, eaten early and out of the house. Lunch is rice with several dishes, often from a canteen-style place, eaten around eleven or twelve. The afternoon is coffee. Dinner is later and more social, and is where the grilled food, the hotpot and the beer happen.

Eating on that rhythm rather than a Western one is the single easiest way to find the good places open.

Ordering

Pointing works. So does the name of the dish, which is usually also the name of the shop. Prices at specialist street places are generally fixed and posted; where they are not, ask before you sit down.

And eat what the place sells. Asking a bun cha shop for pho is how you get the worst version of both.
excerpt: How the cuisine is organised, why it changes as you travel, and the dishes that cover most of it.
author: Editorial

title: Pho, Bun Cha and Banh Mi: What to Order
content:
These are the three Vietnamese dishes with international recognition, and all three are easy to eat badly in Vietnam by going to the wrong kind of place. Here is what each one is, where to eat it, and what to look for.

Pho

A rice noodle soup built on a long-simmered broth, served with beef or chicken. Everything is the broth: it is simmered for hours with charred onion and ginger, star anise, cassia and cloves, and a good one is clear, deeply savoury and only faintly sweet.

Northern pho is the original and the plainer version — clear broth, few accompaniments, maybe some spring onion and a wedge of lime. Southern pho is sweeter, usually comes with hoisin and sriracha on the table, and arrives with a plate of bean sprouts, Thai basil, sawtooth herb and lime.

The cuts

Pho bo tai is rare beef, sliced thin and cooked by the hot broth at the table. Chin is well-done brisket. Gau is fatty flank, nam is flank, gan is tendon, bo vien is beef ball. Tai nam is the common default and a good first order. Pho ga is the chicken version, lighter and underrated.

What a good one looks like

Clear broth, not cloudy. Noodles that are soft but still separate. A smell of spice and beef rather than of stock powder. And a shop that sells pho and essentially nothing else, is busy at breakfast, and has a large pot at the front.

Pho is a breakfast and early-lunch dish in Vietnam. A pho shop at eight in the morning and the same shop at four in the afternoon are not the same proposition, and many of the best simply close when the pot is finished.

Bun cha

A Hanoi dish, and arguably the one that rewards a visit to the north most. Grilled pork — both patties and slices of belly — arrives in a bowl of warm, sweet-sour, diluted fish sauce with slices of pickled green papaya and carrot floating in it. Alongside: a plate of cold rice vermicelli and a mountain of herbs.

You assemble it. Noodles and herbs into the bowl of broth and pork, a few at a time, and eat with chopsticks. It is not a soup and the broth is not meant to be drunk, though nobody will stop you.

What to look for

Charcoal. The pork should be grilled over coals, and in Hanoi you can usually smell a bun cha shop before you see it — the smoke from the grills on the pavement at lunchtime is the signal. Pork that has been cooked on a flat-top is a different and much duller dish.

Bun cha is lunch. Most shops open late morning and are done by early afternoon.

Banh mi

A Vietnamese baguette, light and crisp-crusted from the rice flour in the dough, split and filled. The standard build is pate, some form of pork, pickled carrot and daikon, cucumber, coriander, chilli and a sauce.

The variations are endless: banh mi thit nuong with grilled pork, banh mi xiu mai with pork meatballs in tomato sauce, banh mi op la with fried eggs, banh mi cha ca with fish cake. Hoi An has a particularly strong reputation for it.

What separates a good one

The bread, first. It should be audibly crisp and light enough to compress, warmed or toasted before filling. A dense, bready roll is the most common failure.

Then the balance: the pickles and the herbs are not optional, and a banh mi that is mostly meat and mayonnaise has missed the point. A cart with a queue and a charcoal brazier is a better bet than a shop with a photo menu.

The accompaniments, and what to do with them

With pho, in the south: tear the basil and sawtooth herb rather than dropping leaves in whole, add bean sprouts a few at a time so the broth stays hot, and squeeze the lime at the end. Hoisin and sriracha are for the side dish, not for the bowl, if you want to taste the broth you came for — though plenty of Vietnamese people put them straight in.

With bun cha, work in small batches rather than tipping everything in at once; the noodles go soft and the herbs wilt. With banh mi, there is nothing to assemble, but ask for extra chilli if you want it, because the default is mild for a foreign customer.

Prices and how to order

All three are inexpensive at the places that specialise in them, and several times the price at restaurants aimed at visitors. Prices are generally posted at street stalls; where they are not, ask first.

Ordering is usually a matter of saying the dish name and holding up fingers for how many. At a pho shop, saying "tai nam" after "pho" gets you the standard mixed-beef bowl.

Where to eat each one

Pho is everywhere, but the northern version in Hanoi is the one to seek out. Bun cha is a Hanoi dish and is best there. Banh mi is at its best in the south and in Hoi An. If your route covers the whole country, eat each one where it belongs.
excerpt: Three dishes you already know by name, and what actually distinguishes a good one from a bad one.
author: Editorial

title: Street Food Safety in Vietnam
content:
Street food is a large part of why Vietnam is worth visiting, and avoiding it means missing most of the country's best eating. It also carries a real risk of stomach illness, which is the most common thing that goes wrong on a trip here. Both of those are true, and the sensible approach sits between them.

Start before you travel
