The vaccinations are the part you can actually control, and they are decided before you arrive. The CDC's list for Vietnam includes Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, and typhoid for most travelers, and the scope of each is worth stating precisely: Hepatitis A for unvaccinated travellers aged one and over, Hepatitis B for unvaccinated travellers of all ages, and typhoid for most travellers. Hepatitis A and typhoid are both food- and water-borne, which is the relevant category here.

Talk to a travel clinic as early as you can, because some of these need more than one dose spaced out. A late appointment is still worth making — a clinic can advise on what is useful at short notice — but earlier gives you more options.

How to choose a stall

The principles are the same ones Vietnamese people use, and they are about turnover rather than appearance.

Busy is the most useful indicator. A stall with a queue is selling its stock fast, which makes it less likely that anything has been standing around. It is a clue rather than proof. An empty stall at a busy hour usually has a reason for being empty.

Watch the food being cooked. Grilled, fried and boiled to order, in front of you, is the lowest-risk category. Food that has been cooked and is sitting at room temperature is the highest.

Look at where the raw and the cooked sit. Separate surfaces and separate tongs are a good sign. One board and one pair of tongs for everything is not.

Specialist beats general

A stall that makes one dish all day gets through its ingredients, and the cook has made that dish thousands of times. A cart offering fifteen things is keeping most of them waiting between customers.

Water, ice and salads

Drink bottled or filtered water and check the seal. Tap water is not for drinking anywhere in Vietnam, and that includes brushing your teeth if you want to be careful in the first few days.

Ice is less of a worry than its reputation suggests at established places: commercial ice in Vietnam is generally factory-made from treated water, and the uniform cylinders with a hole through the middle are the industrial kind. Irregular hand-chipped ice is the one to be wary of.

Raw herbs and salads are the genuine grey area, because they are washed in whatever water the stall has. They are also an integral part of most dishes. The CDC's advice is to avoid raw salads. If you want to follow that strictly, you will skip a real part of the cuisine; if you do eat them, higher-turnover places are the lower-risk end of the range rather than a safe one. If your stomach is already unhappy, skip them.

The things most likely to cause trouble

If you want a short list rather than principles: shellfish that has been sitting out, cut fruit prepared hours earlier and kept at room temperature, anything with raw egg or mayonnaise in the heat, and the leftover accompaniments on a table that have clearly been there a while. Rice that has been held warm for a long time is another.

None of these is an absolute rule — a busy stall selling cut fruit all afternoon is turning it over constantly. The underlying question is always the same: how long has this been sitting there?

Easing in

A common approach is to start with the cooked-to-order things in the first day or two — grilled meat, fried rice, noodle soups where the broth is boiling — and add the raw accompaniments after that.

This is about giving yourself a gentler start, not about any one food being dangerous and another safe.

What to carry

Oral rehydration salts are the most useful thing in the bag, and they are cheap and available in any Vietnamese pharmacy. An anti-diarrhoeal is worth having for travel days specifically. Hand sanitiser matters more than most people expect, because you eat with your hands a lot here and many stalls have no washing facilities.

When to see a doctor

Most stomach upsets resolve in a day or two with fluids and rest. Seek medical care for a high fever, blood in the stool, severe or persistent symptoms, or signs of dehydration — and sooner rather than later if you are travelling with children. International clinics operate in the main cities.

Travel insurance

Worth having and worth reading before you need it. Check that it covers medical treatment abroad and, if relevant, evacuation. The international clinics in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City are good and expect payment or a direct insurance arrangement at the point of treatment.

What this all adds up to

Vietnamese street food is not a risk to be endured for the sake of the experience. It is a food culture with its own hygiene logic, and the way to eat it well is to read the signals — turnover, cooking to order, separation of raw and cooked — rather than to avoid the category.

Getting vaccinated, drinking bottled water and choosing stalls by turnover are the things within your control, and they lower the risk rather than remove it. Some people get ill anyway, here as anywhere, and carrying rehydration salts is the part of the plan that assumes it.
excerpt: The cautious advice is to avoid street food. The better advice is to choose it well, and to get the right vaccinations first.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnamese Coffee: What to Order
content:
Vietnam grows an enormous amount of coffee and has built a drinking culture around it that owes very little to European or American habits. Ordering it well is one of the quickest ways to get something genuinely local for almost nothing.

The bean

Most Vietnamese coffee is robusta rather than arabica — stronger, more bitter, higher in caffeine and with a heavier body. That is not an accident of quality; the drinks are built around it. Robusta is why condensed milk works, and why a Vietnamese coffee can take that much sweetness without disappearing.

Arabica and specialty-grade coffee are grown in Vietnam too, mostly around Da Lat, and the third-wave cafes in the cities serve it. That is a parallel scene rather than the mainstream one.

The classic drinks

Ca phe sua da — iced coffee with condensed milk. The default, and the one to start with. Strong coffee dripped through a small metal filter onto a layer of sweetened condensed milk, stirred, poured over ice.

Ca phe den da — iced black coffee, usually with sugar unless you say otherwise. Bracing.

Ca phe sua nong and ca phe den nong are the hot versions of both, more common in the cooler north.

The phin

The small stacked metal filter that sits on top of the glass. It drips slowly, which is part of the experience — ordering coffee here means waiting while it brews rather than being handed a cup. Plenty of places now pre-brew for speed, but the phin is still the standard in the north and at traditional cafes.

The ones worth seeking out

Ca phe trung — egg coffee, a Hanoi invention. Egg yolk whipped with condensed milk into a thick sweet foam, poured over strong coffee and served hot in a bowl of warm water. It tastes like liquid tiramisu and it is better than it sounds.

Ca phe muoi — salt coffee, from Hue. A lightly salted cream on top of iced coffee. The salt cuts the sweetness and it is extremely drinkable.

Ca phe cot dua — coconut coffee, blended with coconut cream and ice into something close to a dessert. Common in Hanoi.

Bac xiu — a southern drink, much more condensed milk and much less coffee. The gentle option.

How to order it the way you want it

Four words cover most of it. "Da" means iced, "nong" means hot, "sua" means with condensed milk, "den" means black. So ca phe sua da is iced with milk, ca phe den nong is hot and black. If you do not want sugar in a black coffee, say "khong duong" — black coffee usually arrives sweetened by default.

Where to drink it

Three distinct kinds of place. The pavement cafes — low plastic stools, a glass of free iced tea alongside, the cheapest coffee in the country and the one most embedded in daily life. The Vietnamese chains, air-conditioned and ubiquitous, which are reliable and a reasonable place to work. And the independent specialty cafes, which are serving arabica and pour-overs to a more international standard.

All three are worth using for different things. The stool on the pavement is the one that is specifically Vietnamese.

The sitting

Coffee in Vietnam is not a takeaway habit. The phin takes its time, the stools face the street, and the expectation is that you stay. Pavement cafes are not run on table turnover, and sitting a long while over a single glass is ordinary rather than awkward.

The iced tea

Almost every cafe gives you a glass of weak iced tea, tra da, alongside the coffee, free. It is there to drink between sips; the coffee is strong and the tea resets your palate.

Buying beans to take home

Vietnamese coffee is cheap and travels well, and the supermarkets and specialty roasters both sell it ground or whole. A few things to know: a lot of mass-market Vietnamese coffee is roasted with butter, oil or other additives, which gives the characteristic flavour but can clog a home machine. Check whether what you are buying is pure coffee if that matters to you.

A phin filter costs almost nothing and is the right way to make it at home. Buy one with the drink.

Da Lat and where the coffee comes from

Most of Vietnam's coffee is grown in the Central Highlands around Buon Ma Thuot and Da Lat, at altitude and inland from the coast. Da Lat in particular has become a destination for farm visits and cupping, and the town's own cafe scene is among the best in the country.

If the coffee is a serious interest rather than a daily habit, that is where to go for it, and it fits into a route between the coast and Ho Chi Minh City.

A note on strength

Robusta carries roughly twice the caffeine of arabica, and Vietnamese coffee is brewed strong. Two iced coffees in an afternoon is more caffeine than most visitors are used to, and the effect is noticeable. Pace it, especially if you are drinking it in the heat.
excerpt: The second-largest coffee producer in the world drinks it differently from anyone else. What the drinks are, and where to have them.
author: Editorial

title: Bia Hoi: Vietnam's Fresh Beer, Explained
content:
Bia hoi is fresh, unpasteurised draught beer, brewed daily and delivered to the bars that sell it the same day. It has no preservatives and does not keep, which is why it is sold and drunk within hours and why it costs almost nothing. It is one of the most distinctive things to drink in Vietnam.

What it actually is

A light lager, low in alcohol, served from kegs or plastic barrels into glasses on the pavement. Because it is not pasteurised and not bottled, the economics are different from packaged beer: no bottling, no long distribution chain, and no shelf life to pay for. The price reflects that.

It is mild. Nobody drinks bia hoi for the strength; they drink it because it is cold, cheap and endless, and because of where it is drunk.

Where it is

Bia hoi is a northern institution, concentrated in Hanoi and the surrounding provinces. It exists in the south, but it is not part of daily life there in the way it is in the north — the southern equivalent is bottled Saigon or 333 on the same plastic stools.

In Hanoi, the junction known as Bia Hoi Corner in the Old Quarter is the famous one and is heavily touristed. The better experience is at any of the hundreds of neighbourhood bia hoi places away from the centre, where the clientele is local and the price is lower still.

How it works

You sit on a low plastic stool at a low table, usually on the pavement. Beer arrives in glasses and keeps arriving; you are generally charged at the end for what you drank. Food is ordered alongside and is the other half of the attraction.

The beer is often poured ahead into rows of glasses, which is normal. It is delivered fresh each day and the places that sell a lot get through it.

What to eat with it

Bia hoi places are drinking-food places. The standard range is nem chua ran, fried fermented pork; lac rang, salted peanuts; nom, a shredded green papaya salad with beef jerky; grilled skewers; and fried tofu. It is salty, sharp food designed to keep you drinking.

Ordering a few plates between a group and letting the beer keep coming is the whole format.

How to find a good one

Away from the Old Quarter, look for the signs: a corner with low tables spilling onto the pavement, a steel keg or a plastic barrel with a tap, and a crowd that is mostly local and mostly after work. The word "bia hoi" on a sign is literal — these places are not trying to be discovered.

There is no need to book, there is rarely a menu in English, and pointing at what the next table is eating works. If the place is full at six in the evening, that is the recommendation.

The hours

Bia hoi is an after-work drink. Places fill up from late afternoon, peak in the early evening, and many have sold their day's supply and closed by nine or ten. This is not a late-night activity, and arriving at eleven expecting to find it in full swing is how people conclude it does not exist.

The price

It is the cheapest beer you will encounter, and considerably cheaper than bottled beer in the same establishment. Prices are posted at most places; at the tourist-facing corners in the Old Quarter they are higher and sometimes not posted, so ask.

Practical points

The glasses are often rinsed rather than washed, which is worth knowing. The beer itself is brewed, alcoholic and delivered daily, which is a different risk profile from the food on the table — but it is not a guarantee of anything.

Do not drive afterwards. Vietnam enforces zero alcohol while driving, and that is not a graduated limit — any alcohol at all is an offence. Take a Grab.

The etiquette

Glasses are raised together rather than drunk individually — "mot, hai, ba, vo" is the count and the toast, and you will hear it across the room all evening. Topping up other people's glasses before your own is normal courtesy. None of it is demanding, and nobody expects a visitor to know it.

Beyond bia hoi

Vietnam has a serious craft beer scene now, concentrated in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, brewing with local ingredients. It is a different evening and a different price, and it is genuinely good. Bia hoi is not competing with it.

Bottled Vietnamese lagers — Bia Hanoi in the north, Saigon and 333 in the south, Huda in the centre — are the everyday alternative and are sold everywhere.

Taking beer home

Bia hoi cannot travel; it has no shelf life. Bottled Vietnamese beer can, within the customs allowance you are flying into. Vietnam's own inbound allowance is 1.5 litres of spirits at 20% ABV or above, or 2 litres under 20%, or 3 litres of beer, and your own country's rules apply on the way back.
excerpt: Draught beer brewed that morning, sold on the pavement at a price nothing else competes with. What it is, where it is, and why it belongs to the north.
author: Editorial

title: Vegetarian and Vegan Food in Vietnam
content:
Vietnam looks like an easy country to eat vegetarian in — the herbs, the vegetables, the rice — and then you discover that fish sauce is in almost everything, including dishes with no visible animal protein. It is still very manageable, but it needs a strategy rather than optimism.

The problem, stated plainly

Nuoc mam, fish sauce, is the base seasoning of the cuisine in the way salt is elsewhere. It is in dipping sauces, in marinades, in broths, in dressings for vegetable dishes. Shrimp paste, mam tom, appears in northern and central cooking. Pork or chicken stock underlies many broths that arrive looking vegetable-based.

A dish of stir-fried morning glory is not vegetarian by default. Neither is a bowl of noodles with tofu in it. This is not a matter of carelessness on the cook's part; it is how the food is seasoned.

Com chay: the real answer

Vietnam has a large Buddhist vegetarian tradition and, with it, a whole category of restaurant: com chay, literally vegetarian rice. These kitchens cook without meat, fish or fish sauce, which is the thing that makes them useful. They are inexpensive, common, and often found near pagodas.

Look for the word "chay" on a sign, or the Buddhist swastika symbol, which in this context marks a vegetarian kitchen. Many are canteen-style: you point at what you want from a tray of dishes and pay by the plate.

The lunar calendar

Many Vietnamese Buddhists eat vegetarian on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month. On those days, com chay places are at their busiest and best stocked, and ordinary restaurants often add vegetarian options. It is a good time to be eating this way.

Regional differences

The south is the easiest. Buddhist practice is more widespread there, com chay places are more numerous, and the southern cooking's heavier use of coconut milk and vegetables translates well. Ho Chi Minh City in particular has a dense network of both canteens and modern vegan restaurants.

The centre is harder, because Hue and Hoi An's signature dishes are built around pork, shrimp and fish — though Hue, as a Buddhist centre with a long monastic tradition, has excellent vegetarian cooking if you look for it. The north sits between the two, with shrimp paste appearing more often than elsewhere.

The useful phrases

Toi an chay — I eat vegetarian. This is the single most useful thing to be able to say, and in a Buddhist context it is well understood to mean no meat, no fish, no fish sauce.

Khong nuoc mam — no fish sauce. Say it explicitly, because "vegetarian" in a non-Buddhist restaurant may not be heard as excluding it.

Khong thit, khong ca, khong trung, khong sua — no meat, no fish, no egg, no milk, for vegan requirements. Writing these down and showing them works better than pronunciation.

Dishes that work

Many standard dishes have genuine chay versions: pho chay, bun rieu chay, banh mi chay, goi cuon chay with tofu and herbs, com tam chay. These are not compromises invented for visitors — Buddhist cooking has made mock-meat versions of the national dishes for a long time, and some of them are very good.

Beyond that: fresh spring rolls without the shrimp, banh xeo made without pork, rau muong xao toi if you confirm no fish sauce, and the enormous variety of vegetable, tofu and mushroom dishes in a com chay canteen.

Vegan specifically

Com chay cooking is often vegan as well as vegetarian, since dairy barely features in the tradition and many kitchens avoid egg too. That makes the chay network the practical starting point for vegans — but confirm egg and dairy at the individual place rather than assuming the category.

Outside it, egg is the common hidden ingredient — in banh mi, in some noodle dishes, in desserts. Dairy barely features in traditional Vietnamese cooking, but condensed milk is everywhere in drinks. Ask for coffee black, or with coconut milk where it is offered.

Where it gets hard

Street food, ironically, because stalls make one dish one way and have no vegetarian version. Smaller towns, where com chay places are fewer. And group situations, where the shared dishes are the point.

Finding places

The mapping apps list com chay restaurants and the vegetarian-specific apps cover the cities well. In Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi there is also a growing number of modern vegan restaurants aimed at a younger Vietnamese and international clientele, which are a different and more expensive proposition from the canteens.

Looking near a significant pagoda is the most useful search heuristic, in small towns as much as in cities. It is where chay kitchens tend to cluster.

Breakfast

The hardest meal, because the standard Vietnamese breakfast is a meat-based noodle soup. The workable options are xoi, sticky rice, sold from baskets in the morning in both sweet and savoury versions; banh mi ordered without the pork and pate; and the com chay places that open early, which many do.

How it actually goes

Most vegetarian visitors to Vietnam eat extremely well, and the ones who struggle are usually the ones who tried to make the general restaurant scene work rather than using the chay network. Switch your default from "what can I remove from this dish" to "where is the nearest chay place", and the country becomes straightforward.
excerpt: Harder than it looks and easier than you fear. The com chay network is the answer, and fish sauce is the problem.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnamese Desserts and Sweet Things
content:
Vietnamese cooking does not really do dessert as a final course at the end of a meal. What it has instead is a large category of sweet things eaten through the day — from stalls, from carts, from dedicated shops — and they are among the easiest and cheapest pleasures of the country.

Che

The central category. Che is a family of sweet soups and puddings, served hot or cold, built from beans, pulses, jellies, tapioca, fruit and coconut milk. A che shop will have a long row of them on the counter, often in glass jars, and you point.

The common ones: che dau xanh, mung bean; che ba mau, the three-colour one with red bean, mung bean and pandan jelly over crushed ice and coconut milk; che chuoi, banana with tapioca and coconut; che troi nuoc, glutinous rice balls with mung bean filling in a ginger syrup, served warm.

It is sweet, it is texturally busy, and it is worth going in without strong preconceptions. Che is not trying to be a Western dessert and it does not taste like one.

Sticky rice and cakes

Xoi is glutinous rice, and it runs both savoury and sweet. The sweet versions — xoi xeo with mung bean, xoi gac with its orange gac fruit colouring, xoi la dua with pandan — are breakfast and snack food sold from baskets on the pavement.

Banh chung and banh tet, the square and cylindrical glutinous rice cakes wrapped in leaves, are lunar new year food and are savoury rather than sweet, filled with pork and mung bean. You will meet them around Tet and not much otherwise.

Banh flan

Crème caramel, inherited from the French and completely absorbed into Vietnamese food. Sold everywhere, often with coffee poured over it or with crushed ice, and usually very good.

Banh and the leaf-wrapped things

A whole family of small cakes steamed in banana or pandan leaf, sold in markets and at pagodas. Banh da lon is a layered steamed cake of mung bean and pandan with a distinctive chewy texture. Banh bo is a honeycomb-textured rice cake. Banh ran and banh cam are the sesame-coated fried glutinous rice balls with a mung bean filling.

These are snack food rather than dessert, eaten through the afternoon, and they cost very little.

Fruit

The thing most visitors underuse. Vietnam grows an enormous range, and the markets sell it cut and ready. Mangosteen, rambutan, longan, dragon fruit, jackfruit, custard apple, pomelo and several varieties of mango, depending on the season.

Durian divides people exactly as advertised; it is banned in many hotels for its smell, and that is not a joke. Try it from a stall rather than bringing it to your room.

Sinh to is the fruit smoothie, blended with ice and condensed milk. Nuoc mia is fresh sugarcane juice, pressed in front of you, and is the best thing to drink in the heat.

The coffee-adjacent sweets

Sua chua — yoghurt — is a serious category here, and not a health food. Sua chua nep cam is yoghurt with fermented black sticky rice. Sua chua ca phe is yoghurt with coffee, which sounds wrong and is excellent. Frozen yoghurt stalls sell it as a block to be eaten with a spoon.

Egg coffee, the Hanoi invention, sits somewhere between a drink and a dessert and belongs in both conversations.

Regional specialities

Hue has its own family of che, including one made with candied lotus seeds wrapped in longan, which was court food. Hoi An has banh it la gai, a dark sticky cake wrapped in leaves. The south has the widest range of coconut-based sweets, and the Mekong delta is where the coconut candy workshops are.

Kem

Ice cream, and Vietnam has a long history with it. Trang Tien in Hanoi is the institution, sold from a window to a permanent crowd, in flavours including green bean and coconut sticky rice.

What to expect from the sweetness

Vietnamese sweets are sweet in a different register from European ones — less fat, less flour, more texture from beans, jellies and tapioca, and coconut milk doing the work that cream does elsewhere. There is very little baking in the tradition; almost everything is steamed, boiled or fried.

That means a plate of che is lighter than it looks, and also that someone expecting cake will not find it. The French-derived things — the flan, the baguette, the pastries in the old patisseries of Hanoi and Da Lat — are the exception.

Where to find all this

Che shops are their own category of business and are usually open from the afternoon into the evening. Markets sell cut fruit and sticky rice in the morning. The yoghurt and ice cream places run late.

Almost none of it is expensive, and the whole category is best approached by pointing at something you do not recognise and finding out what it is.
excerpt: Che, sticky rice, fruit and yoghurt coffee. Dessert here is mostly a street snack rather than a course.
author: Editorial

title: Street Food Tours in Hanoi and Saigon: Worth It?
content:
Street food tours are one of the most heavily sold activities in both Vietnamese cities, and the honest answer about whether to take one depends almost entirely on when you take it.

What a tour actually gives you

Three things you cannot easily get on your own, at least not on day one.

Navigation. The good street food is sold by places with no English, no menu, one dish, and a specific hour. A guide takes you to a series of them in an order that makes sense, and you eat things you would have walked past.

Explanation. What is in it, why it is made that way, which region it comes from, how to eat it. That turns a meal into a framework you then use for the rest of the trip.

Confidence. This is the underrated one. Being shown how to read a stall — what to look at, what the queue means, how to order — tends to take the apprehension out of eating this way for the rest of the trip.

So: the first evening

That is the argument for taking one early rather than late. A tour at the end of a trip is a nice meal. A tour at the start is a set of tools you then use on every meal after it.

Walking or on the back of a scooter

Two formats. Walking tours cover a neighbourhood — usually the Old Quarter in Hanoi, District 1 or District 4 in Ho Chi Minh City — and move between stops on foot.

Scooter tours put you on the back of a bike with a driver-guide and cover much more ground, including the districts a walking tour cannot reach. They are the more memorable of the two and they are also a motorbike ride through Vietnamese city traffic, which some people will not want.

As a passenger, you do not need a licence. Riding yourself is a different matter and not what these tours involve.

How much food is involved

More than people expect. A six-stop tour is a full dinner and then some, and the better guides pace it deliberately — a half portion here, a shared plate there. Do not eat beforehand, and say early if you are slowing down; a good guide adjusts rather than marching you through the remaining stops.

Ask how long the tour runs and at what time of day. Evening tours are the common format; morning tours exist and are the better option if you want to see pho and the breakfast culture rather than the evening food.

What separates a good tour

Ask these before booking. How many people are in the group — four to eight is workable, fifteen is a procession that changes how the stalls treat you. How many stops, and is each one a dish or a taste. Is the guide a local resident of that neighbourhood. Are drinks included. Does it finish with a beer somewhere, which the better ones do.

Ask also whether the stops are places the guide eats at or places that have an arrangement with the company. The answer tells you a lot, and a guide who answers it straightforwardly is usually the right guide.

Dietary requirements

Tell them when you book, not on the night. Vegetarian street food tours exist in both cities and are a better option than a standard tour with substitutions, because the stops themselves change.

Hanoi versus Saigon

The two cities give quite different tours. Hanoi's Old Quarter is dense and walkable, the food is northern — bun cha, pho, cha ca, bun rieu — and a walking tour covers a lot in a small area. It usually ends with bia hoi.

Ho Chi Minh City is spread out, which is why the scooter format originated here and works so well. The food is southern and more varied, with more Chinese influence in Cholon and the seafood and snail restaurants in the outer districts.

If you are doing both cities, taking a tour in each is not redundant. The food is genuinely different.

What it costs, and the alternative

A tour costs many times what the food itself does. You are paying for the guide, and on the first night that is good value. For the rest of the trip, the alternative is to use what you learned: find the specialist places, go at the right hour, eat where the queue is.

A cheaper version of the same thing is a food-focused free walking tour, which several student groups run in both cities, where you pay for your own food and tip the guide.

Safety and hygiene on a tour

A guide takes you to places they use, which is a reasonable filter, but it is not a guarantee against an upset stomach and no tour can offer one. The usual precautions apply the same as anywhere: the vaccinations are the part decided before you travel, and carrying rehydration salts is the part that assumes it might happen anyway.

The verdict

Take one, early, in whichever city you reach first. Choose a small group. Ask about the stops. Then spend the rest of the trip eating on your own, which is what the tour is for.
excerpt: Yes, and early in the trip rather than late. What a good one gives you that is hard to get on your own.
author: Editorial

title: Cooking Classes in Vietnam: What to Look For
content:
Cooking classes are offered in every town a visitor passes through, and they range from genuinely instructive half-days to a token chopping session attached to a lunch. The difference is visible in the itinerary before you book.

The market visit is the test

Almost every class advertises a market visit. The question is whether it is forty-five minutes of actually buying the ingredients you will cook, with the teacher explaining what each one is and how to choose it, or a ten-minute walk-through for photographs before the minibus.

The market is where you learn the things that stay with you: what the herbs are called, how to tell good fish sauce, what rice paper thickness is for, why there are four kinds of basil. The cooking itself is mostly following instructions.

Ask how long is spent at the market and whether you buy the ingredients there. A class that cannot answer is telling you the answer.

Group size and stations

The second question. A class where everyone has their own station and cooks every dish is a different thing from a demonstration where the group collectively makes one dish and watches the rest.

Eight to twelve is a workable group with individual stations. Twenty-plus is a demonstration regardless of what it is called. Ask explicitly: do I cook each dish myself, or do we share?

What you will actually cook

The menus you will see advertised tend to draw from the same pool: fresh spring rolls, a salad such as green papaya or banana flower, a main — banh xeo, clay pot fish, or a grilled dish — and sometimes a soup. These are dishes that are quick, forgiving and photograph well. Read the menu before booking rather than assuming it.

Nothing wrong with that, but if you want to learn pho you will need to look specifically, because a proper broth takes longer than a class does. Classes that teach it generally start the stock the day before and show you the finishing.

Where to take one

Hoi An is the most established place for it, with classes on farms outside town, on boats, and in restaurant kitchens. Many include a bicycle ride or a basket-boat trip to the herb village at Tra Que, which is a genuine working market garden rather than a set piece.

Hanoi teaches northern food — bun cha, cha ca, pho — and the classes are more often city-based, built around a market trip to one of the Old Quarter markets.

Hue is the interesting one if you already cook. The court cuisine is more technical, the dishes are smaller and more precise, and a Hue class will teach you things the others do not.

Ho Chi Minh City covers southern cooking and has the widest range of formats, from hotel schools to home kitchens.

Home kitchens

Smaller operations run classes in a family home for a handful of people, and often cook the family's own dishes rather than the standard tourist menu. They are harder to find because they advertise less, and they are worth looking for.

What you should come away with

A good class sends you home with the recipes in writing, in quantities you can actually buy, with notes on substitutions for ingredients you will not find. Ask whether recipes are provided.

It should also teach you the two or three things that are structural rather than dish-specific: how nuoc cham is balanced, how to handle rice paper, how a Vietnamese plate of herbs is put together. Those transfer to anything you cook afterwards.

What it costs relative to other activities

A half-day class is among the more expensive single activities in a Vietnamese town, several times the cost of a street food tour per hour, because it includes ingredients, a teacher and a meal. The home-kitchen operations are usually the cheapest and often the best, and the hotel schools the most expensive.

Practical points

Most classes run a morning or an afternoon and include the meal you cook, which means you do not need to plan lunch or dinner around it. Say in advance if you are vegetarian — most will adapt the menu properly if given notice.

Wear clothes you can cook in and shoes you can walk a market in. Markets are wet underfoot. Book a day or two ahead in Hoi An, where the good classes fill.

With children

Several classes take families and are good at it — the spring-roll rolling and the pancake flipping are the parts children engage with. Check whether knives and hot woks are part of what they will be doing and whether that suits.

Is it worth the half day

If you cook at home, yes, and the Hue or home-kitchen versions especially. If you do not cook, a class is still a good way to spend a morning in a market with someone who can explain it, which is most of the value anyway.

If your time is tight, a street food tour is generally the shorter commitment and gives you more of the eating and less of the technique. They are different activities, and the choice between them is about whether you want to understand the food or to find it. Compare the actual scheduled times before deciding.
excerpt: The market visit is the part that matters, and it is the part to ask about. How to choose one worth the half day.
author: Editorial

title: What to Bring Home from a Vietnamese Kitchen
content:
Vietnam is a good country to shop in for a kitchen, because the things worth buying are cheap, light and hard to get at home. Here is what actually earns its space, and what to know about getting it back.

Fish sauce

The one to buy properly. Good nuoc mam is made from anchovies and salt and nothing else, fermented in wooden vats for a year or more. Phu Quoc has a protected designation for it and the island's warehouses sell it directly; Cat Hai in the north is the other named producer.

Look at the label for the degree of protein, usually given as a number of degrees N. Higher is stronger and more expensive, and the best is drunk-tasted the way olive oil is. Buy glass if you can and bubble-wrap it; a bottle that breaks in a suitcase is a memorable problem.

Coffee and a phin

Vietnamese coffee is cheap and good, and the small metal phin filter costs almost nothing and is the right way to brew it. Buy both together.

Check whether the coffee is pure or roasted with butter or other additives — much mass-market Vietnamese coffee is, which gives the characteristic flavour but behaves differently in a home machine. Specialty roasters in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Lat sell single-origin Vietnamese arabica if that is what you want.

Pepper

Vietnam is one of the world's largest pepper producers and the stuff sold in the markets is fresher than most of what reaches a Western supermarket. Phu Quoc pepper has a reputation of its own. Buy whole peppercorns, not ground.

Dried and shelf-stable things

Rice paper for fresh rolls, which is light, flat and almost indestructible in a bag.

Dried rice noodles in the widths you cannot buy at home — the flat pho noodles and the thin bun vermicelli.

Shrimp paste and fermented bean curd if you are serious; both are pungent and need sealing well.

Dried shiitake, wood ear and lily buds, which are light and keep for years.

Cinnamon and star anise, both grown in Vietnam, for pho broth.

Sauces beyond fish sauce

Hoisin and chilli sauce are made everywhere and the Vietnamese versions differ from what is sold abroad. Tuong ot, the Vietnamese chilli sauce, is thinner and sharper than the better-known Thai kind. Mam nem, fermented anchovy sauce, and mam ruoc, shrimp paste, are the strong ones and need serious sealing.

Sate, the chilli-and-lemongrass oil served with bun bo Hue, is underrated as a thing to bring back and transforms a bowl of noodles at home.

Tea

Vietnamese green tea, lotus tea and the artichoke tea from Da Lat all travel well. Lotus tea in particular is specific to here and makes a good present. The tea shops in the markets will vacuum-seal it.

Kitchen equipment

A claypot, a rice paper mould, a wooden mortar — all cheap, all heavy. The phin is the one piece of equipment that is genuinely worth the weight.

Lacquerware, textiles and the non-edible

Outside the kitchen cupboard, the things that travel well are lacquerware bowls and trays, which are light and genuinely made here; embroidered and block-printed textiles; and the conical hat, which is impossible to pack and which people buy anyway.

Ceramics from Bat Trang, the pottery village outside Hanoi, are the other category — heavy, breakable, and worth it if you are checking a bag and pack carefully.

Where to buy

Supermarkets are the easiest and the prices are fixed: the large Vietnamese chains stock everything above, often better packaged for travel than the markets. Markets are cheaper and more interesting but you are buying loose and bargaining.

Airport shops sell most of this at a premium, which is worth knowing as a fallback rather than a plan. Buy the liquids in town and the last-minute things at the airport.

What not to bother with

Fresh herbs, which will not survive and will not clear customs. Fresh lemongrass and galangal, for the same reason — the frozen versions at an Asian supermarket at home are better than what arrives after a long flight. Anything requiring refrigeration. And the branded instant noodles, which are sold at home for roughly the same price.

Getting it home

The rules that will actually catch you are your own country's, on arrival home. Agricultural and customs restrictions on food are stricter than most people expect. Processed, commercially packaged, shelf-stable goods are generally the straightforward category; fresh produce, meat and some seeds are generally not.

Check your own border agency's current list rather than assuming, and declare food when the form asks. An undeclared prohibited item is the expensive outcome; a declared one is a conversation.

Liquids and flights

Fish sauce, chilli sauce and any liquid go in checked baggage, double-bagged. The smell survives a loose cap, and so does the stain.
excerpt: What is worth the suitcase space, where to buy it, and what to check before you pack it.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Itinerary: 10 Days
content:
Ten days on the ground is the first length at which all three of Vietnam's regions fit without the trip turning into a sequence of airports. A week forces you to pick two. Fourteen days gives you slack. Ten sits between them, and the plan has to be tighter than the one for two weeks because there is no room to absorb a mistake.

The frame

Fly into Hanoi, out of Ho Chi Minh City, open-jaw. Two internal flights: Hanoi to Da Nang, and Da Nang to Ho Chi Minh City. The ten days below are days in Vietnam, counted from the day you land — day one is the arrival day, and most of it is gone. The flights themselves are on top of that: budget a day in each direction for the crossing when you work out your leave.

There is no nonstop from the United States to Hanoi, so a north-first trip means a connection. If you are flying the nonstop from San Francisco to Ho Chi Minh City, run everything below in reverse.

Days 1 to 3 — Hanoi

Arrive, lose the afternoon, and give the city two full days. Hoan Kiem and the Old Quarter on foot, the Temple of Literature, the Ho Chi Minh complex in a morning, and one museum. Bun cha for lunch, pho for breakfast.

Two days is enough for Hanoi on a ten-day trip, and the temptation to make it three is what costs you the centre later.

Days 4 to 5 — the northern excursion

One, not two. The realistic options are an overnight cruise on Ha Long or Lan Ha bay, or two days in Ninh Binh, which is about two hours from Hanoi and gives you the same karst landscape on rivers.

Sapa is the one to leave out at this length. It is five to six hours each way, which is most of two days of the ten spent on the road, and the trek itself wants more time than what remains.

If the bay is the image you came for, take the cruise. If you would rather walk and cycle than sit on a boat, take Ninh Binh — it costs less travel and you can do it as a long day trip or an overnight.

Days 6 to 8 — the centre

Fly Hanoi to Da Nang early on day six and transfer to Hoi An, about forty-five minutes. That gives you an afternoon, two full days and a morning in the centre.

Spend them on the Ancient Town at its quiet hours, a day for My Son or the Marble Mountains, and a beach afternoon at An Bang. If you want clothes made, order on the first morning — two fittings need the time.

Hue can be added as a day trip, but Hoi An has no station — it means a car to Da Nang, the train north from there, and the same in reverse at the end of the day. It is a long day and the Imperial City deserves better. On ten days, either give Hue a night of its own and take a day from somewhere, or leave it.

Days 9 to 10 — the south

Fly Da Nang to Ho Chi Minh City on the morning of day nine. Two days there covers the War Remnants Museum and Reunification Palace, Ben Thanh and the markets, a street food evening, and the Cu Chi tunnels if the war sites are a priority.

Leave the Mekong Delta out. The packaged day trip from the city is widely reported as the weakest day on a Vietnam itinerary, and the version worth doing needs an overnight in Can Tho for the dawn floating market. Neither fits in ten days without taking the centre apart.

The alternative: centre and south, slower

If three regions in ten days sounds like too much movement, the other shape is two regions done properly. Four nights in Hoi An with Hue as an overnight, then four in Ho Chi Minh City with an overnight in Can Tho for the floating market, and one internal flight instead of two.

That version loses Hanoi and the bay, which for most first visits is a large thing to lose. It is the better plan if you are returning to Vietnam, or if the pace matters more than the coverage.

What the plan is actually trading

Three things get cut to make ten days work: Sapa, Hue as a proper stop, and the Mekong. Each of those is a real destination and each would be in a two-week version. If one of them is the reason you are going to Vietnam, the plan changes shape around it rather than adding to it.

The other honest limitation is the weather. Vietnam's regions have different wet seasons, and ten days moving through all three means at least one region is likely to be in its difficult months whatever you do.

Booking order

International tickets first, because they set the direction and everything else follows. Then the two internal flights, which are cheap and fill at the useful hours. Then accommodation. Then the cruise or Ninh Binh. Tours and classes can wait until you are in the country.

Which region to build the trip around when the month you can travel does not suit it is a question the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: Ten days is the length where three regions become possible without becoming a transit log. Here is the shape that works.
author: Editorial

title: A First Vietnam Itinerary: How to Decide the Shape
content:
Most Vietnam itineraries go wrong before any days are assigned, because the shape of the trip was decided by accident. Four questions settle it, and they have to be answered in order, because each one closes off options for the next.

One: how many days on the ground

Not how many days of leave. Vietnam is a long flight from the United States and the crossing eats a calendar day each way, with the arrival day largely written off. Ten days of leave is seven or eight days of Vietnam.

Count the real number first, because every subsequent decision scales off it. Seven days on the ground is two regions. Ten is three, tightly. Fourteen is three with slack. Three weeks is three regions plus the things everybody cuts.

Two: which regions

Vietnam divides into north, centre and south, each about an hour's flight from the next. The north is Hanoi, Ha Long, Ninh Binh and Sapa. The centre is Hue, Da Nang and Hoi An. The south is Ho Chi Minh City, the Mekong Delta and the islands.

On a short trip, pick adjacent regions. North plus centre, or centre plus south. The north-plus-south combination skips the middle, which is where Hoi An and Hue are, and is the one people most often regret.

The thing that actually decides it

Whichever region holds the thing you most want to see. If that is Ha Long Bay, you are starting north. If it is Hoi An, you are building around the centre. Pick that anchor first and let the adjacent region be the second one.

Three: which month

Vietnam does not have one dry season. The north is coldest and greyest from roughly December to February and hottest and wettest in summer. The central coast has a storm season from September to November. The south is wet from May to October, in the afternoon-downpour way rather than the all-day way.

There is no month that is perfect everywhere, which means the month you can travel partly decides which regions are worth the days. Travelling in October with the centre as your anchor is a plan with a problem in it.

Four: which direction

North to south is the more common shape and suits most itineraries: the harder city first, the weather-sensitive north early, and a departure from the city with the widest choice of onward flights.

South to north is the right answer if the nonstop from San Francisco to Ho Chi Minh City is what makes the trip work, or if the season favours finishing in the north. Open-jaw tickets into one city and out of the other are widely available, so there is rarely a reason to backtrack.

This decision is effectively locked when you buy the international tickets, which is usually before anything else is planned. That is why it belongs in the first four questions rather than the day-by-day.

What the month does to the answer

Worked examples. December: the north is cold and often grey, the centre is coming out of its storm season, the south is dry. A southern-weighted trip makes sense. June: the north is hot and wet in the afternoons, the centre is dry, the south is in its wet season. A centre-weighted trip makes sense. March and April are the closest the country comes to working everywhere at once, which is also why they are busy.

Then, and only then, the days

With those four answered, the day plan writes itself from a small number of rules. Two nights in any city worth stopping in, unless you are deliberately buying a single sight with a one-night stop. One overnight excursion per region at most. A transfer day is a half day gone, not a free one. And the internal flights are short and cheap, so use them rather than overland for the long legs.

The things people underestimate

How long Hanoi to Hoi An takes door to door, which is a flight plus two transfers rather than an hour. How much of a cruise day is the coach. How much time the Mekong needs to be worth doing. And how tired the first forty-eight hours are.

What to book and when

International flights first — they lock the direction. Internal flights next: they are short and inexpensive and the useful departure times go first. Then accommodation in the places you have fixed. Then one or two anchor experiences, such as a bay cruise, that need a date.

Everything else — day tours, cooking classes, drivers, food tours — can be arranged in the country a day or two ahead, usually more cheaply and with better information about the weather.

A sanity check before booking

Write the plan out and count the half-days lost to movement. If more than a quarter of the trip is transfers, remove a region rather than compressing the stays. A shorter list done properly is the thing people remember; a longer list done at speed is the thing they describe as exhausting.

And leave one unplanned day in anything longer than a week. It will be used, either by weather or by a place that turned out to be better than expected.
excerpt: Before the day-by-day, four decisions set everything else. Make them in this order.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam with Children: Planning the Trip
content:
Vietnam works well with children. The food is mild by default and endlessly snackable, Vietnamese attitudes to children travelling are warm to the point of enthusiastic, and the costs are low enough that a family can afford space and comfort that would be out of reach elsewhere. There are three real constraints, and the plan is built around them.

Constraint one: the traffic

Road traffic is the hazard the State Department emphasises most for Vietnam, and city streets are the part of the trip that demands most attention with small children. Crossing a busy road in Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City with a child is a different exercise from doing it alone.

What this means practically: hold hands and cross as a unit at a steady pace; use Grab rather than walking long distances in the cities; and choose accommodation on a quieter street rather than the busiest one.

Car seats are not standard in Vietnamese taxis or ride-hailing cars. Families travelling with small children either bring a portable seat or accept the arrangement as it is, and that is a decision worth making before you arrive rather than at the airport.

Constraint two: the distances

Vietnam is long, and the trip shape that works for adults — three regions in ten days — is punishing with children. Fewer places and longer stays is the single most useful adjustment.

A family week is best as one region. A family fortnight stretches to two comfortably, or three if one of them is a beach stay you barely move within. Use the internal flights rather than overnight buses or long drives.

Constraint three: the heat

Most of Vietnam is hot and humid for most of the year, and children tolerate it less well than adults. Build the day around it: out early, back for the middle of the day, out again in the late afternoon. Accommodation with a pool stops being a luxury and becomes the thing that makes the afternoon work.

What children actually enjoy here

Water, mostly. The bay cruises, the kayaking, the beaches at An Bang, Da Nang and Phu Quoc, and the delta boats. Ba Na Hills, with the cable car and the games area, is the most deliberately child-oriented day out in the country. The water puppet theatre in Hanoi is short and genuinely engaging.

Also: lantern-making and cooking classes in Hoi An, cycling through the rice paddies at Tra Que, the Marble Mountains caves, and the sheer novelty of the street life.

What to go lightly on

The war sites. The War Remnants Museum in Ho Chi Minh City presents the conflict unsparingly, and parents of younger children often choose Reunification Palace instead. Cu Chi involves confined tunnels and a firing range whose noise carries across the site. These are decisions to make deliberately rather than on arrival.

Ages and what changes

With a baby or toddler, the heat and the pavements are the constraints: Vietnamese city pavements are frequently occupied by parked motorbikes and stalls, and a pushchair is often more trouble than a carrier. With primary-age children, the water activities and the sheer sensory volume of the place do most of the work. Teenagers do well here, particularly with the food, the markets and the motorbike-passenger side of it.

Ages also change the war sites, the length of the days and how much heritage anyone will tolerate before lunch.

A shape that works for two weeks

Four nights in Hanoi including one on a bay cruise; a flight to Da Nang and six nights in Hoi An, using the beach from there rather than moving again; a flight south and four nights in Ho Chi Minh City, or in Phu Quoc if the trip should end on sand. That is fourteen nights, three regions, and two internal flights.

The point of that shape is that only two of the fourteen nights involve changing where your bags are, and the longest stay has a pool.

Practical points

Nappies, formula and familiar medicines are available in the cities and harder to find in small towns; buy in Hanoi, Da Nang or Ho Chi Minh City. Pharmacies are everywhere and well stocked.

Apartments and family rooms are cheap by American standards and far more useful than two hotel rooms. Many hotels will add a bed for very little.

Food is easy: rice, noodles, grilled meat, fresh spring rolls and fruit cover most children, and chilli is almost always served on the side rather than cooked in.

Getting around with children

Grab is the default and the fares are low enough that taking cars everywhere in the cities is affordable. For longer legs use the internal flights, which are short. The overnight train is a genuine option with older children and an adventure in its own right; the sleeper bus is not, with any age.

Health before you go

Talk to a travel clinic about the routine and recommended vaccinations well in advance, since some need more than one dose. Carry oral rehydration salts, which are the single most useful thing in the bag with children in a hot country.
excerpt: A good country for family travel, with three genuine constraints. How to build around them.
author: Editorial

title: Temples and Pagodas in Vietnam: What You Are Looking At
content:
Vietnam's religious buildings come from several different traditions, and a visitor who treats them all as "temples" misses most of what is interesting. Here is what the main kinds are, how to recognise them, and how to behave inside.

Chua — the Buddhist pagoda

The most common. A chua is a Buddhist place of worship, usually a complex of halls around courtyards rather than a single building, with a main hall holding Buddha statues, incense burners, and often a bell and a drum.

Vietnamese Buddhism is predominantly Mahayana in the north and centre, which is why you will see Quan Am — the bodhisattva of compassion, the Vietnamese form of Guanyin — very frequently, often as a white standing figure outside. In parts of the south and the Mekong, Theravada Buddhism of the Khmer tradition appears instead, and those temples look quite different: taller, more ornate, closer to Cambodian architecture.

Den — the temple

A den honours a person or a spirit rather than the Buddha: a national hero, a historical general, a mother goddess. Den Ngoc Son on Hoan Kiem lake in Hanoi is one; the Tran Hung Dao temples across the north are others. They often look similar to a chua from outside and the difference is who is on the altar.

Van Mieu — the Confucian temple of literature

Dedicated to Confucius and to scholarship rather than to a deity. The one in Hanoi was Vietnam's first university and has stone stelae on turtles' backs recording the names of doctoral graduates from the fifteenth century on. Several provincial cities have smaller versions.

Dinh — the communal house

The village hall and the shrine of the village's tutelary spirit, usually the oldest and most elaborately carved wooden building in an old village. These are not tourist sites and are often closed, but the woodwork inside the ones that open is some of the best in the country.

Cham towers

Brick towers from the Cham civilisation, Hindu rather than Buddhist, found along the central and southern coast. My Son near Hoi An is the largest group; Po Nagar in Nha Trang and the towers around Phan Rang are others. The architecture reads closer to Indian and Khmer temple building than to anything else in Vietnam.

Cao Dai temples

Cao Dai is a Vietnamese religion founded in the 1920s, syncretic and visually unmistakable: bright colours, a divine eye above the altar, and a congregation in white. The Great Temple at Tay Ninh, north-west of Ho Chi Minh City, is the centre and is the usual place visitors see one. Services run at set times and visitors are welcome at the back.

Churches

Vietnam has a substantial Catholic population and the French-era churches are a visible part of the urban landscape — St Joseph's in Hanoi, the Notre-Dame basilica in Ho Chi Minh City, the pink church in Da Lat, and the stone cathedral at Phat Diem, which was built in Vietnamese temple style.

What is usually inside a chua

The layout repeats enough to be worth learning. A triple gate or an entrance arch; a courtyard, often with a bodhisattva figure and a pond; the main hall with tiered altars, the largest Buddha figures at the back and offerings of fruit and flowers in front; a bell and a drum, either in the hall or in their own small towers; and behind or beside it, an ancestral hall with photographs of the dead and the monks of the pagoda.

Incense burners stand outside the hall doors. The smoke and the stacked coils hanging from the ceiling in busier pagodas are the first thing you will notice.

How to behave

Cover shoulders and knees. Remove shoes where you see others doing so, which is usually at the threshold of an inner hall rather than the courtyard. Step over the raised threshold rather than on it.

Do not point your feet at an altar or a statue, which means watching how you sit. Walk around a statue rather than in front of someone praying. Ask before photographing people at worship, and look for signs prohibiting photography inside halls.

If you want to offer incense, buy it at the gate, light it, hold it at forehead height with both hands, bow, and place it in the burner. It is a normal thing for a visitor to do and it is not expected of you; at a few sites photography or lay offerings are restricted, so look for signs first.

The ones worth going out of your way for

The Perfume Pagoda south of Hanoi, which is a boat trip and a climb. Bai Dinh and the Trang An complex at Ninh Binh, vast and modern. Thien Mu above the Perfume River at Hue. The Marble Mountains caves near Da Nang, where the shrines are inside the rock. Linh Ung on the Son Tra peninsula with its tall Lady Buddha. And the Cao Dai Great Temple at Tay Ninh, which is unlike anything else in the country.

Most of these are covered in their own right elsewhere on this site; what they have in common is that the setting is as much the point as the building.

Donations

Boxes are provided and contributions are voluntary. At some popular sites you will be offered incense or a blessing by someone who then expects payment; that is a transaction rather than a temple custom, and declining is fine.
excerpt: Buddhist, Taoist, Confucian, Cham and Cao Dai, often in the same town. A short guide to telling them apart.
author: Editorial

title: War History Sites in Vietnam: A Guide for American Visitors
content:
For a lot of American visitors the war is part of why they are going, and Vietnam has preserved a great deal of it. The sites are spread the length of the country, they vary enormously in what they offer, and they are presented from a Vietnamese perspective — which is the point of visiting them rather than a caveat.

The south: Ho Chi Minh City and Cu Chi

The War Remnants Museum is the main one. It presents the conflict unsparingly, with heavy emphasis on civilian casualties, chemical defoliants and their consequences. Aircraft and armour in the courtyard, photojournalism upstairs. It is a difficult couple of hours and it is the single most visited war site in the country.

Reunification Palace, a short ride away, is preserved roughly as it was in April 1975 — the cabinet room, the president's quarters, the basement command bunker. It completes the picture the museum starts: the museum shows the war as it was experienced, the palace shows the government conducting it and the rooms where that ended.

Cu Chi is an hour and a half to two hours out of the city, a tunnel system with sections widened for visitors, a firing range whose noise carries, and displays of the tunnels' construction. Two sites operate; Ben Duoc is the quieter of them and is worth asking for.

The centre: the DMZ out of Hue

The old demilitarised zone along the seventeenth parallel is about two hours north of Hue and is a long day out. The circuit takes in the Ben Hai river and the old border, the Khe Sanh combat base, and the Vinh Moc tunnels.

Vinh Moc is the one most people remember. A village lived underground there through years of bombardment, and the tunnels were dug for civilians to live in rather than for fighters to move through. They are reported to be close to their original dimensions rather than widened for visitors.

Khe Sanh divides opinion — a museum, a stretch of airstrip, equipment in the open, and the hills the 1968 siege was fought over. If it is specifically why you are going, say so when booking, because some itineraries allow very little time there.

The north: Hanoi

Hoa Lo Prison, the "Hanoi Hilton", is now a museum. Most of it covers the French colonial period and Vietnamese political prisoners; a smaller section covers the American pilots held there and is presented in terms American visitors generally find striking for its framing rather than its content.

The B-52 wreckage in Huu Tiep lake, in a residential street in the Ngoc Ha district, is a fragment of a bomber left where it came down in December 1972. Allow ten minutes for it. It is the most unexpected of these sites.

The Vietnam Military History Museum has moved to a large new building on the western edge of the city with a substantial outdoor collection of aircraft and armour.

What is not a war site, and still is

Some of the most affecting things are not presented as sites at all. The Long Bien bridge in Hanoi, bombed repeatedly and still carrying trains and bicycles. The war cemeteries along Route 9 and at Truong Son, which are enormous and almost entirely visited by Vietnamese families. The ordinary presence of people with disabilities attributed to defoliant exposure, which the War Remnants Museum addresses directly and which is visible outside it.

None of them is a ticketed attraction, and between them they change the register of the trip considerably.

What to expect from the framing

These are Vietnamese national sites, and the war is called the American War. The presentation is unambiguous and in places polemical, particularly at the War Remnants Museum. Going in expecting a balanced international account is the wrong expectation; going in to see how the war is remembered here is the right one.

That is a different thing from the reception you get. Visitors commonly report being treated with ordinary warmth at all of these places, by staff and by other visitors.

A note on the ground itself

Unexploded ordnance remains a real hazard in parts of central Vietnam, concentrated at construction sites and away from populated areas; the landmine risk is low in urban and populated areas, including tourist destinations. Stay on marked paths at the DMZ sites and do not pick anything up.

Going with a guide

At the DMZ sites a guide is close to essential, because most of what you are looking at is terrain and the interest is in what happened on it. At the museums it matters less — the exhibits carry their own captions, in English.

Veterans and families of veterans travelling to specific locations are generally better served by a private guide and driver than by a group tour, and there are operators who specialise in it. Be clear about the places you want when you book; a standard circuit will not go to them.

How to sequence them

If you are doing the whole country, you will meet these in order: Hanoi's sites early, the DMZ from Hue in the middle, the museum and Cu Chi at the end. That is a reasonable progression, and it means the heaviest material comes last rather than on your second day.

Doing the War Remnants Museum and Cu Chi on the same day is possible and compresses a great deal into one day with a long drive in the middle. Splitting them gives each room.
excerpt: Where the war is on the ground rather than in a museum, how the sites are framed, and what to expect as an American.
author: Editorial

title: Vietnam Itinerary: 3 Weeks
content:
Twenty-one days on the ground is the length at which Vietnam stops being a choice between regions and becomes a question of what to add. The fourteen-day shape already covers the country north to south; three weeks buys you the places that get cut from it, plus slack for weather.

The fourteen-day spine

Start from the standard two-week route, because three weeks is that plus additions rather than a different plan. Hanoi; a northern excursion; the centre around Hue and Hoi An; Ho Chi Minh City. Open-jaw into Hanoi and out of Ho Chi Minh City, with two internal flights and the Hue to Da Nang leg by train.

What three weeks changes is that you no longer have to choose between the northern options, and the south becomes a region rather than a two-day stop.

What to add, in order of value

Both northern excursions rather than one. On two weeks, Ninh Binh and Sapa are a fork. On three, take both — Ninh Binh and Sapa are each a trip out from Hanoi by road, with the bay cruise as a third. That is the biggest single gain and it is why the north grows most.

The Mekong properly. A night in Can Tho so you are on the water at dawn for the floating market, which is the version that works, rather than the day circuit out of Ho Chi Minh City.

Hue as its own stop. Two nights, the Imperial City and two tombs, instead of a rushed day trip.

And then one of these

Phu Quoc or Con Dao for a beach ending; Da Lat and the Central Highlands for coffee country and a cooler climate; Ha Giang for the far northern loop, which is the most demanding addition. Pick one, not two — and note that each of these is a substitution rather than an extra. A beach ending replaces the delta days; Ha Giang replaces Sapa and wants more than Sapa's three; Da Lat comes out of the centre or the south. Con Dao is the most expensive in days, because its flights and its minimum stay take four or five.

A shape that works

Days 1 to 4, Hanoi. Days 5 to 6, Ninh Binh. Days 7 to 8, Ha Long or Lan Ha. Days 9 to 11, Sapa, including the road travel each way. Day 12, fly Hanoi to Hue and take the afternoon there. Day 13, Hue. Day 14, train to Da Nang and transfer to Hoi An. Days 15 to 17, Hoi An and the centre. Day 18, fly Da Nang to Ho Chi Minh City and take the afternoon in the city. Day 19, the city. Day 20, down to Can Tho for the night. Day 21, Cai Rang at dawn, back up to Ho Chi Minh City, and out.

That is twenty-one days and the same two internal flights as the fourteen-day shape — Sapa and Ninh Binh are reached by road from Hanoi, and the delta by road from Ho Chi Minh City. Day 21 is the tight one, so check the departure time before committing to the dawn market.

The south at three weeks

On two weeks the south is Ho Chi Minh City and little else. On three it becomes a region: two days in the city for the museums and the markets, two nights in the delta at Can Tho, and either a beach ending or the long way out through Chau Doc if you are continuing to Cambodia.

That last option is worth knowing about. The boat up the Mekong from Chau Doc to Phnom Penh turns the end of a Vietnam trip into the start of another one, and at three weeks there is room for it.

The things three weeks does not fix

The weather, mostly. Vietnam's regions have different wet seasons and three weeks moving through all of them means at least one is likely to be in its difficult months. Three weeks gives you slack to reschedule a cruise or a trek, which two weeks does not, but it does not give you a dry country.

It also does not make the long legs shorter. Sapa is five to six hours from Hanoi each way whatever the length of the trip, and that is a real cost against two days in Ninh Binh.

Pace

The commonest mistake at this length is filling the extra week with more places rather than more time in the same ones. Three weeks at a two-week pace with an extra region is more tiring than two weeks, not less.

Build in at least two unplanned days. On a trip this long they will be used — by weather, by something you did not know existed, or by needing to do nothing for a day.

What three weeks is actually worth

The honest summary: the extra week buys you the north twice over and the delta properly. It does not come with spare days built in — the route above has none. If you want weather contingency, you have to leave a day unbooked in Hanoi and another in Hoi An, which are the two places where an empty day is no hardship. It does not buy you a fourth region or a different country.

If the additions you want are Ha Giang and the Central Highlands rather than Sapa and the delta, that is a different three weeks and a more demanding one, weighted away from the standard route.

Booking order

International tickets first; they set the direction. Then the two internal flights, which are inexpensive and fill at the useful hours. Then the accommodation in the fixed stops, then the cruise, then the Sapa trek. Everything else can be arranged a day or two ahead in the country.

How a trip this length should be sequenced against the seasons in three different regions is a question the complete Vietnam decision manual works through.
excerpt: Three weeks is where the things a fortnight cuts come back in. What to add, and in what order.
author: Editorial

title: Mekong Delta Homestays: Which Province, and Why It Matters
content:
The Mekong Delta homestay is sold as an upgrade on the day trip, and it is not — it is a different thing entirely. The day trip shows you a circuit of stops. A homestay puts you in one place for a night and the value is in what that place is. Which means the province matters more than the operator.

What a homestay actually is here

Typically a family house or a small guesthouse on a canal or an orchard, with a few rooms, mosquito nets, a shared dinner cooked by the household, and a morning on the water. Some are genuinely a family home with guests; others are purpose-built guesthouses using the word. Both can be good; they are not the same experience.

What you are buying is the slow part of the delta — the hours when the coaches have gone, the canals at dusk and before dawn, and a household's normal evening.

The provinces, and what each gives you

Ben Tre is the closest to Ho Chi Minh City and the coconut province. Narrow palm canals, coconut-candy workshops, and the easiest access of the four. It is also the most visited of the near provinces, so the homestays sit alongside the day-trip circuit rather than away from it.

Vinh Long is further in, on the island between the river's two main branches, with orchards and brick kilns and the Cai Be floating market nearby. Quieter than Ben Tre, and the homestays feel more rural.

Can Tho is the delta's city and the base for Cai Rang, the big dawn wholesale market. Homestays here are on the surrounding canals rather than in the city, and the reason to be here is the market.

An Giang, out towards Chau Doc and the Cambodian border, is the furthest and the least visited, with the flooded Tra Su forest, Cham and Khmer communities, and Sam Mountain.

How to choose between them

By what you want the morning to be. If it is the floating market, you need Can Tho and you need to be on the water before dawn. If it is canals, orchards and a quiet night, Vinh Long gives you more of that for less travel. If it is the shortest trip from Ho Chi Minh City, Ben Tre. If you are crossing to Cambodia afterwards, An Giang puts you at the border.

The common mistake is booking a homestay for the idea of it without checking which province it is in, and then discovering that the dawn market you pictured is in a different province entirely.

Questions to ask before booking

Which province and how far from the nearest town. Is it a family home or a guesthouse. How many rooms. Is dinner with the family or served separately. What the morning activity is and what time it starts. Whether transport from Ho Chi Minh City is included or arranged separately.

The answer about the morning start time is the one that matters most, because the delta's best hours are early and an operator who sets off at nine has sold you a different day.

What an evening and a morning look like

Arrive in the afternoon, usually by road from Ho Chi Minh City or from a neighbouring delta town. A boat or a bicycle before dark through the orchards and along the canals. Dinner with the household, which is where most of the value is and which tends to involve more food than anyone expects. An early night, because the morning starts early.

Then the water before or around dawn: the floating market if you are near Can Tho, otherwise the canals when the fishing boats are out and the light is low. Back for breakfast, and generally away by late morning.

Getting there independently

Buses run frequently from Ho Chi Minh City's western bus station to all the delta towns, and private cars are not expensive split between a few people. Most homestays will arrange a pickup from the nearest bus station if you ask.

Booking directly rather than through a packaged tour is usually cheaper and gives you the morning at your hour rather than the operator's.

Practical points

Bring mosquito repellent; the delta has more mosquitoes than anywhere else you will go in Vietnam, and nets are standard for a reason. Bathrooms are usually shared and simple. Cash, because card payment is rare outside the towns. And a torch, because the paths between buildings are not lit.

If you have a dietary requirement, say so when you book rather than at dinner — the meal is cooked for the household and the guests together.

The decision underneath this

Here is the part that is not really about homestays. If your days are already allocated and what remains is a fixed block before the flight out, then the delta, Phu Quoc, Con Dao and a slower few days in Ho Chi Minh City are competing for the same block — and they do not cost the same. A delta night out of Ho Chi Minh City is two days. Phu Quoc is a flight each way and wants three or four. Con Dao is a limited flight schedule and a three-or-four-night minimum, so four or five days. Extra days in the city cost only themselves.

So the choice is not simply which ending appeals. It is which ending the remaining block can actually absorb, given where you fly out of and what the month is doing to each of them. That kind of ordering problem is what the complete Vietnam decision manual is built around.
excerpt: A homestay is not a longer tour. It is a different product, and the province you pick decides what you get.
author: Editorial

title: Con Dao Islands Guide
content:
Con Dao is a group of islands about 230 kilometres off the southern coast, reached by air or a long ferry. It has empty beaches, a national park covering most of the land and the surrounding sea, and a prison complex that is one of the most significant historical sites in the country. Very few foreign visitors get there, which is most of its appeal.

The two reasons to go

The first is that it is quiet in a way no other Vietnamese beach destination is. The main island has one small town, a handful of hotels and resorts, and long stretches of coast with nobody on them. There is no development at Phu Quoc's scale and no sign of it arriving at that pace.

The second is the history, and it is heavy. The French built a prison on Con Son in the nineteenth century and it was used through the colonial period and the war that followed, including the cells known as the tiger cages. The site is preserved and open, and Hang Duong cemetery holds thousands of graves, including that of Vo Thi Sau, a young resistance fighter executed here and now venerated — Vietnamese visitors come overnight to her grave in large numbers.

How the two sit together

Awkwardly, and that is honest. Con Dao is simultaneously a beach holiday and a place of national mourning, and most Vietnamese visitors are there for the second. Visitors who treat it only as an island resort miss what the place is, and the prison is not an optional half hour.

The beaches and the water

Dam Trau, near the airport, is the best known and the one with a beach bar or two. An Hai and Lo Voi are walkable from the town. The quieter ones need a motorbike or a boat.

The sea around the islands is a marine protected area with better coral and visibility than most of the Vietnamese coast, and diving and snorkelling trips run from the town. Sea turtles nest on several of the outer islands between roughly June and September, and the national park runs supervised visits in season.

The national park

Most of Con Son and the smaller islands are protected. There are marked walking trails through the forest, including one to Dam Trau and another up to a viewpoint over the bay, and the park office in town arranges permits and guides for the longer ones and for the outer islands.

The forest holds the Con Dao black squirrel and the long-tailed macaque, and the birdlife is good. Dugong are present in the seagrass beds and are rarely seen.

The prison, in more detail

Several sites make up the complex and the usual circuit takes a morning. Phu Hai, the largest of the camps, with its communal cells. The tiger cages, small open-topped cells built under the French and used afterwards, which became internationally known in 1970. Phu Binh camp, built later. And the museum, which sets out the chronology.

Hang Duong cemetery is a short distance away and is a working place of commemoration rather than a monument. Vietnamese visitors come at night to Vo Thi Sau's grave; if you are there in the evening, stand back and watch rather than walking through it.

Getting there

Flights run from Ho Chi Minh City and from Can Tho to the island's small airport, and the schedule is limited — book early, and build in the possibility of weather cancelling a flight. A high-speed ferry runs from Vung Tau and from Soc Trang; it takes several hours and does not sail in rough conditions.

Neither route is a casual day trip. Con Dao is a three- or four-night destination at minimum, and the transport is the reason.

Getting around

The main island has one road around the inhabited part and very little traffic. Hotels rent bicycles and electric scooters.
